Sports.title: Norris snatches pole position off Hamilton, Antonelli under investigation | 2026 Hungarian GP qualifying report
Sports.content:
Lando Norris claimed his first pole position as reigning world champion with a superb final lap in qualifying at the Hungaroring.

The McLaren driver was one of few people to improve on their final runs in Q3. Lewis Hamilton held provisional pole position after the first runs but failed to find any further time, allowing Norris to pip him by just 0.012 seconds.

Hamilton therefore fell to second on the grid ahead of Charles Leclerc. Andrea Kimi Antonelli had to settle for fourth place despite beginning his final lap well – he encountered yellow flags at the final corner.

The yellow flags were caused by Max Verstappen, who had his third significant spin in the last four weekends. As in Austria, it occured late in qualifying, the Red Bull driver spinning at the final corner.

Verstappen’s spin also obliged George Russell to slow down. The Mercedes driver then came to a stop at turn one immediately after finishing his final lap. Verstappen and Russell will line up immediately behind Oscar Piastri. The McLaren driver and Hamilton are under investigation for a potential impeding incident.

Isack Hadjar rebounded from a spin in Q2 to claim eighth on the grid ahead of Arvid Lindblad and Nico Hulkenberg. Antonelli also had a drama in Q2 as his first flying lap was deleted as he cut the inside of turn seven, and the decision came so late he had already committed to starting his final run on a used set of tyres. Nonetheless, he pulled out a quick enough time on old rubber to reach the top 10.

However as the session came to an end race control announced Antonelli was under investigation for a potential yellow flag infringement.

Aston Martin’s upgraded car proved quick enough for the team to earn their first fully-merited participation in the second round of qualifying this year (Fernando Alonso have reached SQ2 in Montreal, but not participated in it, after crashing). He did his final run in Q2 early, however, and ended up 16th.

Liam Lawson failed to join his team mate in the final 10, saying the Racing Bulls was difficulty to drive. He took 11th ahead of the Alpines. Gabriel Bortoleto, 14th, lost his first attempt to a track limits infringement like Antonelli.

Alonso reached Q2 at the expense of Oliver Bearman, who had been less happy with the balance of the Haas than his team mate after sitting out first practice. The dejected Williams pair also fell at the first hurdle.

Lance Stroll, whose Friday was badly disrupted by a suspension failure, ended up half a second behind Alonso in 20th place. The Cadillac drivers occupied the back row.

Sports.title: Norris heads Hamilton in final practice at the Hungaring | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lando Norris denied Ferrari a sweep of all three practice sessions for the Hungarian Grand Prix, setting the fastest time of the weekend so far in his McLaren.

With the soft tyres surprisingly proving resilient enough to yield two competitive times, Norris lowered the benchmark to a 1’17.939. That ensured he came out on top after a spate of runs by the drivers from the leading teams.

Norris displaced Lewis Hamilton from the top of the times by a tenth of a second, the Ferrari driver enjoying a strong run through the final sector. There was almost nothing to choose between him and Andrea Kimi Antonelli in third.

Charles Leclerc put his Ferrari fourth while Oscar Piastri and George Russell were each almost half a second slower than their respective team mates.

The Red Bull drivers did not look especially happy with their cars, Isack Hadjar branding his “undriveable” after a mistake at turn 12. Max Verstappen was the quickest of the pair, albeit seven-tenths of a second off Norris.

Liam Lawson took ninth for Racing Bulls but his team mate Arvid Lindblad missed most of the session with a technical problem. He emerged from the pits just in time for a single flying run. The Audi drivers completed the top half of the field.

Sergio Perez failed to set a time as he came to a stop immediately after leaving the pits. The Cadillac driver’s rear brakes were smoking alarmingly, prompting race control to red-flag the session.

Without that, the Williams drivers might have ended the session slowest of all. Valtteri Bottas outpaced his former team’s drivers and the upgraded Aston Martins were ahead of all four.

Fernando Alonso ended practice just under two-and-a-half seconds off the pace, but set his time early in the session, indicating there could be more pace in the heavily revised AMR26. The team had a fright early in the session, however, when Alonso caught his team mate at turn 12, who did not seem to realise he was there, provoking a worrying near-miss.

Sports.title: Tim Tszyu Outworks Errol Spence Jr. Over 12 Rounds
Sports.content:
The opening rounds were competitive. Tszyu stunned Spence with a right hand in the closing seconds of the first round, but Spence answered in the second with effective body work and a hard left that briefly shifted the momentum. The third round also favored Spence, although Tszyu finished strongly with another right hand.

Tszyu regained momentum in the fourth before another close fifth round. He began taking control in the sixth and seventh, landing the cleaner punches while increasing his work rate. Both fighters developed swelling under their left eyes.

Referee Will Soulos warned Spence several times for low blows in the eighth round as blood began flowing from Spence’s nose. Tszyu continued pressing the action over the final four rounds, repeatedly landing right hands while Spence’s output slowed.

Tszyu finished strongly in the twelfth, rocking Spence with another right hand during the closing minute to seal the victory.

Following the decision, Spence applauded Tszyu before announcing his retirement from boxing.

Reda Defeats Fleming

In the co-feature, Ahmad “Bloodshot” Reda earned a unanimous decision over former Olympian Paul “Showtime” Fleming after 10 entertaining rounds.

Reda controlled most of the early action with his speed and activity, although Fleming enjoyed his best success in the fifth after inviting Reda to exchange while standing against the ropes.

A clash of heads opened a cut over Fleming’s left eyebrow in the seventh. Reda continued to outwork the veteran over the closing rounds despite suffering a cut late in the fight.

The judges scored the bout 99-91, 97-93 and 96-94.

Peters Stops Actis

Australian Olympian Callum “50 Cal” Peters remained unbeaten by stopping Ivan “Gringo” Actis in the seventh round.

The opening rounds featured heavy exchanges before Peters gradually took control with sharper punching. A right hand opened a cut over Actis’ left eye in the fourth, and Peters continued to wear him down until referee Will Soulos halted the bout at 55 seconds of Round 7.

Aokuso Knocks Out Tejeda

Former Olympian Paulo “Sweet P” Aokuso captured the vacant IBF Intercontinental light heavyweight title with a dramatic 10th-round knockout of Luis Antonio Tejeda.

Aokuso rocked Tejeda early, but the Dominican battled back and had the Australian badly hurt against the ropes during the seventh round.

The fight ended suddenly in the final round when Aokuso landed a crushing counter left hand that flattened Tejeda for the count.

Rahimi Wins Pro Debut

Former Olympian Tina Rahimi opened her professional career with a unanimous decision over Sacha Ryan Dryden.

Rahimi boxed well throughout the four-round contest, using her speed and combinations to edge most of the rounds before finishing strongly.

The judges scored it 40-36, 40-36 and 39-37.

Grach Defeats Pluto

Heavyweight Brandon “The Bull” Grach earned a unanimous decision over Ike “From Pluto” Pluto in a five-round battle.

Grach hurt Pluto with a right hand in the third round and scored a knockdown in the fourth. Pluto rallied late and landed several solid punches in the fifth, but Grach had already done enough to secure the victory.

The judges scored the fight 49-45, 49-45 and 48-46.

Jimmy Lennon Jr. served as the ring announcer for the main event.

Sports.title: Errol Spence Jr. Retires After Tim Tszyu Loss
Sports.content:
Errol Spence Jr. brought his boxing career to an end Saturday night after losing a unanimous decision to Tim Tszyu, saying his health, family and financial security made retirement an easy choice. The former unified welterweight champion made the announcement moments after suffering a 12-round defeat at Afterpay Arena in Sydney, Australia.

“It was a great fight. Congratulations to Tim and Jeff Fenech. It was a good showing by Tim. I answered a lot of questions about myself, and now it’s time to go home with my family and start a new life,” Spence said before confirming his decision. “Yeah, for sure. I’ve got my faculties intact. My money is good and working for itself, so everything’s good, man. I’ve got a beautiful family and I thank God that I’m able to leave this sport with my faculties intact and my family by my side. Everything’s going to go well.”

The judges scored the fight 117-111, 117-111 and 118-110 for Tszyu, who gradually took control after a competitive opening. Spence was returning from a layoff of nearly three years and showed flashes of his former ability, but Tszyu’s pressure and higher punch output proved decisive over the second half of the contest.

Sports.title: Tim Tszyu Hands Errol Spence Jr. Tough Return Defeat
Sports.content:
“Middleweight is my new division and I feel strong,” said Tszyu. “This was one hell of a show. There were sleepless nights where I was thinking about facing a legend like Spence. I understand why he’s one of the greats.”

The opening rounds were competitive, with Spence finding success behind his jab and left hand while investing in body shots. Tszyu refused to give ground, walking the former unified welterweight champion down and landing hard right hands whenever Spence paused in front of him.

The fight changed as the rounds wore on.

Tszyu began timing Spence with increasing regularity, connecting with right hands to the head and body while forcing the Texan backward. Spence’s timing and punch output declined as the pace caught up with him, a predictable challenge after such a lengthy absence from the ring.

By the championship rounds, Tszyu had taken firm control. Spence continued fighting back and showed the toughness that defined much of his career, but he spent long stretches covering up, holding and trying to slow the Australian’s momentum. Tszyu never allowed him to regain control, continuing to press forward and outwork him until the final bell.

“The advice from corner was to get in there,” said Tszyu. “I’m trying to replicate Kostya Tszyu and my trainer Jeff Fenech. if I can be half as great as them, I’ll go down as a great man.”

The victory gives Tszyu one of the biggest wins of his career and strengthens his position among the leading names at 160 pounds. He entered the bout under pressure after a difficult run over the last two years, but responded with a disciplined performance against one of boxing’s most accomplished former champions.

“I’d love to fight for a world title. I want Erislandy Lara and all the champions,” said Tszyu. “That’s what I’m aiming for. But beating a great like Errol Spence tops any world title for me.”

After the fight, Spence addressed his future while giving Tszyu credit for his performance.

“It was a good fight and congratulation to Tim,” said Spence. “It’s been a great event and everyone has treated me well. It was a good showing by Tim.

For Spence, the defeat raises fresh questions about what comes next. His decision to return after nearly three years away was one of the sport’s biggest stories, yet the layoff appeared to take its toll as the fight progressed. Although he lasted the full 12 rounds, Tszyu’s steady pressure exposed the difficulty of returning against a proven contender without a tune-up first.

“I answered a lot of questions for myself and now it’s time to go home with my family and start a new life. I’ve got my faculties intact and my money is working for itself. I’m thankful to leave this sport with my family by my side.”

Sports.title: Josh Kelly Eyes Boots Ennis After Bloody Title Defense
Sports.content:
His ambition is understandable. Ennis owns the WBA and WBO titles at 154 pounds, making a unification bout one of the biggest opportunities in the division. Eddie Hearn also backed the idea after the fight, pointing toward a possible event in the United States later this year.

The bigger issue is recovery.

Kelly didn’t leave the ring looking like someone ready to begin another training camp. Agyarko landed plenty of hard punches throughout the contest, and Kelly’s injuries weren’t limited to accidental head clashes. He also complained afterward that the referee allowed too much roughhouse work, describing stretches of the contest as feeling like “an MMA fight.”

That criticism comes with some irony. Kelly repeatedly landed rabbit punches during the fight and eventually had a point deducted for hitting behind Agyarko’s head. Both fighters contributed to the physical nature of the contest.

Kelly has made it clear he wants Ennis next. The bigger question is how long it will take for the damage from the Agyarko fight to heal before he can begin preparing for a unification bout.

Sports.title: Bill Haney Claims Keyshawn Davis Has Gone Missing
Sports.content:
Under the WBO order, the winning bid would be split 75 percent to Haney as champion and 25 percent to Davis as the mandatory challenger. The organization has set a minimum bid of $200,000, although the sides remain free to reach their own agreement before the scheduled hearing.

Bill Haney’s latest post appears aimed at increasing the pressure with little time left on the negotiating clock. Rather than discussing specific terms, he questioned Keyshawn Davis’ willingness to complete a deal while portraying the challenger as absent during one of the biggest business opportunities of his career.

No agreement between the camps has been announced, leaving Monday’s purse bid on course unless a deal is reached beforehand, with time still remaining.

Sports.title: Eddie Hearn Thought Anthony Joshua’s Career Was Over
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua’s dramatic comeback knockout of Kristian Prenga left Eddie Hearn celebrating by the end of the night, but the Matchroom promoter admitted his thoughts were very different after the opening round.

Joshua climbed off the canvas twice before stopping Prenga in the second round at the Jeddah Superdome, surviving a scare that nearly derailed his comeback.



“When he got dropped, I was like, that’s career over,” Hearn said to Charlie Parsons at The Stomping Ground. “I’m kind of thinking to myself, ‘You know what? I’m proud of him for even getting back in the ring.’ If it ends like this, he should be really proud of the fact that he even returned to boxing. He had 24 breaks in his ribs or something. He couldn’t move, was in hospital for weeks and weeks. To even be in the ring was incredible.” Hearn said Joshua’s recovery changed everything. “He held on. He walked onto an uppercut and somehow found a way to recover,” Hearn said. “When he got back to the stool, I felt if he could just find his legs, this guy had thrown a lot of punches in the first round and was going to wear himself out. AJ has incredible knockout power. It doesn’t matter if he’s hurt. He has the ability to take you out with one punch.” Joshua answered those concerns by stopping Prenga in the second round, but Hearn did not ignore the warning signs. He believes the performance should not overshadow the determination Joshua displayed by overcoming the knockdowns and finishing the fight. Share via: Facebook

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua Survives Two Knockdowns To Stop Kristian Prenga
Sports.content:
The fight changed completely in the second round.

Joshua came out with greater urgency, established his jab, and began landing the right hand that had been missing during the opening three minutes. Once he found his rhythm, Prenga’s confidence disappeared. Joshua pinned him on the ropes with a series of heavy shots before finishing the job with a crushing combination that forced the referee to stop the contest.

The victory gives Joshua the result he needed after months away from the ring following his car accident, but it also leaves plenty to discuss. Getting dropped twice by an opponent who entered as a sizeable underdog is unlikely to inspire confidence among those already questioning where Joshua stands at this stage of his career.

The dramatic comeback kept plans for a proposed clash with Tyson Fury alive, though the opening round also provided future opponents with a blueprint. Prenga had success by taking the initiative immediately and forcing Joshua into exchanges before he could settle behind his jab.

Joshua ultimately delivered the knockout the crowd came to see, but the first-round scare may become the lasting memory from a fight that raised almost as many questions as it answered.

Ghana News.title: Opoku-Agyemang delivers keynote address at Sister Cities International 70th anniversary
Ghana News.content:
Vice President Professor Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang has delivered the keynote address at the 70th anniversary celebration of Sister Cities International in Washington, DC.

Sister Cities International, founded in 1956, is a non-profit network headquartered in Washington, DC, that connects communities in the United States with global partners through cultural, educational and trade exchanges.

A statement issued by the Office of the Vice President said Prof Opoku-Agyemang, speaking on the theme: “Forging Stronger Partnerships in Africa for Sustainable Economic Development,” underscored the importance of city-to-city diplomacy in advancing development, strengthening institutions and fostering international relationships.

“City-to-city partnerships continue to provide solutions to shared challenges and create opportunities for investment and mutual learning,” Vice President Prof Opoku-Agyemang said.

She reiterated Ghana’s commitment to strengthening local governance through decentralisation and noted that under President John Dramani Mahama’s Reset Agenda, Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies remained central to national development.

The Vice President explained that the Assemblies were being empowered with greater resources and responsibilities to improve the delivery of quality education, healthcare, infrastructure and other essential public services.

Prof Opoku-Agyemang also highlighted Ghana’s strategic role as host of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Secretariat and pointed to the vast opportunities for inter-city collaboration across the continent.

She said city diplomacy had the potential to stimulate trade, entrepreneurship, innovation, digital transformation and investment, while creating opportunities for the youth.

The Vice President noted that cultural and educational exchanges remained critical to building trust and strengthening bonds between communities.

She said Ghana’s long-standing commitment to reconnecting with the African diaspora demonstrated how people-to-people engagement could develop into enduring partnerships that contributed significantly to development.

“As cities worldwide face common challenges, including rapid urbanisation, climate change, waste management, public health, and disaster preparedness, we need greater collaboration among municipalities to share knowledge, strengthen institutional capacity, and develop practical solutions that enhance our quality of life,” Vice President Prof Opoku-Agyemang stated.

Prof Opoku-Agyemang congratulated Sister Cities International on its 70 years of promoting global friendship and cooperation and reaffirmed Ghana’s commitment to partnerships that advanced sustainable development, institutional learning, economic opportunity and shared prosperity.

Ghana News.title: Mahama leads Ghanaians to mark 14th Anniversary of Prof Mills’ passing
Ghana News.content:
President John Dramani Mahama on Friday led Ghanaians to commemorate the 14th anniversary of the passing of President Professor John Evans Atta Mills with the laying of wreaths at his tomb at the Asomdwe (Peace) Park in Accra.

President Mahama said the greatest tribute Ghanaians could pay to the late President was their commitment to the principles he cherished and exemplified, including integrity in public life, respect for democratic institutions, tolerance of differing views, compassion for the vulnerable, and an unwavering belief that Ghana’s progress must benefit all citizens.

He noted that the late President’s vision of a peaceful, just and prosperous Ghana remained a work in progress.

“I pledge to the memory of President John Evans Atta Mills that I shall continue to walk in the footsteps he left behind,” President Mahama stated.

The President said Prof Mills’ dream now belonged to all Ghanaians and called on citizens to work together towards its fulfilment.

He also expressed appreciation to Mrs Ernestina Naadu Mills, former First Lady, and the Mills family for sharing with the nation a man whose life continued to illuminate Ghana’s path.

President Mahama said the annual gathering at Asomdwe Park was not merely to lay wreaths but to renew gratitude for a life that enriched and strengthened the nation.

He observed that while time softens grief and pain, it also sharpens memory.

“Fourteen years after Professor John Evans Atta Mills left us, I find that what endures most after his departure is not merely the memory of a President, but the memory of a man, a gentle soul whose character was his greatest strength,” the President said.

He noted that some leaders command attention by the force of their personalities, and that President Mills commanded respect through the strength of his character and his values.

He said the late President Mills believed that kindness was not a weakness, humility was not timidity, and decency was not incompatible with effective leadership.

President Mahama said the late President Mills demonstrated that one could occupy the highest office of the land without losing one’s humanity.

“I had the rare privilege of serving by his side. Beyond Cabinet meetings, official engagements and the weighty affairs of state, I came to know a leader who listened more than he spoke, who reflected before he acted, and who never allowed the burdens of office to diminish his compassion for the ordinary people he served,” he said.

President Mahama described the late leader as a statesman who commanded respect through the strength of his character and values rather than through force of personality.

According to him, Prof Mills believed that kindness was not weakness, humility was not timidity and decency was fully compatible with effective leadership.

He noted that the late President demonstrated that one could occupy the highest office in the land without losing one’s humanity.

He said Prof Mills’ leadership was anchored in conscience and reminded Ghanaians that history ultimately judges leaders by the depth of their convictions and the impact of their service rather than by the bitterness of political contests.

“That is why his legacy continues to resonate. He taught us that public office is not a prize to be claimed, but a trust given by the people to be honoured.”

President Mahama added that the late President understood that leadership was most effective when it sought to unite rather than divide, heal rather than injure, and inspire rather than intimidate.

He said Prof Mills’ quiet wisdom and steady temperament continued to guide him in discharging the responsibilities entrusted to him by Ghanaians.

The President expressed the hope that future generations who never had the opportunity to know Prof Mills would come to appreciate that true greatness is often quiet, genuine strength is often humble and enduring leadership is measured by service rather than acclaim.

The commemoration, organised by the National Democratic Congress in collaboration with the J.E.A. Mills Memorial Heritage, was attended by Mr Alban Sumana Kingsford Bagbin, Speaker of Parliament, Ministers of State, Members of Parliament and other dignitaries.

Ghana News.title: Police urge peaceful Homowo celebration, warn against violence
Ghana News.content:
The Tema Regional Police Command has appealed to residents to celebrate this year’s Homowo Festival peacefully and refrain from acts that could disrupt public order.

Deputy Commissioner of Police (DCOP) Eric Asamoah Asiedu, Tema Regional Police Commander, said the festival period would witness traditional rulers, priests and priestesses performing customary rites before, during and after the celebrations, including the sprinkling of kpokpoi, the traditional Homowo meal.

DCOP Asiedu noted that disputes over who had the authority to perform the sprinkling of kpokpoi had, in previous years, led to confrontations, violence and breaches of the peace.

He, therefore, urged residents to celebrate the festival in an atmosphere of peace, unity and mutual respect while adhering to the laws of the country.

The Regional Commander cautioned celebrants against engaging in violence, unnecessary confrontations, disorderly conduct and other acts capable of endangering public safety.

He assured the public that the Police would provide adequate security throughout the festival period and deal decisively with individuals who engaged in criminal activities under the guise of the celebrations.

DCOP Asiedu also expressed concern over growing tensions arising from chieftaincy disputes in some traditional areas.

He urged all factions, supporters and interested parties to avoid acts of provocation, violence, unlawful assembly and the use of vigilante groups.

The Regional Commander said chieftaincy disputes should be resolved through the appropriate legal and traditional mechanisms, warning that anyone whose actions threatened public peace would be arrested and prosecuted.

DCOP Asiedu further warned armed robbers, drug traffickers and other criminal elements operating within the Tema region that the Police had intensified intelligence gathering, patrols and collaboration with other security agencies to combat crime.

He stressed that there would be no safe haven for criminals in the region and reaffirmed the Command’s commitment to protecting lives and property.

Ghana News.title: Leila Djansi questions NFA’s appeal for Film Fund donations
Ghana News.content:
Ghanaian-American filmmaker Leila Djansi has criticised the National Film Authority’s (NFA) appeal for public donations to the Ghana Film Fund, arguing that the fund should generate investment rather than rely on public contributions.

Reacting to the NFA’s fundraising appeal in a Facebook post, Djansi said it was wrong to ask Ghanaians to contribute when structures to make the film industry commercially viable had not been established.

“Back to the NFA. why ask Ghanaians to donate instead of using the government’s allocation to generate more money?” she questioned.

She added: “A Film Fund should be an investment that generates more investment, not a charity that begs for donations.”

The award-winning filmmaker argued that authorities should establish structures that would enable Ghana’s film industry to generate sustainable revenue before seeking public support.

“Again, I ask: what structures have been put in place to sustain the industry and ensure these films generate revenue?” she wrote.

Djansi also rejected the notion that YouTube could serve as the industry’s long-term economic solution.

“YouTube is a platform. It is not an industry. It will not replenish a government film fund,” she stated.

According to her, Ghana should stop modelling its film industry on Nigeria’s because the two countries have different market realities.

“Nollywood should not be Ghana’s standard. Copying Nigeria contributed to the collapse of Ghana’s industry years ago. Doing it again will not produce a different result. What works for Nigeria will not necessarily work for Ghana. You gotta find your own beat.”

She explained that Ghana lacked Nigeria’s population, celebrity ecosystem, distribution network and audience size, making it unrealistic to expect the same results from the YouTube-driven model.

Instead, she proposed using the Film Fund to attract international productions through competitive tax incentives and grants tied to minimum spending thresholds.

“Use the Film Fund to attract foreign productions through competitive tax incentives and grants. Give them a minimum spend. $1.5 million and up,” she said.

Drawing comparisons with film incentive programmes in the United States, Djansi noted that Georgia offers a 35% tax credit for qualifying productions, while New Jersey provides 40%, attracting productions that spend heavily in local economies.

She argued that international productions filming in Ghana would spend money on hotels, transport, catering, construction, equipment, locations and local crews, generating revenue that government could reinvest in the Film Fund.

“That economic activity generates revenue for the country. Government can then reinvest those returns into the Film Fund, creating a cycle of growth instead of a cycle of fundraising,” she wrote.

Djansi also suggested that Ghana should pursue a film industry strategy tailored to its own market, saying: “Instead of chasing Nigeria’s numbers, Ghana should build a model that reflects Ghana’s audience and strengths.”

Her latest comments are consistent with views she has expressed previously. In an opinion article published in March 2025, Leila argued that government should “fix foundations before funding Ghana’s film industry”, insisting that proper industry structures must be established before public money is invested in film production.

She made a similar argument during an interview on Hitz FM last year where she said she did not believe in establishing a film fund without a viable distribution system, warning that relying on YouTube was not a sustainable business model for Ghanaian filmmakers.

Ghana News.title: The ‘Our Day’ Dilemma: A cherished Ghanaian tradition that has become a high-pressure cooker
Ghana News.content:
The day that was once the most anticipated day on the school calendar, the day filled with laughter, juice boxes, and paper baskets of colour, has become a war zone of outrage.

As basic schools across the country officially end the term on Thursday, July 23, 2026, social media has exploded into a heated debate. The trigger? A wave of mounting allegations from frustrated parents claiming that the once beloved end-of-term “Our Day” tradition has been hijacked and turned into financial extortion.

For decades in Ghanaian culture, showing gratitude to educators was simple but spontaneous and heart-driven. But recent claims paint a vastly different picture of today’s classrooms where direct solicitations are used.

According to reports monitored on social media, parents now report receiving direct messages and phone calls from teachers nudging them to fund end-of-term "appreciation packages."

Some of the requests have reportedly ballooned from small tokens of appreciation to high-ticket items, including home appliances such as microwaves and substantial cash demands.

The situation has pushed parents, especially those with wards in private schools, into a corner, fearing their kids will be embarrassed or treated differently if they go to school empty-handed. “Our Day” then and now

The controversy stands in stark contrast to the memories of older generations.

Gone are the days when ‘Our Day’ meant excitement, laughter, and sharing, not expectations.

Growing up, while living with my late grandmother, my school was just behind our house. I could easily read between the lines when classes were about to begin. I would quickly prepare myself and rush off to school, eager to join my friends.

Those were our “Syto” days in public schools. Our biggest excitement back then was not about buying gifts for teachers; the real deal lay in “Our Day” celebrations.

Going to school with biscuits, drinks, and food packed in beautifully decorated baskets covered with white cloth was the ish of the day. It was a real joy.

"When I was in primary school, our biggest excitement was not about buying gifts for teachers. We looked forward to bringing biscuits, drinks, and food packed in beautifully decorated baskets covered with white cloth. That was the real joy. It was never a rule. No parent was forced, and no child felt embarrassed."

Pupils brought small tokens like drinks or biscuits in appreciation of their teachers, who accepted them with utmost pride.

But it was a voluntary gesture, as no parent was forced, and no child felt embarrassed because they could not offer a gift to their teacher.

It was simply an expression of a show of love and appreciation. But society over time is changing, forcing the meaning attached to Our Day gifts to change too.

There is no doubt that teachers deserve to be appreciated. They shoulder bigger responsibilities even beyond the walls of classrooms.

They provide guidance and counselling and, in some instances, spend financially on their pupils. Those teachers deserve recognition.

For instance, if a parent recognises the influence of a teacher on a ward and showers gifts on him or her willingly, there is absolutely nothing wrong with that.

After all, appreciating people for their good deeds is sacrosanct with the Ghanaian upbringing.

A small gesture from a grateful heart can mean a lot.

But the real problem begins when appreciation becomes an expectation.

When parents are asked to exchange expensive gifts such as microwaves or large sums of money, then it raises concerns.

Some overburdened parents already struggling to make ends meet will be put under unbearable pressure.

A gift should bring happiness, not stress.

Some people argue parents who choose private schools over public ones should be ready to meet the expectations that come with them. institutions. While parents certainly want the best for their children, appreciation should never feel like a compulsory payment.

Perhaps a better approach is to allow parents to raise specific concerns instead of blaming teachers for their predicaments. If a particular teacher or school makes unreasonable demands, that situation should be addressed directly rather than painting every teacher 'black'.

Because the truth is, many teachers continue to serve with dedication and commitment.

At the same time, we should not allow this conversation to destroy our culture of kindness and generosity.

Giving has always been part of who we are as Ghanaians.

When we are kind and loving to others, God is pleased.

So, let us continue to appreciate teachers, but let that appreciation come from the heart — not from pressure, fear or obligation.

Perhaps the greatest gift a teacher can receive is not an expensive item wrapped in a package but the appreciation of their patience, sacrifice and hard work that have helped shape the life of a child.

Ultimately, the essence of Our Day is not about the gifts. It was always about gratitude, love, and appreciation.

Source: Dorcas Abedu-Kennedy

Ghana News.title: UHAS celebrates 2026 International Day
Ghana News.content:
The University of Health and Allied Sciences in the Volta Region has hosted the 2026 edition of its annual International Day.

The event was aimed to commemorate and celebrate the cultural diversity of the University, which seeks to foster a community welcoming people of various nationalities and promote international collaborations.

The Vice-Chancellor, Prof Lydia Aziato, revealed that the University currently maintains 94 international partnerships worldwide, aimed at enriching student training and faculty development. She stated, “this is no mean achievement.”

She praised the significant contribution of the Cuban faculty in helping the University gain accreditation to establish the School of Medicine, among other accomplishments.

“On behalf of staff and management of UHAS, without you, we wouldn’t have a School of Medicine that is making waves both nationally and globally,” she said.

She also recognised the contributions of stakeholders, including Nigerian, Indian, and South African faculty, in guiding the University towards its goal of delivering quality training in diverse health disciplines.

“We are grateful to everyone who made this possible,” she emphasised.

The Dean of International Programmes, Prof Elvis Tarkang, stated that UHAS acknowledges the importance of cultural diversity in fostering a vibrant and intellectual environment.

He added that a culturally diverse university environment “strengthens our institutional identity, broadens perspectives and enhances the quality of teaching, learning, research, and service.”

He noted that through internationalisation, UHAS has equipped students to address complex health issues within different communities.

“Diversity is not just something to be acknowledged but a source of strength that promotes institutional growth, academic excellence, and meaningful partnerships,” he explained.

Dr Carlien Jooste, Director of Internationalisation at Sefako Makatho Health Sciences University in South Africa, highlighted the importance of internationalisation in modern universities.

She described it as a platform for students and staff to gain comprehensive training and participate in exchange programmes to share knowledge.

She urged universities to integrate internationalisation into their vision and strategic plans, invest in staff development, and regularly assess international initiatives.

She also pointed out that curricula should incorporate global and diverse perspectives, while university management should foster opportunities for intercultural engagement.

“Successful internationalisation is not measured by the number of international partnerships or international students on campus. Its true success lies in creating a university where every individual feels respected, included, and empowered to contribute,” she concluded.

Ghana News.title: Maison Yusif launches ‘The Beast’ fragrance, eyes global expansion from Ghana
Ghana News.content:
Ghanaian luxury perfume house Maison Yusif has unveiled its latest fragrance, The Beast, as it intensifies efforts to position African-made perfumes on the global luxury market.

The fragrance was launched on Saturday, July 25, at the Pelican Hotel in Accra, where the fragrance house described the new Parfum Extrême as a bold expression of African craftsmanship, confidence and uncompromising luxury.

Screenshot

The Beast was created for individuals who command attention through their presence rather than words.

The Beast is designed to be remembered as a scent that embodies confidence, discipline and fearless ambition while delivering depth, elegance and timeless luxury.

The fragrance draws inspiration from leaders, entrepreneurs, creators and visionaries, with every bottle handcrafted in Accra to reflect the brand’s commitment to modern perfumery and African luxury.

As part of the launch event, guests participated in a live product demonstration and fragrance experience, giving them the opportunity to experience The Beast up close and gain a deeper appreciation of its unique composition and character.

The event also featured customer testimonials, with early users of the fragrance sharing their experiences and impressions of some of Maison Yusif's products, highlighting its distinctive scent profile and lasting appeal.

Speaking to journalists after the launch, the Founder of Maison Yusif, Yusif Jnr Meizongo, said the company has remained focused on building an internationally recognised African fragrance brand.

“Since we started, so far we have been targeting international, and it has been great for us, and I think Ghanaians also support its exposure,” he said.

He added, “Maison Yusif wants to take over the world and represent Africa.”

Mr Meizongo said the company is determined to redefine perceptions about African luxury products instead of following trends established elsewhere.

“Honestly, I’m sick and tired of replicating the white people in terms of everything that we do. So here we’re trying to take a new step to let the world know that Africa is what it is and Africa is the next big thing,” he said.

He stressed that Maison Yusif is focused on carving its own identity in the luxury fragrance industry.

“Maison Yusif is not a competition. We’re doing it in our own race. We’re a royal fragrance house, truly niche, made in Ghana, by a Ghanaian, from Ghana and in Ghana.”

Looking ahead, Mr Meizongo expressed confidence in the company’s growth ambitions.

“In the next five to 10 years, we look to conquer Africa and the world with our royal fragrance,” he stated.

Explaining the inspiration behind the new product, he said the creative team wanted a fragrance that projected strength and dominance.

“We wanted to create a fragrance that was very dominant, and my creative team and I were looking for a very dominant name, and we came across The Beast. I’m not the only one who comes up with the names, or the scent, etc.,” he said.

The launch forms part of Maison Yusif’s broader vision of establishing Ghana as a producer of world-class luxury fragrances while showcasing African creativity and craftsmanship on the international stage.

Ghana News.title: NSMQ 2026 : St. Louis SHS returns to nationals after thrilling comeback in Ashanti region qualifiers
Ghana News.content:
St. Louis SHS fights back to reach NSMQ 2026 nationals

St. Louis Senior High School has secured a place at the 2026 National Science and Maths Quiz (NSMQ) national championship after producing a remarkable comeback victory in Contest Two of the Ashanti Regional Qualifiers.

The Kumasi-based school recovered from an early deficit to finish with 53 points, sealing automatic qualification after a closely contested battle in which several schools held the lead at different stages.

Jachie Pramso SHS finished second with 45 points, followed by Kumasi Girls' SHS on 42 points. Esaase Bontefufuo Senior High Technical School scored 37 points, while Jacobu Senior High Technical School ended the contest with 15 points.

The victory marks a return to the national stage for St. Louis SHS after the school narrowly missed out on the 2025 championship, having been eliminated during the regional qualifiers.

Speaking after the contest, the team's coach expressed appreciation for the victory but admitted the team had aimed for a more convincing winning margin.

"We thank God for the victory, but we wanted a much bigger margin. We know we can do better, and we'll work harder ahead of the national championship," the coach said.

The contestants also expressed confidence ahead of the national championship, signalling their intention to make a strong impact when the competition begins.

While St. Louis SHS claimed the only automatic qualification slot from the contest, Jachie Pramso SHS and Kumasi Girls' SHS remain in contention for qualification as potential best-performing losing schools.

Their chances of reaching the national championship will depend on how their scores compare with those recorded by other non-winning schools across the regional qualifiers.

With momentum on their side, St. Louis SHS will now look to improve on its previous best performance at the NSMQ, having reached the semi-finals in 2023, as it prepares for another shot at Ghana's most prestigious academic quiz competition.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: House of Hope: New film follows a Waldorf-inspired school in the West Bank
World.content:
A documentary about a primary school in the West Bank follows children under occupation and the couple who run it even as Israel’s war persists.

At one point in the documentary, House of Hope, the protagonist, Manar Wahhab, breaks down in a classroom corner in the school she founded with her husband in the occupied West Bank. The cameras keep rolling.

“To step into someone’s life with a camera at the moment when they’re really down, it feels a little bit uncomfortable, but we made the choice together to keep filming during these moments. I wanted the audience to be there with them,” director Marjolein Busstra told Al Jazeera.

The film follows Wahhab, a Palestinian woman who established a Waldorf school with her husband, Milad Vosgueritchian, in al-Eizariya in the occupied West Bank.

House of Hope Vision Kindergarten & School teaches the Waldorf philosophy of non-violent resistance and offers children a space to express their emotions and cope with the trauma and difficulty of living under occupation.

“The school protects the children’s dignity in the present moment. It’s more about refusing to let occupation shape their inner world, so that they can actually be children and have agency,” Busstra said. “It’s in Waldorf philosophy that they make space to express the feelings.”

Working with a Palestinian crew, Busstra spent three years with Wahhab, travelling to the occupied West Bank nine times throughout the course of the documentary. She first met Wahhab 18 years ago during a film workshop in the West Bank.

Although the documentary centres around the elementary school, Wahhab is the story’s driving force. The story follows Wahhab and Vosgueritchian, both at the school and at home with their children.



“I started filming the school, but right away, I knew I wanted to do it about Manar’s inner life,” Busstra said. “I think hope is a difficult word at the moment, but I have a deep awe for Manar, who keeps creating and teaching even while carrying so much herself.”

For Wahhab, her respect for Busstra and their existing friendship helped her trust the film crew during vulnerable moments.

“We both believe deeply in education, in children’s creativity and freedom and in seeing the human being as something whole and beautiful in mind, soul and spirit. Those shared values created openness and trust between us and helped shape a film that is not only about events but also about humanity,” Wahhab told Al Jazeera.

The film was produced by Think-Film, the company behind The Voice of Hind Rajab, which tells the story of the five-year-old Hind killed by Israeli forces in 2024. Soldiers fired 335 bullets into the car carrying the girl and six of her family members – a story that became a symbol for the system failure to protect children in Gaza.

Although sometimes difficult, Wahhab said she made an effort to let the crew document multiple facets of her life.

“Over those three years, the crew met many versions of Manar. Sometimes they arrived, and I was fresh, energetic and cooperative. Other times, they found me exhausted, angry, overwhelmed, or ill,” she said. “I understood that I had to be as authentic as possible, because I was representing not only myself, but also my community, hope, peace and the voice of Palestinians.”

Wahhab and Vosgueritchian founded the school out of a desire to offer a different kind of education to Palestinian children and to provide a place where they felt safe and could share their emotions.

“The school was born many years ago when we saw the hardships surrounding our community and wanted to create something different, a space of love, safety, creativity and healing,” Wahhab said. “House of Hope is an idea, a mission and an energy that we carry wherever we go.”

In an increasingly violent Israeli occupation, Wahhab considers the Waldorf philosophy essential.

“I do not see nonviolence as weakness. Actually, I believe the opposite. Violence is easy. Nonviolence requires courage, awareness, patience and inner work. It asks us to see beyond our own pain and ego and to hold on to our humility even when circumstances are trying to pull us away from it,” she said.



“The world absorbs the energy that we create, and right now, there is so much fear, anger and violence in our world. I think we need more peace within ourselves, peace with one another and peace with nature,” Wahhab added.

After Hamas’s incursion into southern Israel on October 7, 2023, came Israel’s brutal military response. Life became increasingly difficult for Wahhab, Vosgueritchian and the children at House of Hope, but the crew continued to document their realities.

“The story I wanted to create with Manar stayed the same, but after October 7, everything became heavier. They were so down for a while. They were like different people, like they lost all hope,” Busstra said. “The school built this safe haven, but the occupation is always rattling at the door.”

Israel’s intensified military actions in the West Bank, including the shooting and killing of children, are a constant spectre. In another scene, Wahhab watches her son leave for school and checks to see if he has a phone charger and spare clothes in case he is held at a checkpoint for hours.

“The energy is so heavy now. I hope people understand that we are not asking for something extraordinary. We are asking for basic human rights, the right to live with dignity and freedom, the right to safety and the right to be fully human beings,” Manar said.

Busstra, who closely followed Wahhab for three years, said she wants audiences to go “beyond the framing of us vs them”.

“I hope that this stays with people, not as something distant that happens to others, but something they can locate within their own understanding of what it means to love someone in an unsafe world.”

Wahhab believes the film offers a more nuanced perspective of Palestinians.

“I think that in the West, many people see a very limited picture of Palestine and the Middle East. Sometimes they see us through stereotypes as terrorists, as people who are undeveloped or somehow less than themselves,” she said. “I hope this film helps people look beyond those images. The news does not tell the full reality. It often shows only violence and people killing one another. It doesn’t show the essence of people’s lives. It shows negativity,” she said.

Wahhab encouraged people to consider the documentary through a lens of shared humanity.

House of Hope won the best international feature documentary prize at the Hot Docs Canadian International Documentary Festival in May 2026 and was recently screened at UNESCO in Paris. It will soon be screened at the Jerusalem Arab Film Festival.

“Even though our story is deeply rooted in the West Bank, its message is universal. Our hope is that people everywhere can see our story and take something meaningful from it.”

World.title: Typhoon Noul makes landfall in China, with hundreds of thousands evacuated
World.content:
Noul hit southern Guangdong province and neighbouring Hong Kong, bringing strong winds and heavy rain to the region.

Typhoon Noul has hit southern China, including Hong Kong, bringing strong winds and heavy rain to the region and prompting the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people in Guangdong province.

China’s national weather centre said Noul made landfall on the coast of Huidong county in Huizhou, southern Guangdong province, at approximately 3:50am local time on Sunday (19:50 GMT on Saturday).

China’s official Xinhua News Agency said Noul was the strongest typhoon to make landfall in China so far this year.

Hong Kong’s Observatory said Noul, with maximum sustained winds of 110 kilometres per hour (68 miles per hour) near its centre, was moving Sunday into inland Guangdong and weakening progressively, bringing strong winds and heavy rain to parts of the region.

More than 715,000 people had been relocated for safety by early Sunday in Guangdong province, according to state-owned China National Radio. On Saturday, authorities said some 340,000 people were evacuated.

China’s National Meteorological Centre expected parts of southern Guangdong and southeastern Fujian provinces to experience heavy rain and strong winds over the weekend.

Many trees were seen uprooted in Huilai county, located on the coast of Guangdong province, state broadcaster CCTV reported.

Hong Kong’s airport authority said about 350 flights were cancelled on Sunday. At least nine people were injured across the city during the typhoon period, according to Hong Kong authorities.

As Noul approached Hong Kong, parts of a large scaffolding on a high-rise building collapsed on Saturday afternoon, local police said, although initial reports indicated there were no injuries.



Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration said Noul was bringing rainfall to parts of southern and eastern Taiwan. It was passing over waters south of Taiwan and was moving away from the island Saturday.

Earlier this month, Typhoon Bavi brought strong winds and rain to eastern China, leading to the evacuation of more than two million people. It made landfall on July 11. Another, Maysak, made landfall in southern China on July 3.

World.title: New front in US-Iran war escalates as Houthis fire at Saudi oil facilities
World.content:
Conflict also spreads to Caspian Sea as Tehran accuses Ukraine of a deadly attack on an Iranian vessel.

Tehran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen have fired missiles and drones at two of Saudi Arabia’s most strategically important oil facilities on the Red Sea, in a major escalation of the latest simmering regional conflict to be reignited by the war launched by the United States and Israel against Iran.

But the skies over the country at the epicentre of the widening war were quiet for a second successive night, with no new US attacks on Iran reported by Sunday morning.

Iran had been pounded by 13 consecutive waves of overnight US air strikes since July 11, after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) attacked tankers trying to transit the Strait of Hormuz. As hostilities escalated, both sides declared that an interim peace agreement signed in June was dead, and a second phase of talks to finalise a comprehensive peace deal appeared doomed.

But there have been no US air strikes since Friday, and tentative signs are emerging that Washington and Tehran are still talking via mediators and might return to more meaningful discussions.

Even if another fragile truce is agreed, however, the cascade of consequences unleashed by the war is still stoking conflict and confrontation elsewhere.

Iran’s attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have put a stranglehold on exports of oil and raw materials for fertiliser, sending energy prices soaring and raising the risk of a food security crisis in some of the world’s most vulnerable countries.

In March, in response to attacks on Iran, the Tehran-backed Hezbollah movement in Lebanon resumed missile attacks on Israel, which then launched a devastating invasion of southern Lebanon that has displaced 1.2 million people.



Now, another smouldering regional conflict has erupted again, between US-allied Saudi Arabia and the Houthi movement which controls most of northern and western Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa. Saudi Arabia and its regional allies joined a brutal civil war against the Houthis in 2015, until a truce was agreed in 2022.

Risk of global crisis

The truce collapsed this month after an attack on Sanaa airport to stop an Iranian plane landing provoked the Houthis to fire ballistic missiles at Saudi Arabia. Last Monday, the Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia, and late on Friday the Saudis launched air strikes on the Houthi-held city of Hodeidah.

In retaliation, Houthi forces launched Sunday’s attacks on facilities belonging to Saudi state oil giant Aramco in the coastal cities of Jizan and Yanbu, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said.

There has been no comment from Saudi Arabia on the extent of any damage to Aramco’s refinery in Jizan, but a large column of smoke was seen rising after the attack.

In Yanbu, Saudi Arabia’s principal west coast export gateway, two ballistic missiles aimed at oil installations were intercepted by a Patriot battery operated in Saudi Arabia by the Greek military under an agreement ‌with Riyadh.

The escalating conflict has raised fears that the Houthis could block the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. If both the Bab al-Mandeb and Hormuz straits were blocked, the resulting supply chain crisis would cause major economic damage across the world.

Entangled wars

Besides spreading to the Red Sea, the US-Iran war has become entangled with the deadliest active conflict in the world – Russia’s attempted conquest of Ukraine.

A long-range strike on an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea on Saturday caused an explosion that killed one sailor and wounded another, according to Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which blamed the attack on Ukraine and summoned Kyiv’s charge d’affaires in Tehran to convey its condemnation of the “hostile and criminal” act.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X that Kyiv had achieved “very strong results” with long-range strikes in the Caspian Sea, hitting “vessels used in military cargo shipments involving Iran, as well as a warship”.

Zelenskyy claimed in further comments on X on Saturday that since the start of July, Kyiv had detected “active Russian satellite ⁠surveillance of the Gulf states and US military facilities located there”. He said the satellite images were passed to Tehran to help the IRGC identify targets for ballistic missile and drone attacks.



US President Donald Trump has not given a reason for the sudden cessation in air strikes on Iran, but a senior administration official told the Reuters news agency that Trump “has always been clear that his preference is diplomacy, but he has shown Iran what will happen if they fail to come to the table in a serious way”.

Trump said on Friday that there was still some communication with Iran.

“They are talking to us right now; they’d love to make a deal,” he said. “I don’t think they’re ready to … but I’m willing to listen.”

Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar, reporting from Tehran, said Iranian officials had confirmed the two sides were exchanging messages.

“There have been proposals conveyed by the mediators, and Tehran is still reviewing them,” Serdar said, adding there was “not much progress yet” due to “fundamental differences” in their positions and deep mistrust.
