World.title: The men’s World Cup is over, now Mexico’s women are ready for their moment
World.content:
With the 2026 edition of the men’s World Cup behind us — in which Mexico became the first country to host the sporting event on three separate occasions (1970, 1986 and 2026), leaving an indelible impression on fans worldwide who openly celebrated Mexico’s culture, gastronomy and spirited fandom — the “summer of North American soccer” is coming to a close. Well, sort of. It’s not completely over.

Luckily for fans of fútbol (also known as fút or balompié in Mexico), on-pitch action will resume with a different set of national heroes, as Mexico and the rest of the globe prepare for the upcoming 2027 Women’s World Cup.

World Cup qualifying has already begun

View this post on Instagram A post shared by FOX Sports MX (@foxsportsmx)

Though the tournament won’t actually take place until next summer — hosted in Brazil, marking the first time the FIFA women’s edition will take place on Latin American soil since debuting in 1991 — the race for the trophy is already underway.

Last winter, World Cup qualifying games began; this fall, North American qualifiers, which determine which teams from the region will compete in the World Cup, will conclude.

Here’s a look at Mexico’s national women’s squad and how they have fared so far on their historically arduous journey for sporting glory.

A history of women’s professional soccer in Mexico

Like all women’s sports around the globe, Mexico’s Liga MX Femenil is relatively new and lags behind its male counterpart league in terms of financial support, national investment, media coverage and, as a result, fandom. Despite those barriers, it has been celebrated as a highly successful effort.

The league was announced in late 2016 and officially played its first game in 2017. Since then, it has quietly developed into one of the world’s leading women’s leagues, with the Associated Press reporting that “women’s pro soccer is thriving in Mexico” and The New York Times citing it as the most-watched women’s league on the planet.

That said, it hasn’t been a path without systemic and cultural resistance. Instances of gender bias, sexism and a massive gap in pay and resources have endured. Last summer, Mexican men’s national team legend and former superstar Javier “Chicharito” Hernández was fined by the Mexican Football Federation for demeaning comments on social media that portrayed women as “failing” and “eradicating masculinity,” prompting a response from President Claudia Sheinbaum. In 2023, former Club América Femenil player Scarlett Camberos chose to leave the team and country due to excessive sexual harassment and cyberstalking.

Liga MX Femenil and the birth of the FIFA Women’s World Cup

Though Liga MX Femenil — both its successes and its accentuated reminder of Mexico’s machismo — is relatively nascent, pro women’s soccer in Mexico can be traced back to 1970. Before FIFA’s involvement, an unofficial Women’s World Cup existed as a series of international events independently sponsored by various nations. In those times, Mexico finished in third place at the 1970 World Cup in Italy and ended as runner-up in the largely erased 1971 World Cup in Mexico. It is estimated that the 1971 final at Estadio Azteca drew 110,000 fans. Unofficial tournaments continued throughout the 1980s under non-FIFA-sanctioned entities like the Chinese Taipei Football Association.

Pressure for an official FIFA Women’s World Cup mounted, crescendoing in 1986 when Norwegian delegate Ellen Wille famously urged FIFA to legitimize a women’s tournament in a speech that “changed the course of women’s football,” according to the BBC. In 1988, FIFA organized a trial tournament, the FIFA Women’s Invitation Tournament in China. Overwhelming success resulted in the debut of the official Women’s World Cup in 1991 in China.

Surprisingly, since the FIFA era of the World Cup began, Mexico’s women’s team hasn’t shown much promise. That is finally changing.

The road to the 2027 World Cup is off to a perfect start

In February, Mexico’s women’s team kicked off its World Cup campaign in the preliminary qualifying rounds of the Concacaf W Championship. Concacaf is the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football, representing one of FIFA’s six continental governing bodies, which divides competition into regional tournaments that funnel teams into the World Cup every four years. Under this format, all North American, Central American and Caribbean teams face off, with the four quarterfinal winners earning direct berths to the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil.

Currently, Mexico is among the remaining eight North American countries with a chance to secure a World Cup ticket this year. It can do so by defeating Haiti on Nov. 28 at Texas Health Mansfield Stadium in Texas.

Mexico’s women haven’t reached a World Cup since 2015. Unlike the Mexican men’s national team — which has qualified 18 times dating back to 1930 — the women have appeared only three times (1999, 2011 and 2015). While the Women’s World Cup has taken place only nine times compared to 23 for the men, El Tri Femenil has struggled to assert regional dominance, holding a 33.3% qualification rate compared to the men’s nearly 80% rate over a much longer period.

A thus-far ‘flawless’ qualifying journey

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Concacaf W (@concacafw)

However, this World Cup cycle is proving to be different: Mexico’s women have been perfect in their qualifying run, an unprecedented feat. In 2023, Mexico also went undefeated for the first time at the Pan American Games in Santiago, Chile, en route to claiming its first gold medal, proving this current team’s success is no fluke.

El Tri has topped Group A of the Concacaf W Championship qualifiers with a flawless 12 points — going unbeaten in four matches and scoring 36 goals while conceding zero. That places them among the continent’s strongest units and makes them favorites to advance. While they have primarily played lower-ranked competition — such as Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, which Mexico defeated 14-0, and Puerto Rico — the core of the 2023 Pan American Games roster remains intact, leading many to consider this the best women’s team Mexico has ever fielded.

‘The Sorceress’ and other Mexico stars to watch

The roster is headlined by Lizbeth “La Maga” Ovalle (whose nickname translates to “The Sorceress”). Having debuted professionally in 2017, the winger — originally from Aguascalientes, who gained fame as one of Mexico’s top scorers with Tigres UANL — set a record in 2025 by signing a US $1.5 million contract with the Orlando Pride of the National Women’s Soccer League, making it one of the most lucrative deals in women’s soccer history. That same year, Ovalle won the FIFA Marta Award for “Best Goal of the Year” at The Best FIFA Football Awards ceremony for her spectacular “scorpion kick” goal.

Behind Ovalle, Mexico boasts a depth of experience and skill with team captain Rebeca Bernal and the formidable striker Charlyn Corral, one of Mexico’s all-time leading goal scorers. Complementing the veteran leadership is “Concacaf Best Young Player” award winner Alice Soto, a 19-year-old dynamic midfielder who debuted professionally at age 13 and has been scoring in Liga MX Femenil ever since.

Why upcoming qualification matters

Against Haiti, Mexico can automatically claim a direct spot in the 2027 World Cup. A loss would send the team to a playoff round for a second chance.

Haiti is coming off its inaugural appearance in the 2023 Women’s World Cup in Australia and New Zealand. Les Grenadières, as they are known, are a rising team led by attacking duo Melchie Dumornay and Nérilia Mondésir, supported by a defense that has allowed only one goal during qualifiers.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mente Mujer (@mentemujer_)

Though the Women’s World Cup does not begin until next June, the matches will stream on Netflix for the first time, with Mexico’s women primed for their deepest run in tournament history. Furthermore, the 2031 Women’s World Cup will be co-hosted by Mexico, the United States, Costa Rica and Jamaica, marking the first time Mexico will host the FIFA women’s event.

Until then, El Tri Femenil hopes to deliver the nation its first World Cup trophy — regardless of gender.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: US crimes against Mexico from an immigrant’s perspective
World.content:
There is nothing like living outside of your native country to make you reflect on the meaning of its actions, especially if your native country happens to be the United States of America.

Living in Mexico, of course, makes you an automatic representative of your country. This is not a fair position to be in, but it is the story of immigrants everywhere. For the most part, I benefit from my country of origin: whereas plenty of people in the U.S. might look down on an immigrant from Mexico, here it is the opposite. Most people expect me to be cool and interesting, and maybe a little sneaky, scary or both.

We may all be individuals, but the human brain only has so much capacity to think of people as individuals. Gather too many foreign individuals into the same place, and the borders between us blur and blend until we are collectively “others.”

Proud and ashamed

Many things about the U.S. make me very, very proud to be from there: like jazz music, the advancement of civil rights and feminism. First in flight. Customer service agents who are mostly empowered to actually help you. Clean public restrooms with toilet paper, for free!

Other aspects of my home country, however, make me feel deeply, deeply ashamed. A less-than-stellar record when it comes to genocide and enslavement, for example. And oh, Lord, influential religious leaders who would love to send us back to those “good old days.” Deliver us!

When it comes to current events, our treatment of immigrants is at the top of my list right now.

In case you have been protecting your peace more than I have and have abstained from the news, here is a sad summary: Donald Trump returned to office with as much of a mandate as you could suppose to reduce the “out of control” immigration in the U.S.

The killing of innocents and deportation of US citizens

More Latinos in the U.S. than ever voted for him. Strangely, they seemed to believe his promise that he would only target and deport “the criminals” among them. Who would not get behind that?

As it turns out, there are a lot fewer “immigrant criminals” than most people thought. So, unfortunately for the law-abiders, the net was pretty much immediately cast much, much wider to meet detention quotas set by the administration. It caught mothers and fathers taking their children to school. It caught lots and lots of people here legally, papers be damned. It caught those who were brought as children and have known no other life than that of an American.

On top of the generalized horror of being torn from one’s life, there is the very suspicious fact that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has been extremely cagey, caught in lies more than once. It is a fight every time a local official wants to enter a (privately run) detention facility. Those who have come out of them have described the places as unfit for human beings. Rotting food, freezing temperatures and medical needs that are ignored. It is not hard to imagine how over 50 people have died since detentions were ramped up upon Trump’s return, some by suicide. Seventeen of these deaths have been of Mexican nationals (14 in custody, three during “operations”).

A lack of institutional control

Then, of course, there are the vehicle stops and shootings under extremely suspicious circumstances. One of the latest, of course, was that of a Mexican national, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, who turned out not to even be ICE’s target. ICE’s story is that he tried to “weaponize his vehicle” against them. Witnesses say it was quite the opposite. The feds had to be blocked from deporting the witnesses. Weird behavior from an institution that has nothing to hide, right?

In short, things are truly out of control.

The U.S. and Mexico are supposed to be allies. What is going on here?

‘A general lack of accountability’

The main thing that is going on, I believe, is that the wrong people are in charge. Unhappy people voted them in, believing their lies about what the source of their unhappiness actually stemmed from. A threadbare social safety net paired with barely-there labor laws that are happy to let people simply fall through the net and onto the concrete pavement? Nah, that cannot be it … transgender people and immigrants, that is who is hurting you!

Social media — what was supposed to bring us together — and a general lack of accountability to the truth that the internet age has wrought have been excellent at getting people all riled up for stupid reasons.

The U.S. is really pushing it with Mexico right now.

Can Mexico do anything about it?

I personally think that is doubtful, but who knows? I have been wrong before. But if ICE cannot even be held accountable for its on-camera killings of U.S. citizens, who is going to put a boot on its neck over immigrant killings?

And when the offending country has been essentially in charge of international justice for decades, it is hard to tap the brakes. After all, who do you go to for help when the police themselves are corrupt?

Mexico, of course, understands this conundrum in a literal sense. But Mexico also does not claim to be the distributor of justice for the world, either.

Of all the words I might use to describe Mexicans, “proud” would be in the top five. While it seems that a few insults here and there will always be tolerated because of the particular power dynamic the two countries have, you cannot just start letting its citizens die and not even apologize for it.

Mexico files criminal complaints

Claudia Sheinbaum, thankfully, is not letting this go. Criminal complaints, cease-and-desist letters to the private companies in charge of detention, the United Nations. They are going at it from all angles.

The Secretariat of Foreign Affairs is “filing a criminal complaint against whoever is responsible.”

But, gosh. “Whoever is responsible.” Hmm. There is our first issue right there.

Would that be the president, for insisting that as many immigrants be tossed out of the U.S. as possible? Stephen Miller, the architect of the whole thing? Agency heads? Those who hire and “train” (or don’t) ICE officers? The private companies who feel no need to provide adequate living conditions? The offending/negligent immigration officers themselves? It truly is a long list of candidates.

The known reality, of course, is that in the end, it is unlikely anyone will be held to account. I mean, we cannot even get the U.S. to acknowledge that it dropped a bomb on an Iranian girls’ school, killing hundreds of children. Sanctity of life, indeed.

‘The twin monsters of incompetence and cruelty’

How are we supposed to get anyone who has been given “free rein” to carry out the president’s signature plan to play fair?

One of the biggest crimes that humans commit against each other is allowing the twin monsters of incompetence and cruelty to go on … and right now, those twin monsters have the full backing of the U.S. federal government.

This is what happens when you remove the shackles of accountability from institutions filled with the kinds of people who see the world as a fight between those who hunt and those who get hunted.

And many people who work in ICE fancy themselves hunters; they like to prey on people who are running or scared, or just trying to stay out of trouble’s way. They are hunted by the same types of people who used to catch (and torture) runaway slaves. They sniff out fear and relish the capture.

So here we are, many of us, living in a country that has welcomed us in ways that the U.S. would not dream of welcoming our neighbors. It is a strange and sad position to be in. It is also worth remembering that the tables could always turn.

We are the “others” here, after all.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: World Cup glow fades as tariffs and security challenges take center stage
World.content:
This week marked the end of the 2026 FIFA World Cup and the conclusion of Mexico’s third turn as a host country. The week opened with President Sheinbaum’s attendance at the World Cup final in New Jersey, where brief exchanges with Trump, Carney and other officials set the tone for USMCA review talks that resumed in Mexico City. Sheinbaum later called the tournament a diplomatic success, and world leaders had high praise for Mexico’s performance as a host nation.

As World Cup excitement faded, security stories dominated elsewhere. Zacatecas authorities linked the multihomicide of 10 people, including a former mayor, to extortion and official collusion, while a Sinaloa Cartel kingpin, “El Mayo” Zambada, was sentenced to life in prison in the U.S. While El Mayo’s court case has run its course, infighting within the cartel he once led prompted 900 more troops to deploy to Mazatlán, Sinaloa. The week ended with the annoucement of sweeping U.S. sanctions against an opposing organized crime syndicate, the Jalisco New Generation Cartel.

On the economic front, inflation fell to its lowest level since 2020 and a new round of U.S. tariffs largely spared Mexico.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Security: Homicides fall, but high-profile violence persists

México state’s homicide rate has dropped to its lowest level in 19 years, officials said Wednesday, citing a “unified command” strategy that cut daily killings by 58% since September 2024. In Morelos, Governor Margarita González’s administration touted a 54% homicide drop alongside improving public perceptions of safety, even as the state investigated the murder of a mayor with alleged ties to organized crime.

That progress contrasted with events in Sinaloa and Oaxaca. The Zacatecas multihomicide, which included a former mayor of Sombrerete and two Fresnillo officials, is being investigated as a possible case of extortion and collusion between criminals and public officials. In Mazatlán, a string of targeted attacks over the past two weeks left at least a dozen dead, prompting the arrival of 900 additional troops, bringing the security deployment to more than 1,300 personnel. Authorities attributed the violence to the ongoing feud between Sinaloa Cartel factions that intensified after Zambada’s 2024 arrest. Separately, journalist Alejandro Leyva was shot dead in Oaxaca on Wednesday, the second journalist killed in Mexico in less than a week. Federal prosecutors took over the case at the request of state officials.

On Thursday, the U.S. Treasury sanctioned 39 individuals and 16 companies linked to the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, including the CJNG’s new leader, Juan Carlos Valencia González, a.k.a. “El Pelón.” The U.S. called it the largest action ever taken against the group, and Mexico’s financial intelligence unit blocked the same accounts.

El Mayo’s sentencing and its aftermath

Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, Sinaloa Cartel co-founder, was sentenced to life in prison and ordered to forfeit $15 billion by a U.S. federal judge on Monday. In court, Zambada urged young people to avoid a life of crime. President Sheinbaum said she agreed with the sentiment but declined to explicitly endorse a message from a convicted trafficker. Mexican officials said Wednesday it remains unclear whether Zambada could ever be transferred to a Mexican prison, a decision that depends on whether the Attorney General’s Office pursues extradition.

Trade and economy: Inflation eases, tariff fights continue

Mexico’s annual inflation rate fell to 3.10% in the first half of July, the lowest for any comparable period since December 2020, driven largely by falling produce prices. Meanwhile, the tariffs Mexico implemented this year on countries without free trade agreements — chiefly targeting China — cut affected imports by 23.2% between January and May, even as overall imports from Asia rose on surging Taiwanese semiconductor purchases.

On the U.S. side, President Trump’s re-imposed tariffs took effect Friday on dozens of countries, but Mexico avoided major new costs: About 80% of Mexican exports remain tariff-free under the USMCA, according to Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard. While dozens of other countries faced increased tariffs, Mexico’s rate remained at 10%. The U.S. gave Mexico a heads-up before the announcement, as U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer visited Mexico City this week to meet with Sheinbaum and press for stricter automotive rules of origin in the ongoing USMCA review, citing a growing U.S. auto trade deficit with Mexico.

Health, migration and infrastructure

Deputy Health Minister Eduardo Clark reported that 30 public hospital projects have been completed since October 2024, adding 1,474 beds toward a goal of 9,000 by 2030, with 33 more projects due this year. Health officials also moved to calm fears over a U.S. Cyclospora outbreak initially attributed to lettuce from Guanajuato: After the FDA retracted a positive test result, Mexican authorities said there was no evidence of contamination in Mexican-grown produce.

A new report from the Migration Policy Institute found the Mexican-born population in the U.S. has fallen to 11.1 million, down more than 500,000 since a 2007 peak, a decline researchers said could accelerate amid stepped-up immigration enforcement. On infrastructure, the government launched the second construction phase of its passenger rail program, which will link central Mexico to Saltillo and the Pacific coast, while separate data showed Mexico is drawing more international tourists but earning less per visitor as land-crossing traffic outpaces higher-spending air arrivals.

Also this week, the federal government joined Jalisco state officials in announcing a joint effort to rehabilitate Guadalajara’s aging water infrastructure and curb industrial contamination of the Lerma River, while Mexico City announced three regional forums to debate social media and AI regulation for minors.

Looking ahead

USMCA negotiations are set to continue following this week’s talks with Greer, with both sides aiming for interim agreements before year’s end even as the review process stretches toward 2036. Security officials face pressure to build on regional and national homicide declines while containing the Sinaloa Cartel factional violence driving unrest in Mazatlán and elsewhere. Investigations into the Zacatecas multihomicide and the killing of journalist Alejandro Leyva remain open, with federal authorities now involved in both cases.

World.title: Postcards from Mexico: On the Cabo San Lucas Marina
World.content:
CABO SAN LUCAS, Baja California Sur, Oct. 25 — It’s quiet and cool off the strip. The abarrotes are just opening, and there’s an old man in a vest up the block pushing a shopping cart full of empty beer cans. That might be mop-up duty from last night’s debauchery, or this morning’s. Stray dogs patrol the streets, trotting from one garbage pile to the next like derelict show ponies. In their glory days, they guarded the now-abandoned buildings that flank the street, too pure for this world with their barbed-wire crowns of thorns.

Baby birds are just waking up, warbling. They were promised a worm, like all early birds, but maybe they’ll settle for the gnats buzzing around my face, plentiful at these hours when it’s still not hot enough for the sun to burn them out of the air midflight.

It doesn’t take much to drown out the noise they make. Every half-minute, buses rattle up the sand-dusted Narciso Mendoza and down the Leona Vicario. As I turn onto Lázaro Cárdenas, I’m presented with a beautiful bouquet of belching tubas courtesy of the music blaring from the back of a black vocho. One doesn’t question who would blast banda music at this hour. “Reveille.” “La 4 x 4.” Same tiger, different stripes.

The soundtrack of the Cabo San Lucas Marina

The playlist in the Cabo San Lucas Marina is different. You might still hear some classics, depending on whose boat you walk by, but the shops and kiosks pander to a different demographic. I still haven’t quite figured out which. Daft Punk begets Murray Head, which begets Katy Perry. Speaking of which, Señor Frog’s is still thriving. Even at this hour, I spot a gringo retiree in board shorts and a tank top loitering in front, presumably curious about hours of operation. He’s in good company.

Along the esplanade, you hear far more English than Spanish. Much of that comes from merchants stumbling through back-of-the-napkin phrases they’ve committed to memory to entice newly arrived tourists to buy their wares. Though I also hear an old woman muttering something to her dog about one of the boats they pass by, so I guess even the dogs here are fluent.

‘A parking lot for yachts’

Along a wall, a line of men wearing Oakleys, long-sleeved shirts and visors sits idly, taking it easy before heading out on whatever excursions they’ll be leading. Nearby, a bored-looking clerk in a dockside store that looks like Cabo’s version of J. Peterman scrolls on his phone, unfazed about the urban sombrero sales quota he’ll need to meet by the end of the day. Even aboard the boats, on the eve of the world’s biggest marlin tournament, local fishermen prattle, hosing down decks and trying to be heard over the dull roar of idling boat engines.

This marina is like a Costco parking lot for yachts, though instead of an associate in a neon vest checking your ID, there’s a tall, wrought-iron gate with an entrance like a cage that only those with a key can get through. I pause to size it up, then look around to see who’s watching. “I could hop that,” I say to myself.

Ethan Jacobs is a freelance writer and writing coach based in Playa del Carmen. He has written extensively in narrative and short fiction formats, and his work has received recognition both domestically and internationally in microfiction, short fiction and narrative essay formats.

World.title: Is Chipotle in Mexico a good or bad idea? A ‘Confidently Wrong’ podcast
World.content:
Recently, and with much fanfare, Chipotle opened its first restaurant in Mexico. Perhaps not surprisingly, the opening spurred a polarizing debate and discussion about whether a U.S.-based Mexican restaurant chain would do well in the country. Years ago, Taco Bell entered the country and ultimately left in what was considered a disaster.

So what are the arguments for and against Chipotle coming to Mexico? Is it yet another unwanted assault of American culture on another country? Or is it a welcome sign of competition and choice for Mexicans?

Could it lead to lost business for local Mexican restaurants and reduced “authentic” Mexican food options? Or could it create a standard for the trifecta of affordability, service and quality that Chipotle is known for and oftentimes doesn’t exist in many restaurants today? Or perhaps it’s not that big of a deal, and people should move on?

And finally, what does the choice of a ritzy Monterrey suburb as the first restaurant location in the country tell us?

I will admit that while I have been a very frequent customer of Chipotle in the United States, I have actually eaten very few burritos here in Mexico. And the ones I have had have been very different.

In this week’s episode of Confidently Wrong, George and I talk through the arguments on each side of the debate and offer our own thoughts and opinions. Where do you stand on this issue? Check out the discussion here:

Confidently wrong about Chipotle: Episode 5 - Season 3

World.title: US sanctions more than 50 Jalisco cartel-linked individuals and businesses
World.content:
The U.S. Treasury on Thursday imposed sanctions on 39 Mexican individuals and 16 companies it alleges are linked to the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), calling it “the largest action ever taken” against the notorious crime gang.

The measure targets the leadership of the cartel — designated by President Donald Trump as a foreign terrorist organization — and its illicit financing networks across Mexico.

The Treasury Department said in a statement that the goal of the sanctions is to limit the CJNG’s ability to traffic fentanyl and other drugs into the United States.

Shortly thereafter, Mexico’s Financial Intelligence Unit (UIF) reported it had identified “indicators related to possible operations with resources of illicit origin, including cash transactions, acquisition of high-end vehicles, jewelry and real estate,” as well as “international transfers, intensive use of credit and debit cards and transactions using virtual assets.”

As a result of this review, Mexico blocked the accounts of the same 55 individuals and companies sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department.

“The coordinated actions between Mexican and U.S. authorities strengthen mechanisms of international cooperation to prevent abuse of the financial system, combat money laundering and weaken the economic structures of organized crime,” the UIF said.

Among those sanctioned is Juan Carlos González, aka “El Pelón,” identified by U.S. authorities as the new leader of the CJNG following the February death of his stepfather, cartel founder, Rubén Oseguera Cervantes, who was killed in a federal operation.

The U.S. State Department has offered a reward of US $5 million for the capture of González, who holds both Mexican and U.S. citizenship.

Also sanctioned was the network of associates and subordinates linked to Audias Flores Silva, aka El Jardinero, who was arrested by Mexican authorities in April.

The UIF review found “inconsistencies” in tax records involving the accused, saying “they present characteristics of shell companies or with corporate structures of limited or no apparent economic activity.”

A complaint was filed with the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) and the 39 individuals — as well as eight others accused of being part of the same CJNG network — were added to the UIF’s Blocked Persons List (BPL).

The BPL is a public report identifying individuals and legal entities involved in money laundering or terrorist financing. All Mexican individuals and companies are required to immediately suspend any and all acts, operations or services with people or entities on the BPL.

With reports from EFE, Infobae, El Economista and La Jornada

The week turns on whether inflation data from Brazil and growth figures from Mexico and Brazil confirm that Latin America’s largest economies can keep cutting rates while the Federal Reserve stays on hold.

The Federal Reserve decision anchors the week for global rates and Latin American currencies. (Photo internet reproduction)

Investors begin the week with a Brazilian consumer-confidence reading on Monday and close it with a Bank of Japan decision and a Colombian rate call on Friday. In between, the Federal Reserve, Banco Central de Chile and a heavy run of Latin American inflation and activity data will set the tone for carry trades and local-currency bonds.

The dollar will take its cue from the FOMC statement on Wednesday and the first estimate of second-quarter US GDP on Thursday. For Latin American assets, the domestic stories matter more: a soft Brazilian IPCA print on Tuesday would reinforce the Selic-cutting narrative, while a strong Mexican GDP rebound on Thursday could narrow the rate differential with the US and support the peso.

Three Themes for the Week

Disinflation in Brazil is the week’s most tradeable theme, with the mid-month IPCA and the wholesale IGP-M both due.

Monetary policy divergence returns to the fore as the Fed stands still while Chile and Colombia decide whether to cut, hold, or signal a turn.

Growth data from Mexico, Brazil and the euro area will test the assumption that Latin America can decouple from a slowing global economy.

The Week, Day by Day

Monday, July 27, 2026

The session opens with a Singapore monetary policy statement before the Latin American morning brings Brazilian consumer confidence and Mexican trade figures. A FGV confidence print above the 88.5 consensus would suggest that domestic demand is holding up better than the central bank’s cautious tone implies, potentially trimming near-term Selic-cut bets.

The Week in Context

Latin American markets enter the week with carry trades well supported by high local rates and a dollar that has struggled to sustain rallies. Brazilian and Mexican assets have been the primary beneficiaries, but the flow has also reached Andean currencies as global investors search for yield in a world where the Fed appears stuck in a holding pattern.

The risk to this benign setup is a hawkish surprise from the FOMC or a growth shock from China that hits commodity prices. Oil remains in a comfortable range for the region’s producers, but any escalation in Middle East tensions would lift fuel costs for importers and complicate the inflation outlook for central banks in Chile and Colombia.

The Bottom Line

The week’s trades hinge on Brazilian inflation and Mexican growth. A soft IPCA print and a firm Mexican GDP rebound would keep the carry trade alive and favour the real and the peso. The Fed is unlikely to move, but any shift in its statement that suggests a higher-for-longer stance would hit local-currency bonds hardest. Chile and Colombia offer event risk late in the week; both central banks are expected to hold, making the tone of their communications the real market mover.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the single most important data point for Latin American markets this week?

Brazil’s IPCA mid-month CPI on Tuesday. A print below the 0.4 percent consensus would strengthen the case for further Selic cuts and support the real and local bonds.

Will the Federal Reserve move rates this week?

No. The consensus expects the fed funds rate to stay at 3.75 percent. The market will trade the statement, particularly any change in the description of the labour market or inflation risks.

Which central bank decisions outside the US matter most?

Chile on Tuesday and Colombia on Friday. Both are expected to hold, but any signal that cuts are approaching would move the peso and local rates in each country.

World.title: Guyanese Literary Giant Ian McDonald Dies at 93
World.content:
Guyana · Culture

Key Facts —Born c. 1933 —Died 19 July 2026, aged 93 —Known for Caribbean literary giant; author of the novel The Humming-Bird Tree; poet; decades-long editor of Kyk-Over-Al; co-editor of the Heinemann Book of Caribbean Poetry —Roles Novelist, poet, longtime columnist for Stabroek News, former top executive at Guyana Sugar Corporation (GuySuCo), former Chairman of Guyana Publications Inc., editor, anthologist

Dr. Ian McDonald, the Guyanese writer and editor hailed as a Caribbean literary giant, died on Sunday, 19 July 2026, at the age of 93.

A weathered clapboard Georgetown cottage, the kind of quiet street where McDonald might have set a scene, amid the rustle of bougainvillea and the hum of the tropics.

Life and career

Ian McDonald’s life was deeply intertwined with the cultural and economic fabric of Guyana. Born around 1933, he grew up in a period of profound change in the Caribbean, eventually establishing himself as a leading voice in the region’s literature.

While the full arc of his early years remains sparsely documented in the immediate aftermath of his passing, what is clear is that he dedicated decades to writing, editing, and public commentary that resonated across the West Indies.

He moved between the worlds of literature and industry with ease. McDonald served for many years as a top executive management official at the Guyana Sugar Corporation (GuySuCo), the state-owned sugar company that once stood as the backbone of the country’s economy. In this role, he gained firsthand experience of the challenges and rhythms of Guyanese life, a perspective that would inform his writing and his later work as a columnist.

He also held a key position within the media landscape as Chairman of Guyana Publications Inc, the company that publishes Stabroek News, one of the country’s leading newspapers. His regular column in that paper became a fixture of intellectual life in Guyana, offering reflections on arts, society, and the region’s future.

This dual commitment to letters and public service marked him as a singular figure in Caribbean life.

Major works

McDonald’s literary output spanned genres, but he was most celebrated for his fiction and poetry. His best-known work, The Humming-Bird Tree, stands as a hallmark of Guyanese literature.

The novel, widely read and studied, captures the complexities of a society in transition, seen through the eyes of its young protagonists. It cemented his reputation as a writer of sensitivity and insight, and it remains a touchstone for readers seeking to understand the Caribbean experience.

As a poet, McDonald contributed to the broader tapestry of West Indian verse. Although the full bibliography of his poetry collections is not immediately available in the records of his passing, his role as co-editor of the Heinemann Book of Caribbean Poetry underscores his significance.

That anthology, published in the early 1990s, brought together voices from across the region and was hailed as a landmark in the canon of Anglophone Caribbean writing. It served as both a classroom text and a declaration that the islands had a distinct and powerful poetic tradition.

Beyond the page, his poems appeared in journals and newspapers, often reflecting on themes of nature, identity, and the quiet dignity of ordinary life. His literary craftsmanship was paired with a clear, accessible style that made his work beloved by a wide audience.

Kyk-Over-Al and a life in letters

Perhaps no role defined McDonald’s contribution to Caribbean letters more than his decades-long editorship of Kyk-Over-Al. Founded in 1945 by A.J.

Seymour, the magazine quickly became the most important literary periodical in Guyana and one of the most influential in the English-speaking Caribbean. McDonald, who took up the editorial mantle, guided the publication through multiple generations of writers, ensuring it remained a vibrant forum for new poetry, fiction, and criticism.

Under his stewardship, Kyk-Over-Al maintained its reputation as an incubator of talent. Writers who later achieved international recognition first saw their work in its pages, and the magazine continued to publish even as print media faced mounting challenges.

McDonald’s unwavering commitment to the journal reflected his belief in the power of small magazines to build literary communities and to preserve a cultural space distinct from the commercial pressures of mainstream publishing.

His editorship was not merely administrative; he actively mentored young contributors, offering feedback and encouragement. The magazine’s longevity—it remains a fixture in Guyanese cultural life—is a testament to his dedication.

Literary legacy for Guyana and the Caribbean

When news of McDonald’s death broke, tributes poured in, underscoring the breadth of his impact. Kaieteur News described him as a “Caribbean literary giant,” a phrase that captured the esteem in which he was held.

Guyana’s President Irfaan Ali was quoted by Demerara Waves saying that McDonald was “a literary figure of worth and one of the Caribbean’s distinguished sons.” Such recognition was not merely ceremonial; it reflected the deep imprint he left on the region’s cultural identity.

McDonald’s legacy is inseparable from the post-colonial literary awakening of the West Indies. Alongside writers like Wilson Harris, Edgar Mittelholzer, and Martin Carter, he helped articulate a distinctive Guyanese and Caribbean voice that resisted being defined solely by colonial narratives.

His work as an anthologist, particularly through the Heinemann Book of Caribbean Poetry, ensured that this voice was codified and made accessible to students and readers worldwide.

He also served as a bridge between generations. Older writers respected his stewardship of the literary tradition, while younger authors found in him an ally who understood that literature must evolve to speak to contemporary realities.

His influence is now embedded in the curricula of Caribbean universities and in the ongoing conversations about what it means to be a writer from the region.

Beyond the page

For all his literary achievements, McDonald was not a man who lived solely in the world of books. His tenure at GuySuCo placed him at the heart of Guyana’s most important industry. Sugar defined the country’s economy and society for centuries, and McDonald’s executive role gave him insight into the lives of workers, the complexities of production, and the interplay between agriculture and national development. This real-world grounding lent his writing an authenticity rarely matched by purely academic observers.

His column for Stabroek News further illustrated his ability to move between spheres. Week after week, he commented on social issues, politics, and culture, always with the measured, thoughtful tone of someone who had both witnessed and shaped history.

As Chairman of Guyana Publications Inc, he also oversaw the strategic direction of the newspaper, helping to ensure that independent journalism remained a pillar of democratic life in the country.

In all these roles, McDonald personified the ideal of the public intellectual: someone whose expertise and passion could be applied to practical affairs without losing the critical distance that art requires. His career showed that literature and leadership are not mutually exclusive, and his example inspired others to pursue similarly broad engagement with their societies.

Why his work still matters

Ian McDonald’s writing endures because it speaks to universal questions through the particular lens of Caribbean experience. The Humming-Bird Tree, with its delicate exploration of childhood, race, and belonging, continues to resonate in a world still grappling with issues of identity and inclusion.

His poetry, though less widely catalogued in the immediate record, captures the beauty and pain of life in a post-colonial society with a lyrical simplicity that defies trends.

More than his individual works, his stewardship of literary institutions ensures that his impact will be felt for decades. By editing Kyk-Over-Al and co-editing the Heinemann anthology, he helped build the infrastructure that allows writers from small nations to reach global audiences.

This kind of labor—often unsung—is what sustains a literary culture. Future historians of Caribbean writing will inevitably cite his contributions as foundational.

As Guyana and the wider Caribbean navigate the challenges of the twenty-first century, the voice of Ian McDonald—measured, humane, and deeply attuned to the rhythms of the region—will remain a source of guidance and inspiration. His death marks the end of an era, but the work he championed lives on, a testament to a life richly lived in service of art and community.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was Ian McDonald’s most famous book?

He is best known for his novel The Humming-Bird Tree, which has become a classic of Caribbean literature.

What was his role in the sugar industry?

He served as a top executive at Guyana Sugar Corporation (GuySuCo), the state-owned sugar company, combining a successful management career with his literary pursuits.

How did he influence Caribbean writing?

As editor of Kyk-Over-Al and co-editor of the Heinemann Book of Caribbean Poetry, he championed West Indian voices and helped shape the region’s literary canon.

World.title: Brava Board Backs Ecopetrol’s US$534M Takeover Bid
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts —Board Recommendation Brava Energia’s board issued a favorable opinion on Ecopetrol’s tender offer on July 24, 2026, recommending shareholders accept. —Advisory Nature The recommendation is non-binding; each shareholder must decide individually whether to tender shares. —Revised Offer Filing Ecopetrol resubmitted its tender-offer document on July 20, 2026, after CVM’s regulatory review and approval. —Auction Date The auction is scheduled for August 5, 2026, at 3:00 p.m. Brasília time, with financial settlement on August 17, 2026. —Conditions Precedent Completion remains subject to regulatory requirements and conditions outlined in the offer document.

Brava Energia‘s board of directors issued a favorable opinion on July 24, 2026, recommending that shareholders accept Ecopetrol’s tender offer for control, while emphasizing that the final decision rests individually with each investor.

Brava Energia shareholders faced a key decision as the board endorsed Ecopetrol’s tender offer.

Brava Board Backs the Ecopetrol Offer

The board of Brava Energia, the Brazilian oil and gas company, formally recommended on July 24 that its shareholders accept the ongoing public tender offer (OPA) launched by Colombia’s Ecopetrol. The favorable opinion, disclosed in a material fact, marks a crucial endorsement in the multi-month effort by Ecopetrol to acquire a controlling stake in Brava.

However, the board stressed that its recommendation is advisory and non-binding, serving to inform rather than bind investors.

According to the filing, the board’s opinion included certain qualifications (ressalvas), though the exact content of these caveats was not fully detailed in the publicly released summaries. The company reiterated that the decision to tender shares remains an individual choice, dependent on each shareholder’s investment strategy and assessment of the offer’s terms. This advisory approach is standard in Brazilian tender offers, where boards provide a reasoned view but do not approve the transaction itself.

The recommendation comes after Ecopetrol had to overcome regulatory hurdles, including an earlier suspension by Brazil’s Securities and Exchange Commission (CVM). With the board’s backing now public, attention shifts to the upcoming auction date, where the offer’s success will be determined by the level of shareholder participation.

The board’s stance may influence retail and institutional investors who look for guidance, but ultimately the tender’s outcome hinges on collective acceptance.

What the Tender Offer Puts on the Table

A tender offer, known in Brazil as an OPA (Oferta Pública de Aquisição), is a public invitation by an acquirer to purchase shares from existing shareholders, often with the aim of gaining control. In this case, Ecopetrol is seeking to buy a controlling stake in Brava Energia, building on its strategic push into Brazil’s pre-salt and other offshore assets.

The offer allows any Brava shareholder to sell their shares at a predetermined price and conditions.

The specific terms, including the price per share and any minimum acceptance thresholds, were outlined in the revised offer document filed on B3 on July 20. While the board’s recommendation signals that the terms are favorable from a governance perspective, the actual value of the bid was not reiterated in the recent updates.

Earlier reports had indicated a multi-hundred-million-dollar offer, with some sources citing US$534 million as the aggregate amount for the targeted stake, but these figures were not confirmed in the latest regulatory filings.

Completion of the OPA is subject to several conditions precedent, such as regulatory approvals (which already include clearance from Brazil’s antitrust body CADE) and the tender of a sufficient number of shares to achieve control. If the conditions are met, Ecopetrol will become the controlling shareholder, reshaping Brava’s strategy and governance.

For investors, the decision revolves around whether the offered price fairly values the company’s prospects.

How the Ecopetrol-Brava Saga Unfolded

Ecopetrol’s pursuit of Brava Energia gained momentum in early 2026, with the Colombian state-controlled company signaling ambitions to expand in Brazil’s oil sector. In May 2026, Ecopetrol launched the initial tender offer, targeting a controlling equity stake after securing pre-approval from CADE, Brazil’s antitrust authority.

The move reflected Ecopetrol’s strategy to diversify its asset base beyond Colombia and capitalize on Brava’s portfolio, which includes interests in the mature Campos Basin and promising pre-salt discoveries.

The deal hit a snag in June when Brazil’s CVM suspended the OPA, requesting additional disclosures and compliance measures. This intervention cast uncertainty over the timeline.

However, after Ecopetrol submitted supplementary information and appealed, the CVM lifted the suspension, allowing the process to resume. On July 20, Ecopetrol filed the amended tender-offer document, restarting the clock and setting the stage for the July 24 board opinion.

The board’s favorable recommendation now adds a governance seal of approval, though the board had no power to approve or block the offer itself. The sequence of events—from launch to regulatory pause to revival—illustrates the complex nature of cross-border M&A in Brazil’s energy sector.

With all major approvals in place, the transaction’s completion hinges purely on the auction outcome and settlement.

The Auction and Settlement Timeline

The revised schedule sets the public auction on B3, Brazil’s stock exchange, for August 5, 2026, at 3:00 p.m. Brasília time. During this auction, shareholders who wish to accept the offer will formally tender their shares at the agreed price. The auction is a standard mechanism used in Brazilian OPAs to concentrate liquidity and ensure transparent price discovery, though in fixed-price offers like this one, it primarily serves as a settlement mechanism.

If enough shares are tendered to fulfill Ecopetrol’s control objectives and all conditions are met, the financial settlement will occur on August 17, 2026—eight business days after the auction. On that date, selling shareholders will receive payment for their shares, and Ecopetrol will take ownership.

This settlement timeline is consistent with B3’s typical T+8 settlement cycle for such special operations.

It’s important to note that the offer’s completion remains conditional: if any prerequisite is not satisfied by the settlement date, the deal could be delayed or canceled. Shareholders who tender their shares are locked into the transaction once the auction concludes, so they should review the full offer document—available on B3 and CVM websites—for exact terms and risks.

What It Means for Investors

For Brava’s minority shareholders, the board’s recommendation provides a strong signal that the offer’s terms are aligned with the company’s interests. However, the advisory nature means each investor must weigh their own analysis: those who believe Brava’s long-term value exceeds the offer price might hold onto shares, while others may prefer to lock in cash, especially given the oil market’s volatility.

The offer’s control premium—the extra amount over market price to gain control—may not be explicitly separated from the tender price.

If Ecopetrol gains control, Brava Energia will likely undergo strategic changes, potentially accelerating investments or integrating operations. Minority shareholders who remain after the OPA might see their shares trade in a less liquid market, as free float often shrinks after control transactions.

Conversely, a failed bid could leave Brava independent but under pressure to deliver on its existing growth plan.

The next key milestone is the August 5 auction, where participation levels will reveal market sentiment. Investors should monitor any last-minute updates from Brava or Ecopetrol that could affect the offer, such as changes in conditions or competing bids.

With the board now on record, the focus shifts to execution, and the coming weeks will determine whether Ecopetrol’s Brazilian ambitions are realized.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Brava Energia’s board recommendation binding on shareholders?

No, the opinion is purely advisory. Each shareholder must independently decide whether to tender their shares based on their own assessment.

What happens at the August 5 auction?

The auction is a formal session on B3 where shareholders can tender their shares at the offer price. The outcome determines if Ecopetrol acquires the necessary controlling stake.

When will shareholders receive payment?

Financial settlement is scheduled for August 17, 2026—eight business days after the auction—provided all conditions are met.

World.title: Celsia Builds 260 MW of Solar Across Colombia
World.content:
Colombia · Energy

Key Facts —Construction Scale. Celsia is building 17 solar farms with 260 MW across four Colombian departments, using 650,000 panels. —Investment Total. The projects represent over COP 1 trillion (US$255.6 million) in investment through its C2 Energía platform. —Job Creation. The construction phase is generating 3,500 direct and indirect jobs nationwide. —Regional Focus. Farms are concentrated in Valle del Cauca (109.2 MW), Tolima (69.5 MW), Santander (59.7 MW), and Sucre (19.9 MW). —2025 Capex Plan. Celsia earmarked COP 900 billion (US$219 million) of its COP 1.3 trillion 2025 budget specifically for solar energy.

Colombian energy firm Celsia is rapidly expanding its solar footprint, with 260 megawatts currently under construction across 17 new farms, as part of a broader strategy to install 1,000 MW of solar and wind capacity by 2027, backed by heavy investment.

Solar panels being installed at one of Celsia’s 17 new solar farms in Colombia.

Celsia’s Solar Construction Push

Celsia confirmed in a corporate release that it has 17 large-scale solar farm projects currently under construction, totaling 260 megawatts (MW). The projects span the departments of Valle del Cauca, Tolima, Santander, and Sucre.

The buildout involves the installation of 650,000 solar panels and is expected to generate approximately 3,500 jobs during the construction phase. The farms are being developed through C2 Energía, a joint venture with global renewable investor Cubico Sustainable Investments.

This push is part of Celsia’s stated goal to reach 1,000 MW of operational solar and wind capacity in Colombia by 2027, a target the company has reiterated in public filings and media statements.

Investment and Funding Strategy

Total investment for the 17-farm portfolio exceeds COP 1 trillion, equivalent to roughly US$255.6 million at current exchange rates. Celsia is financing the projects through its C2 Energía platform, a partnership with Cubico Sustainable Investments.

In 2025, Celsia plans total capital expenditures of COP 1.3 trillion (US$316.5 million), with COP 900 billion (US$219 million) directed specifically at solar energy, according to figures reported by Reuters. This reflects the company’s prioritization of renewable expansion.

An earlier, smaller project—a solar plant in Buga, Valle del Cauca—required an investment of COP 55 billion (about US$14.1 million), underscoring the scale of the current pipeline.

Regional Breakdown and Local Impact

The 17 farms are distributed as follows: eight in Valle del Cauca (109.2 MW), five in Tolima (69.5 MW), three in the Chicamocha area of Santander (59.7 MW), and one in Sucre (19.9 MW).

Valle del Cauca hosts the largest share, including a recently inaugurated plant in Buga and a 19.9 MW project in Puerto Tejada built for Grupo Familia/Essity. These projects are expected to supply clean energy to local industries and communities.

The construction phase alone is creating thousands of jobs, providing an economic boost in several regions. The solar farms will also help diversify Colombia’s energy matrix, which has historically relied heavily on hydropower.

What It Means for Expats and Investors

Celsia’s large-scale solar investment signals Colombia’s growing commitment to non-hydro renewables, potentially improving energy reliability and creating opportunities for foreign investors in the sector.

The heavy weighting of 2025 capital spending toward solar—coupled with a clear 1,000 MW target—suggests a stable regulatory and business environment for renewable infrastructure. This could attract further international capital and partnerships.

For expats living in Colombia, a more diversified energy grid could mean fewer weather-related power disruptions. The influx of investment may also support jobs, local services, and a greener economy in the regions where farms are built.

Background

Celsia is the energy arm of Grupo Argos, one of Colombia’s largest conglomerates. The company has increasingly focused on renewable energy, stating a goal of operating 1,000 MW of solar and wind by 2027.

Earlier corporate communications mentioned a mid-term target of 600 MW of solar under development plus 330 MW of wind by 2025, but the more recent emphasis is on the 1,000 MW combined goal by 2027.

C2 Energía, the development vehicle for many of these projects, is a joint venture with Cubico Sustainable Investments, a UK-based renewable energy investor. The partnership was designed to accelerate Celsia’s non-conventional renewable portfolio.

The Numbers in Context

Celsia’s own corporate release confirms 260 MW under construction. However, a subsequent report by Colombian newspaper La República quoted a company official saying it had ‘339 MW and another 300 MW under construction,’ suggesting the pipeline may have grown.

Some media outlets have referenced a 580 MWp target for solar by end-2026, but this figure does not appear in any Celsia or Grupo Argos filing verified by The Rio Times. The number may include projects still in early development or unconfirmed stages.

Readers should rely on Celsia’s official communications for project status. The 260 MW across 17 farms remains the only fully verified construction figure at this time.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Celsia’s renewable energy goal?

Celsia aims to have 1,000 megawatts of solar and wind power in operation in Colombia by 2027, according to company statements.

How much is Celsia investing in its current solar projects?

The 17 solar farms under construction represent a total investment exceeding COP 1 trillion (approximately US$255.6 million). Additionally, Celsia has allocated COP 900 billion (US$219 million) of its 2025 budget to solar.

Where are the new Celsia solar farms being built?

The 17 confirmed farms are located in Valle del Cauca, Tolima, Santander, and Sucre, with the largest concentration in Valle del Cauca.

World.title: Namibia Air Plans $33M Embraer Fleet of 7 Aircraft
World.content:
Brazil · Aerospace

Key Facts —Airline. Namibia Air is the carrier pursuing the fleet renewal, not FlyNamibia. —Fleet Plan. The plan includes seven Embraer regional aircraft: four ERJ 145s and three E170/E175-family jets. —Cost. The total investment is reported at N$594 million (approx. US$33 million), with the ERJ 145s at US$3 million each and the E170/E175s at US$8 million each. —Aircraft Type. The larger jets are standard E170/E175 models, not the newer E-Jets E2 family. —Deal Status. It remains unclear whether the plan is a firm order, a memorandum of understanding, or a preliminary fleet strategy.

Namibia Air has reportedly laid out a N$594 million (US$33 million) plan to acquire seven Embraer regional jets—four ERJ 145s and three larger E170/E175-family aircraft—as part of a fleet renewal, though the exact nature of the deal remains unconfirmed.

The E170/E175 family offers larger cabins for regional routes, potentially boosting Namibia Air’s capacity.

The Fleet Renewal Plan

Namibia Air is targeting a fleet renewal with seven Embraer regional aircraft, according to mid-July 2026 reports.

The plan includes four ERJ 145 jets—a 50-seat model widely used for short-haul routes—and three aircraft from the larger E170/E175 family, which typically seat 70 to 88 passengers.

The total cost is pegged at N$594 million, approximately US$33 million at current exchange rates. The ERJ 145s are estimated at US$3 million each, while the E170/E175 jets cost around US$8 million apiece.

For context, Namibia’s aviation market is relatively small by global standards, with a handful of carriers serving domestic trunk routes and regional connections to neighboring countries. A fleet investment of this scale would represent one of the more significant capital moves in the country’s recent civil aviation history.

Understanding the Aircraft

The ERJ 145 is a twin-engine regional jet designed for routes with lower passenger demand, offering airlines a cost-effective solution for connecting smaller cities.

The E170 and E175 belong to Embraer’s E-Jet family, not the newer E2 series. They are larger than the ERJ 145 and are popular with regional airlines worldwide for their fuel efficiency and cabin comfort.

Regional jets in this class allow carriers to serve thinner routes profitably and can open new direct connections without the risk of larger, less efficient aircraft.

In plain terms, “thinner routes” are those with fewer passengers per day—too many for a small turboprop to handle economically, but not enough to fill a larger single-aisle jet. Aircraft like the ERJ 145 and E170/E175 are built specifically to bridge that gap, making it possible to offer daily flights where demand would otherwise not justify the service.

Investing in smaller jets could enable the airline to increase frequencies on domestic and regional routes, improving connectivity for business and leisure travelers.

A modernized fleet may also lower maintenance and fuel costs over time, potentially leading to more competitive fares.

It is worth noting that the reported per-unit prices likely reflect used-aircraft market values rather than new factory deliveries. Both the ERJ 145 and the original E-Jet family have been in service for years, and a healthy secondary market exists for well-maintained examples. This approach can lower upfront costs considerably, though it also raises questions about remaining airframe life and long-term maintenance planning.

What It Means for Expats and Investors

For expatriates in Namibia and neighboring countries, a larger and more modern regional fleet could translate to more flexible travel options and better connections to hubs like Johannesburg or Cape Town.

Investors in Namibia’s tourism and business sectors could benefit from improved air access, which often stimulates economic activity and property markets in well-connected regions.

However, until the deal is finalized and delivery timelines are known, the immediate impact remains speculative.

Background

Namibia Air is the national airline, operating domestic and regional services. It has faced fleet and operational challenges in recent years, making a renewal plan a critical step for its long-term viability.

Regional aviation in Southern Africa is highly competitive, with carriers like Airlink and CemAir also operating Embraer jets. A modern fleet is essential to remain relevant.

The airline’s choice of Embraer aircraft aligns with a trend among African carriers to adopt smaller, more efficient jets for thin routes.

Embraer, a Brazilian aerospace manufacturer, has long seen Africa as a natural market for its regional jets. The continent’s vast distances, combined with uneven passenger demand between city pairs, make the 70-to-90-seat segment particularly relevant. A potential Namibia Air order would add to Embraer’s existing footprint in the region.

Unconfirmed Deal Status

Crucially, the sources available do not specify whether the fleet plan is a firm purchase order, a memorandum of understanding, a letter of intent, or simply a long-term strategy.

Neither Namibia Air nor Embraer has issued an official statement confirming the deal, as of this reporting. The figures cited come from secondary reports and should be treated as preliminary.

Industry observers will look for confirmation from primary sources, such as regulatory filings or press releases, before concluding that the acquisition will proceed.

What to watch next is whether Namibia’s transport ministry or civil aviation authority references the plan in any upcoming budget statement or infrastructure briefing. Another open question is how the airline intends to finance the acquisition—whether through state backing, development-finance loans, or a leasing arrangement—and what that structure might signal about the government’s commitment to strengthening the national carrier.

What aircraft is Namibia Air planning to acquire?

The plan involves four 50-seat Embraer ERJ 145s and three larger E170/E175-family regional jets.

How much is the fleet renewal expected to cost?

Reports indicate a total cost of N$594 million, or about US$33 million, with individual aircraft priced at US$3 million (ERJ 145) and US$8 million (E170/E175).

Has Namibia Air signed a firm order with Embraer?

No, the current information does not clarify whether the plan is a firm order, a memorandum of understanding, or only a preliminary fleet strategy.

World.title: China Beef Surcharge Looms as Brazil Nears Quota Limit
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts —Quota threshold. Brazil’s 2026 beef export quota to China is 1.106 million tonnes; above this, a 55% surcharge applies on top of the 12% tariff, totaling 67%. —JBS vacation. JBS’s Campo Grande unit began a 15-day collective vacation on July 21, affecting over 2,000 workers, to cope with high cattle prices. —Iguatemi slowdown. Iguatemi Beef reportedly implemented collective vacations in Iguatemi, with unconfirmed reports of around 90 workers affected. —Quota used. Brazil had already used 80% of its 2026 beef quota to China when Beijing alerted the market on July 21. —JBS strategy. JBS said the move will cut costs and that it will reroute beef volumes to alternative export markets.

Brazilian meatpackers Iguatemi Beef and JBS have curtailed slaughtering at plants in Mato Grosso do Sul as Brazil’s 2026 beef exports to China near a 1.1-million-tonne quota, triggering the risk of a combined 67% import tariff.

JBS and Iguatemi Beef plants in Mato Grosso do Sul are slowing production as the China beef quota nears its limit.

China Quota and the Tariff Wall

Brazil operates under a 2026 beef export quota to China of 1.106 million tonnes. Once this volume is shipped, any additional beef faces an extra 55% surcharge, bringing the total import tax to 67% when added to the standard 12% tariff.

By late July, the Brazilian industry had used roughly 80% of that quota. China reportedly informed the market on July 21 that the threshold was near, raising alarms among exporters.

This quota mechanism is designed to protect Chinese domestic producers, but it can severely disrupt Brazil’s largest beef export channel, forcing processors to pull back to avoid uncompetitive shipments.

JBS Halts Slaughter in Campo Grande

JBS’s large beef plant on the Sidrolândia exit in Campo Grande, which employs more than 2,000 workers, began a 15-day collective vacation starting Tuesday, July 21.

The company told local media that the reduction in slaughter was a cost-management measure during a period of high live cattle prices and weaker demand. JBS said it would reallocate production volumes to other markets to cushion the impact.

The plant’s temporary halt is one of the most visible signs of the quota squeeze, as JBS typically runs multiple shifts and exports heavily to China.

Iguatemi Beef Slows Operations

In the town of Iguatemi, also in Mato Grosso do Sul, Iguatemi Beef implemented collective vacations or a production slowdown, according to local press reports.

The mayor of Iguatemi mentioned that about 90 workers were dismissed, but the company has not confirmed any layoffs. The exact nature and duration of the workforce adjustment remain unclear.

This uncertainty underscores how quickly the quota threat can cascade into local employment decisions, even when the full surcharge has not yet been triggered.

Industry and Union Response

The meatpacking workers’ union Sicadems confirmed to local media that vacation and slowdown measures were being taken in Mato Grosso do Sul.

Union president Régis Comarella explained that if the quota is exceeded, a 55% surcharge would apply on top of the existing 12% tariff, making it impractical for plants to ship beef to China.

Meanwhile, no detailed public statement has emerged from Iguatemi Beef, and JBS’s official line emphasizes cost control rather than the quota directly.

What It Means for Expats and Investors

For investors, the quota crunch highlights the vulnerability of Brazil’s meat sector to Chinese trade policy. JBS shares (listed as JBSS3 on B3 and as a global ADR) could see short-term volatility if the quota is fully exhausted and plants remain idle.

Expats living in Brazil may observe indirect effects: if Brazilian beef producers divert volumes to the domestic market to offset lost Chinese sales, local meat prices could stabilise or even dip slightly, though cattle prices currently remain high.

Longer term, Brazil’s reliance on China as the buyer of roughly 60% of its beef exports is a strategic risk. Ongoing talks about quota expansion or bilateral agreements will be critical for the industry’s stability.

For those in Mato Grosso do Sul, the temporary plant closures may strain local economies that depend on packinghouse wages, even if the moves are short-lived.

Background: Brazil-China Beef Trade

China is Brazil’s largest beef export destination, accounting for over half of all shipments in value terms. The annual quota was introduced to manage import volumes and protect Chinese farmers from a flood of foreign meat.

Brazil’s beef sector has grown rapidly on the back of Chinese demand, with plants across the country upgrading facilities to meet Chinese sanitary standards. When the quota nears exhaustion, it creates a waiting game: shippers must decide whether to risk the surcharge or hold back.

The surcharge makes Brazilian beef significantly more expensive for Chinese buyers, who can switch to other suppliers like Argentina or Australia. This seasonal quota squeeze has become a recurring feature of the trade relationship.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are Brazilian beef plants shutting down?

They are reducing slaughter to avoid shipping beef to China after the 1.106-million-tonne 2026 quota is exhausted, which would trigger a 67% total import tax, making it commercially unviable.

How does the Chinese beef quota work?

Brazil has an annual quota of 1.106 million tonnes. Once that volume is reached, any additional beef exported to China faces an extra 55% surcharge on top of the standard 12% tariff, totaling 67%.

Will this affect beef prices in Brazil?

Possibly. If plants pivot to selling more beef domestically to offset lost Chinese sales, local supply could increase, potentially stabilising or lowering retail prices, though high cattle costs may limit the drop.

World.title: Brazil’s Banco do Brasil Settles $1.86 Billion in Desenrola 2.0
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts —Renegotiation total. Banco do Brasil renegotiated R$10.4 billion in overdue debts since the launch of Novo Desenrola in May 2026. —Program name. The debt relief is provided under the government’s Novo Desenrola Brasil program, also called Desenrola 2.0. —Eligible borrowers. The program covers individuals, businesses, rural producers, and students with FIES loans. —Discount and terms. It offers 30–90% discounts, up to 48-month terms, and a maximum interest rate of 1.99% per month. —Dollar equivalent. R$10.4 billion equals approximately US$1.86 billion at an exchange rate of R$5.60 per US dollar.

Banco do Brasil has renegotiated R$10.4 billion (US$1.86 billion) in overdue debts for individuals, businesses, farmers, and students under the government’s Novo Desenrola Brasil program since its launch in May 2026, offering deep discounts and extended terms.

A key new feature of Desenrola 2.0 lets Brazilians use part of their FGTS savings to help pay off renegotiated debts.

The R$10.4 Billion Renegotiation Package

The state-owned giant Banco do Brasil reported R$10.4 billion in debt renegotiations under the Novo Desenrola (Desenrola 2.0) program. The figure reflects agreements reached since the program’s launch in May 2026, the bank said.

The total covers a broad range of overdue obligations: personal debts, business loans, rural producer financing, and student loans from the FIES program. The bank did not disclose the total number of clients or contracts tied to this specific sum.

For context, Banco do Brasil is one of Latin America’s largest financial institutions by assets and plays a central role in federal credit policy. Its participation in Desenrola 2.0 carries weight because it reaches millions of account holders across the country, including in remote areas where other banks have a lighter footprint.

How Desenrola 2.0 Works

Novo Desenrola Brasil targets individuals earning up to five minimum wages per month. Eligible debts include credit card balances, overdraft facilities, and personal loans that were in default.

Under the program, banks offer discounts between 30% and 90% on the original debt. Repayment can stretch over 48 months with interest capped at 1.99% per month—well below typical consumer lending rates in Brazil.

A key feature of the new phase is that debtors can use part of their FGTS (employee severance fund) to reduce the amount owed, making it easier to settle large balances.

The FGTS is a mandatory savings account that employers fund with 8% of a worker’s monthly salary. Brazilians can typically access it only in specific situations, such as being fired without cause, buying a home, or serious illness. Allowing its use for debt repayment is a significant policy shift, because it taps into locked savings that many workers already have but could not previously touch for this purpose.
