World.title: China’s Summer Hit Recasts the Eight Immortals as Con Artists
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018801/China’s Summer Hit Recasts the Eight Immortals as Con Artists
World.content:
Before they were immortals, they were scammers.

That’s the irreverent premise behind “All Wishes Come True!,” a new Chinese animated comedy that has turned a band of mythological figures from Taoist legend into a summer box-office hit.

Released July 18, the film recasts the Eight Immortals — traditionally symbols of people from all walks of life — as con artists who impersonate gods and deceive worshippers before achieving immortality themselves.

In less than a week, the film has grossed more than 370 million yuan ($51 million), becoming the second highest-grossing domestic animated film of 2026 behind “Boonie Bears: The Hidden Protector.” It also holds an 8.3 rating on Chinese review site Douban, the highest among this summer’s new releases.

The film’s biggest twist unfolds in Penglai, a fairyland where gods and humans coexist under a surprisingly modern bureaucracy governed by an immortals management bureau. Deities are assigned temples, evaluated on performance targets, and ranked on giant leaderboards based on the incense offerings they receive.

Unlike traditional tales of the Eight Immortals’ journey toward enlightenment, the film gives the legendary figures a new beginning: they first appear as schemers targeting the riches of Fu, Lu, and Shou, the three deities of fortune, prosperity, and longevity.

Zhongli Quan, traditionally portrayed as a general who became a Taoist immortal, is reimagined as a con artist who leads the group in impersonating deities. Cao Guojiu, traditionally linked to the Song dynasty (960–1279) imperial court, appears as an official in the immortals management bureau.

After taking over a temple, the group finds itself responsible for granting wishes — and eventually becomes known for catching thieves. Their journey later leads to a clash with the war god Yang Jian.

Director Mu Zhengyang said he designed Penglai as a “first-tier megacity,” where gods and humans operate within a modern social system. “At first, audiences should feel that they’re entering a traditional Eastern fairyland. But once inside, it becomes much more like an amusement park,” he told domestic media.

The film’s character-driven approach also extends to its voice performances. Voice director Chen Hao, who worked on the popular “Ne Zha” films, voices Zhongli Quan, while Tieguai Li’s Chongqing dialect adds regional flavor to the character.

The film’s cultural references have also fueled online discussion. On streaming platform Bilibili, videos decoding more than 100 Easter eggs and hidden details have each attracted nearly one million views.

One widely discussed clue is the Eight Immortals’ temple number — 1350, the same number associated with Sun Wukong, better known as the Monkey King, in the “Book of Life and Death,” a mythical register of the underworld in “Journey to the West,” hinting at his possible appearance later in the story.

The same reinterpretation has also drawn criticism from some viewers, who argue that the film alters the identities and values associated with traditional mythology.

Yang Jian, for example, traditionally portrayed as a righteous war god who protects ordinary people, is reimagined as a figure willing to sacrifice heaven and humanity to save his mother. The film’s other redesigns have also drawn attention, including Cao Guojiu’s portrayal as an overweight, flamboyant official and Lan Caihe’s depiction as a toddler.

The debate also extends to the film’s portrayal of immortality. Through the line, “Only immortals can do good deeds,” it offers a new interpretation that some viewers praised, while others argued it differs from traditional Taoist ideas of attaining eternal life.

The production team, based in southwestern China’s Sichuan province, said the Eight Immortals offer creative space for reinterpretation because many audiences know their famous stories but are less familiar with their broader legends. The filmmakers said they hoped to introduce the figures to a new generation through a fresh retelling.

“We didn’t want to simply bring the Eight Immortals in front of young audiences and tell the same story again,” producer Ying Xujun told domestic media. “We had to create something new for a new generation.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A poster for “All Wishes Come True!” From Douban)

World.title: At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018802/At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.content:
This year’s World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai was larger, more crowded, and more politically prominent than in previous editions.

President Xi Jinping attended the event for the first time, while more than 1,100 companies showcased computing systems, AI agents, robots, and other products aimed at workplaces, factories, and consumers. In-person visits topped 400,000, and tickets were reportedly resold for more than 1,000 yuan.

Xi called for wider access to open-source AI, and China launched a 29-country AI cooperation body, placing issues of governance, access, and international coordination alongside the usual displays of commercial technology.

Beyond the speeches and packed exhibition halls, the most revealing conversations were practical: lowering computing costs, putting AI agents to work, managing new safety risks, and building businesses that can last.

Here are four takeaways from this year’s WAIC.

Computing power gets practical

Computing power was one of the most discussed topics at this year’s WAIC, second only to AI applications by number of related forums. But the focus moved beyond building more data centers or training ever-larger models.

Two questions dominated: what the next generation of computing power might look like, and how to make today’s resources cheaper and more efficient.

At one flagship forum on the future of computing, scientists discussed emerging approaches including quantum computing and space-based computing. Among the speakers was Pan Jianwei, a leading quantum physicist and recent recipient of a top United Nations science award, who outlined recent advances in the field.

Pan also urged caution. Although the field has reached a series of important milestones, he said, building a general-purpose quantum computer capable of quickly solving problems with clear practical value will still require years of sustained research. The academic community, he added, has a responsibility to help the public assess the technology realistically and guard against an industry bubble.

Companies also seemed more focused on improving the efficiency of existing computing resources and reducing the cost of each AI query.

Some were working to improve the performance of models trained mainly on Nvidia chips when deployed on Chinese chips. Others focused on allocating and managing computing resources more efficiently.

Rather than chasing only the most powerful and expensive models, many Chinese AI companies appeared more concerned with making AI cheaper to run.

AI Governance and Safety

AI governance and safety were prominent throughout this year’s WAIC, from high-level forums to the opening ceremony and President Xi Jinping’s speech.

Brian Tse, an AI safety expert and founder and CEO of Concordia AI, said he has seen more discussion in China around cybersecurity and the protection of critical infrastructure, especially the risks posed by frontier AI models.

“The threat landscape is evolving rapidly,” Tse said. “Many experts at the forums expressed concern that threats and potential misuse are developing faster than society’s current defenses.”

The concerns also appeared to be shifting beyond large language models and the harmful content they can generate. More attention was paid this year to the risks posed by autonomous AI agents, which can plan tasks, make decisions, and interact with other tools.

On July 15, just before WAIC, China’s new rules on AI anthropomorphic interaction took effect, targeting services that simulate human personalities and sustained emotional interaction. The rules prohibit providers from offering virtual partners or relatives to minors and bar services from inducing emotional dependence or addiction.

In May, regulators also released guidance on the standardized application and development of AI agents, including plans to explore digital identity management for them.

“China is positioning itself as an architect of multilateral AI governance,” Tse said.

AI lands at work

One phrase heard often at this year’s WAIC was AI’s real-world “landing” — the push to move the technology out of demos and into everyday work. Companies ranging from Tencent and Alibaba to smaller startups showed AI products aimed at offices, factories, and consumer services. AI agents were among the most visible examples.

At booths run by major tech firms, exhibitors demonstrated how agents could be built into corporate workflows, from searching internal documents to generating reports and coordinating routine tasks.

The impact could be broad because many of these companies’ software systems are already embedded in Chinese workplaces. Adding AI agents to existing platforms may prove easier than persuading companies to adopt entirely new tools.

Still, genuinely effective applications appeared limited. Office productivity remained the most obvious use case, while other areas were less developed.

Robotics and embodied AI occupied an entire floor at this year’s WAIC. Visitors could still see robots performing awkward dances or taking six minutes to make a cup of tea. But some companies were beginning to move beyond staged demonstrations, showing robots designed for inspection, manufacturing, logistics, and other industrial uses.

The founder rush

Some of the most revealing conversations at this year’s WAIC took place after the official sessions ended.

Across after-hours gatherings, private meetups, and open-mic sessions, young founders and industry professionals swapped ideas on AI agents, robotics, and productivity tools. Some gatherings ran late into the night, with almost any topic open for discussion.

Many entrepreneurs seemed eager to absorb every new idea, experiment, business opportunity, and professional connection they could find.

But that urgency also carried risks. Some founders said their AI ventures were burning through years of savings. Many still lacked a convincing answer to a basic question: how their projects would generate lasting value and revenue.

That tension ran through WAIC: crowded halls, founders eager to share projects and failures, and a palpable fear of moving too slowly and missing the AI wave. The mood mixed optimism with anxiety, much of it fueled by the speed of the technology and the sheer volume of information surrounding it.

The conversations also suggested a maturing industry. More speakers and founders were asking not only what AI could do, but where it could be useful, how it could be governed, and which businesses could survive once the initial excitement fades.

(Header image: A humanoid robot from a Chinese robotics firm waves Chinese national flags during the 2026 WAIC in Shanghai, July 18, 2026. Ng Han Guan/AP Photo via VCG)

World.title: The Soybean That Built Northeast China
World.content:
In 2020, I traveled to Kaishantun, a town in the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture near the China-North Korea border. It fit every stereotype of the deindustrialized Northeast. Young people had left. The government had built two rows of barracks-style apartment blocks for the elderly residents who remained. Kaishantun railway station had long been abandoned. On the station sign, the space for the next stop was blank. North Korea lay only a few hundred meters away.

On the walk back, I wandered into a derelict movie theater and discovered several reels of old film. Later restored, they revealed something astonishing: clips of a symphony orchestra and a traditional folk orchestra.

What kind of small town could support two orchestras of its own?

As I dug deeper into the history of my home region, Northeast China, I found that part of the answer lay in a crop that today frequently appears in international headlines: soybeans. A century before China became a major importer of American soybeans, it was the world’s leading producer.

In August 1872, three Japanese army officers, disguised as merchants and acting on the orders of General Saigō Takamori, traveled through “Manchuria,” the term they used for Northeast China. Saigō was studying relations between Japan, Korea, and China as he prepared a future campaign against Korea. A year later, the officers submitted their “Report on an Inspection of Manchuria,” one of Japan’s earliest intelligence briefings on China. The report includes a detailed discussion of soybeans:

“From winter through spring, soybeans are continuously transported by inland waterways. Regardless of the cold, day and night, dozens of horse-drawn carts move in a single direction. Large merchants purchase the beans and pile them into circular mountains more than two rooms across and over 6 meters high … The quantity stored is beyond counting.”

In 1885, another Japanese military officer, Kikuchi Setsuzō, passed through Northeast China on his return from the Russian Empire. Along the way, he studied how Qing forces fed their military horses, which he regarded as superior to those of Japan and Russia. Qing troops processed the residue left after soybean oil extraction into pressed soybean cakes for animal feed. Each cake weighed about 12.5 kilograms and could feed three horses for a day. Kikuchi even claimed such soybean resources would be “indispensable” for training military horses.

In the 19th century, Kikuchi was among the few who grasped soybeans’ strategic significance. The crop had reached Europe and North America in the 18th century but remained largely a botanical curiosity. A handful of enthusiasts, such as the Austro-Hungarian agronomist Friedrich Haberlandt, sought to introduce soybeans into Western diets. Yet while they imported the crop, they did not import the culinary traditions that had made it a staple across Asia.

In East Asia, by contrast, people had accumulated more than a thousand years of experience cooking and consuming soybeans. They also recognized the crop’s value as animal feed. After the Meiji Restoration in 1868, Japanese rice farmers gradually abandoned traditional fish-based fertilizers in favor of soybean cake. Between 1882 and 1902, Japan’s soybean imports increased four-hundredfold.

The Russo-Japanese War of 1904–05 finally alerted the world to soybeans’ importance. European military observers noted that both sides relied heavily on the crop. Japanese forces consumed soybeans directly and used them in military logistics. Russian forces fed them to cavalry horses. Soybean oil served as a raw material for soap and as a lubricant for artillery equipment and wagon axles.

The soybean trade expanded rapidly. A 1911 report from the Customs Service in Shanghai observed that “It is only in the last three years that soya beans have become important in intercontinental commerce,” calling their rapid emergence from obscurity “one of the most remarkable commercial events of recent times.” In the same year, the U.S. ambassador in Beijing told the State Department that Northeast China had until recently been largely unknown for its commercial potential, despite supplying soybeans to global markets. He observed that its economic trajectory was now drawing attention in major cities including New York, London, Hamburg, and Seattle, and attributed this shift to soybeans, whose rapidly growing demand he characterized as “phenomenal in trade annals.”

Estimates suggest that Northeast China accounted for between 16% and 42% of global soybean production between 1908 and 1930, shipping soybeans, soybean oil, and soybean cakes to the rest of China, Japan, and Europe. Until the eve of World War II, China produced more than 80% of the world’s soybeans. The crop became widely known as the “Manchurian bean.”

Soybeans were also among the most important exports of a then largely impoverished China. After World War I, their importance grew rapidly, and by the 1920s they had overtaken tea and silk to become China’s leading export, accounting for more than 20% of export earnings.

As trade expanded, so did Japan’s territorial ambitions. In the run-up to Japan's formal annexation of Korea in 1910, Yanbian became a frontier along the China-Korea border where Chinese and Japanese spheres of influence met directly. Japanese strategists viewed the wider Yanbian area as a gateway to the interior of Northeast China and sought to build a railway linking the Korean port of Chongjin with China’s inland Northeast. General Hasegawa Yoshimichi, commander of Japanese forces in Korea, regarded Yanbian as a vital supply corridor for sustaining colonial rule on the peninsula. He advocated occupying the region to secure access to strategic commodities such as soybeans.

Over the following three decades, Japan steadily expanded its influence in Northeast China. In 1931, Japanese forces seized the region and took control of its economic resources. This expansion, justified in the name of protecting economic “lifelines,” would later extend across Asia during the Pacific War to the oil fields of Burma, Sumatra, and Borneo; the rubber plantations of Malaya; and the chromium and iron deposits of the Philippines.

In Yanbian, war and colonial rule only reinforced the region’s economic importance. Beyond soybeans, Japanese authorities coveted the region’s timber. In Kaishantun they established the Eastern Manchuria Rayon Pulp Company, whose output eventually surpassed that of most producers in Japan. After the Chinese Communist Party won the civil war and founded the People’s Republic of China in 1949, the new state’s flagship pulp and paper enterprise was established in the same town.

Factories brought more than jobs. They brought hospitals, movie theaters, and even symphony orchestras.

Yet by then Northeast China was no longer the sole center of the global soybean trade. By the early 20th century, American farmers were already familiar with soybeans, using them to replenish soil and support other crops. After the Russo-Japanese War, however, the crop’s industrial potential attracted growing attention.

One unlikely champion was Henry Ford. He used soybean protein and soybean-oil derivatives in automotive components and in 1941 unveiled a prototype car with body panels made largely from soybean-based plastic. To demonstrate its strength, he famously struck it with an axe.

Ford’s soybean car was hardly a commercial success, but it generated publicity for the crop. When Japan severed America’s access to Asian supply routes during the Pacific War, soybeans were transformed from an industrial curiosity into a strategic resource. Combined harvesters and advances in plant breeding helped American farmers scale up production.

By the 1950s, the center of gravity in soybean production had shifted decisively to the Americas.

One final piece was still missing from the modern soybean map: Brazil. In the early 1970s, a major El Niño event, a climate pattern that warms the Pacific Ocean, devastated the Peruvian anchoveta fishery, a key source of animal feed, driving demand for soybean meal. Prices surged, and in 1973 the Nixon administration imposed restrictions on soybean exports.

History then took an ironic turn. Japan, heavily dependent on imported American soybeans, increased its investment in South American agriculture, while Brazil’s agricultural research agency, Embrapa, developed soybean varieties suited to tropical conditions. The result was a dramatic expansion of Brazilian production.

In 2024, more than 70% of China’s soybean imports came from Brazil. When trade tensions between China and the United States intensified in 2025, Brazil became China’s principal alternative for former U.S. suppliers.

Northeast China remains the country’s most important soybean-growing region, producing the beans that become tofu and soy milk on Chinese tables. But it no longer supplies the world with soybean oil and soybean meal. Once-thriving industrial towns have been swept up in the tide of deindustrialization, leaving behind abandoned railway stations and empty movie theaters.

From an unassuming plant in Northeast China to one of the world’s most traded agricultural commodities, the soybean’s history is ultimately a story of globalization. A soybean harvested in Paraguay may be processed in Argentina, sold to China by a trading house in Geneva, and eventually find its way into milk, cakes, or meat products. It shapes what we eat, how we farm, and how nations interact with one another. It also shapes the fate of countless small towns, including places like Kaishantun.

(Header image: A soybean field in Xingkai Lake Farm, Heilongjiang province, 2023. VCG)

World.title: Ilocos Norte students turn ‘Bangsak’ into battle royale video game
World.content:
The game’s pixel art is inspired by the cities of Batac and Laoag, the capital of Ilocos Norte

Before graduating from college, four students from the Mariano Marcos State University (MMSU) reinvented a traditional Filipino street game as a multiplayer battle royale video game.

MMSU College of Computing and Information Sciences students Clinton Wayne Visaya, Jansen Espiritu Baloaloa, Gabriel Jerickson Galapin, and Michael Ryann Luen Velasco — collectively known as Mangken Studios — presented their game, BangSak: Water Rising, at the Level Up 2.0: Esports GameDev Challenge during the 2026 ALT+TAB Festival, held on June 20 and 21.

Representing the Ilocos Region, the winning entry from Region I was among the featured titles at the Department of Science and Technology (DOST) Pavilion, where visitors experienced locally developed independent video games.

From the streets to the screen

Bangsak, which the game took inspiration from, is a traditional Filipino hide-and-seek street game. The name comes from the sound of a gun (bang) and pretending to stab (saksak). In this variation of hide-and-seek, the seeker must also shout “bang” and the name of the hider to capture them, while the hider must say “sak” to save the lives of captured players.

While BangSak: Water Rising follows the general rules of the street game, there is an added twist to make the game more interesting: they turned the game into a battle royale.

A battle royale pertains to a competition with multiple combatants, and victory is typically decided when there is only one person or team standing. In video games, to force players to engage with each other, the “safe zone” on the map continuously shrinks.

In BangSak: Water Rising, the game developers shrank the map by adding rising floods because, according to game designer and developer Clinton Visaya, flooding was the most prominent disaster during the game’s development.

“Main inspiration namin ang flood-control projects. ‘Yung game map, may mga sira-sirang tubo at umuulan, so unti-unti siyang bumabaha at ‘yung drainage pipes ay hindi gumagana,” Visaya said.

(The flood-control projects were our main inspiration. The game map has broken pipes, and it’s raining, so it slowly floods because the drainage pipes don’t work.)

Several politicians and officials from the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) are under investigation for alleged anomalous and substandard flood-control projects, which led to nationwide protests to call for accountability from the government.

Meanwhile, the game’s pixel art is inspired by the cities of Batac and Laoag, the capital of Ilocos Norte.

“Sa pag-create ko ng characters, nag-base ako sa typical na uso rito sa Ilocos. At since malapit lang naman ‘yung Batac sa amin dito, tinitingnan ko ‘yung mga outfit ng mga tao kung ano ang swak sa character,” lead artist Gabriel Jerickson Galapin said.

(In the creation of the characters, I based it on what is trending here in Ilocos. And because we are close to Batac, I looked at the people’s outfits and looked at whether they fit the character.)

“Sa pag-design ko ng environment ng game, ‘yung mga buildings and mga trees ay nag-base lang din sa Laoag. Bumisita ako doon sa mga certain places at tiningnan ‘yung colors at structures ng buildings,” he added.

(In the design of the game environment, the buildings and the trees were based on Laoag. I visited certain places and looked at the colors and the structures of the buildings.)

First and last competition win

The team shared that this was not their first competition. Their previous game development challenge landed them in fourth place, which the team said lowered their morale.

“Napakasakit po sa amin na tanggapin noon na hindi kami nanalo,” Visaya said. (It was very painful for us to accept that we didn’t win.)

However, this only motivated them to continue improving until, finally, in their last year in college, they became a finalist.

“Sobrang ecstatic and surreal kasi hindi namin naakala na ‘yung simpleng game namin is ma-award ng ganoong prestige,” Visaya added.

(It felt so ecstatic and surreal for us because we didn’t think that our simple game would be given that kind of prestige.)

Meanwhile, Eloihim Baculpo, MMSU instructor and the BangSak game development team’s mentor, said it was a proud moment for him to see his students break their “fourth-place curse.”

“Every time they have a competition, they always choose me to guide them. When they won, it was a really proud moment and emotional moment for me, because these fresh graduates deserved to win on their very last competition,” Baculpo said.

Keeping tradition alive

According to Jansen Baloaloa, the game’s lead developer, the team chose Bangsak not only for its simple mechanics, but also because they had fond memories of playing the street game as children.

“It has a practical aspect, as well as an emotional aspect, during the development of the game,” Baloaloa said.

The team also credited their vision to recreate Bangsak to remind the youth of traditional Filipino street games.

“Ang end-goal namin ay to spread awareness sa mga cultural games ng mga Pilipino,” Visaya said. (Our end-goal is to spread awareness of Filipino cultural games.)

“It also serves as our hope for it to act as a preservation of our traditional games. We hope that children will play these games again even in the future because there’s still a trace of it in the games in a digital format,” Baloaloa said.

Furthermore, the team hoped that their award-winning game would show that the Philippines has its own creative video game developers.

“We have creative Pinoys and creative games,” Visaya said.

BangSak: Water Rising, which is still in development, is planned to be released on Steam, a digital distribution platform for PC games. – Rappler.com

Jose Emmanuel Thayer is a fourth-year BA Communication student at the University of the Philippines Baguio and an alumnus of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2025.

World.title: Beyond the jersey: Erica Legaspi builds pathway for Filipina rugby
World.content:
Erica Legaspi helps create a global community that offers mixed-race and overseas Filipinas a way to reconnect with their heritage through the sport of rugby

“What am I doing?” It’s a question Erica Legaspi sometimes asks herself during the three-hour round trip home from rugby training.

A member of the Philippine women’s rugby team, Legaspi already has enough on her plate as an athlete. Yet alongside training and competition, she has spent the last several years helping build something much larger than herself.

As a co-founder of the Magandaquins, Legaspi has spent years building a community that offers mixed-race and overseas Filipinas a way to reconnect with their heritage through sport. The name combines the Tagalog word “maganda” (beautiful) with rugby terminology, reflecting the program’s Filipina roots. What began as an effort to bring people together has since evolved into a support system, a legitimate pathway to the national team, and even a family.

Before helping other Filipinas find their place through rugby, Legaspi was navigating her own identity as a Filipino-American. Born and raised in the United States to parents who immigrated from the Philippines, she was primarily raised by her mother and longed for the sense of community she imagined came with her heritage.

Playing rugby since 2007, Erica tried out for the Philippine Volcanoes in 2019 through a Facebook recruitment post. Her quest to explore her untapped physical and competitive potential eventually became an unexpected bridge to her Filipino roots.

Legaspi suddenly found herself surrounded by a community of other Filipinos she had long been searching for. “It sounds cheesy, but I am so proud to be Filipino,” Legaspi said. “I loved being on a team with that many other Filipinos. I’d never had that experience before.”

PODIUM. Erica Legaspi (fourth from right) and the Philippine women’s rugby team celebrate during the 2019 Southeast Asian Games after bagging the silver medal. Photo courtesy of the Philippine Rugby Football Union

The experience stayed with her. For the first time, Legaspi felt connected to a community of Filipinos who shared both her heritage and passion for rugby.

But she soon realized many other Filipina players living abroad did not have the same opportunity. While the Philippine national team provided a pathway for a select group of athletes, there was no dedicated space where diaspora and mixed-race Filipinas could connect with one another, explore their heritage, and learn more about opportunities in Philippine rugby.

Together with fellow players Lauryn Nazareno, Lora Mateo, and Vanessa Cifuentes, Legaspi helped launch the Magandaquins, creating a community where Filipinas from North America could find that connection through the sport.

FOUNDERS. Erica Legaspi (from left) Lauryn Nazareno, Vanessa Cifuentes, and Lora Mateo co-founded Magandaquins, an international Filipina-heritage rugby program which has since grown into a global community and pathway to the Philippine women’s rugby team. Photo courtesy of Erica Legaspi

A small effort among a handful of players has since expanded far beyond what its founders originally envisioned. Since its founding, the Magandaquins has grown into an international Filipina-heritage rugby program with more than 50 registered players across four continents. The roster includes players from the United States, Canada, Australia, Hong Kong, and the Philippines.

Eighteen players from the North American chapter have earned official caps for the Volcanoes after coming through the Magandaquins system. While members train locally through regional chapters, they come together throughout the year for international tournaments and rugby festivals.

CHAMPS. Magandaquins players Patricia Mandon, Lora Mateo, Vanessa Cifuentes, and Lauryn Nazareno celebrate after winning gold at the Asia Rugby Trophy Series. Photo courtesy of the Magandaquins Facebook page

As interest in the Magandaquins grew, Legaspi began hearing from players who wanted to learn more about their Filipino heritage, explore opportunities in rugby, or simply find a community of women who shared similar experiences.

“We started asking people why they wanted to be involved and what their connection to the Philippines was,” Legaspi said.

For Legaspi, some of the clearest signs of the Magandaquins’ impact came away from the rugby field.

After suffering a serious knee injury herself in 2023, she was asked to reach out to another player whose rugby future suddenly seemed uncertain. “Someone was like, ‘Hey, you should reach out to this girl because I think her career might be over for rugby, or at least she’s not doing well mentally,'” Legaspi recalled.

The conversations began with rehabilitation and recovery. Legaspi shared her own experience navigating months away from the sport and the emotional toll that came with it. “There are a lot of dark days and you have to just push through each and every one of them,” she said.

Over time, the relationship grew beyond rugby. They exchanged recommendations for books and television shows and continued talking even after the player returned to competition.

Legaspi said it was one of the moments that confirmed the Magandaquins had become more than a rugby program. “Just to be able to be there for her felt very impactful because I wouldn’t have met her if it wasn’t for the Magandaquins,” she shared.

HAPPY TUMMY. Erica Legaspi (right most) and her Magandaquins teammates have built a strong bond off the field.

Maintaining an international community spread across four continents requires constant work behind the scenes. Aside from her responsibilities as a national team athlete, Legaspi helps coordinate community activities, connect with players from different countries, and think about how the organization can continue to grow.

Combined with training and work, the schedule can be difficult to manage. “Do I get enough sleep? No,” she said with a laugh. The commitment also comes with financial sacrifices. Like many rugby players, Legaspi often shoulders the costs of travel, accommodations, and training.

“You have to pay to get over to the Philippines, and when you’re not in the camp itself, you pay for your accommodations as well,” she said.

What surprised Legaspi most was how much the experience changed her. “I think it’s built more of my confidence in being able to lead others,” she said. “For the most part, I like to be a background player.”

Running the Magandaquins forced her to step into a leadership role she never expected to occupy. “It’s given me a large sense of pride in terms of knowing that I can help give a voice to others, not even just Filipino women, but even Asian women in rugby,” she said.

The experience opened doors beyond the Magandaquins. Legaspi later volunteered as a team liaison officer for the USA Women’s rugby team, a stint that gave her a behind-the-scenes look at how elite programs operate.

“I don’t think I would have had the confidence to even put my name to be a volunteer for these things if it weren’t for Magandaquins in general,” she said. “It’s like you can take control. You can be a leader.”

“But at the end of the day, I have to realize this isn’t for me in terms of these opportunities,” Legaspi said. “These are for other people.”

Asked what she hopes younger Filipino athletes take away from her story, her answer was simple: “That they can do it too, and they can even do it better.”

SQUAD. Members of the Magandaquins, including co-founder Erica Legaspi (left most, top row), gather for a group photo.

Acknowledging that the Magandaquins has grown beyond its founders, she hopes more players will eventually step into leadership roles of their own.

“To be able to do something and create a stronger foundation for others to get into these roles and lead other women is what I’d love to see this program do,” she said. “I am very proud to be a part of it, but it is not my program. I want other people to feel empowered to want to do the work as well.”

For Legaspi, the goal was never simply to build a rugby program. It was to make sure other Filipinas could find the same sense of belonging she once spent years searching for. “If I said my goal was to leave the jersey in a better place than where I found it, I need to do this work,” she said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Pax Silica, El Niño: Environmental issues for SONA 2026
World.content:
From landfill crises to water supply concerns surrounding Pax Silica, which environmental issue do you think should be mentioned in this year's SONA?

MANILA, Philippines – President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ended his SONA last year with a bang: the crackdown on corruption surrounding flood control projects.

What followed were investigations into corruption in the highest echelons of government, the uncovering of scandalous wealth and contractor ties, public condemnation, and the death of a former Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) official.

That all started with an environmental issue: Infrastructure — dikes, pumping stations, retaining walls — that have failed to keep communities safe from floods. Worse, many were even ghost projects.

What are the major environmental and climate concerns of the country today? We made a rundown of the environmental issues that warrant being mentioned in Marcos’ fifth State of the Nation Address (SONA) on Monday, July 27.

Landfill crises: The advent of waste-to-energy?

The first half of 2026 was marked by consecutive landfill incidents: in Binaliw, Cebu City; Rodriguez, Rizal; and Davao City. Several people were killed. A fire erupted in the closed Navotas landfill that led to the evacuation of people in parts of Bulacan.

The landfill crisis even spilled over to political bickering. The closure of the landfill in Davao City caused a spat between Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte and the Palace.

Groups raised alarm over waste pickers’ safety, and called for better implementation of the solid waste management law to prevent more trash slides.

TRASH SLIDE. A drone shot of the Binaliw landfill in Cebu City shows a collapsed structure at the foot of the landfill. Photo by Jacqueline Hernandez/Rappler

In light of these incidents, many environmentalists have expressed caution on waste-to-energy projects as the solution to these landfill incidents.

The Department of Energy has resumed the auction for waste-to-energy projects under its Green Energy Program. We know of at least two companies applying for an environmental compliance certificate for waste-to-energy projects.

How will Marcos address the crisis in waste management? Will he trumpet the waste-to-energy agenda in his SONA?

El Niño and food supply

Still coping with the impacts of the Middle East conflict and high oil prices, farmers and fisherfolk are bracing for the El Niño expected to peak in November.

The El Niño will affect not just livelihoods but food production and supply as well. Fuel and fertilizer prices have eased but remain elevated and at risk of rising again due to renewed conflict between the US and Iran.

Agriculture chief Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. had directed his agency to “fast-track irrigation, water impounding and other climate adaptation projects” before the dry spell hits.

The Philippines suffered a lot in the 2024 El Niño, with a production loss worth P57.8 billion. Will the country be better prepared this year and the next?

Pax Silica and water woes

On April 16, the Philippines joined the Pax Silica – the United States’ initiative to grow supply chains for the artificial intelligence era. Under this initiative, the Philippines is set to build a 4,000-acre industrial hub in New Clark City. The country is being eyed for its reserves of nickel, copper, chromite, and cobalt.

What’s the primary reason for outcry over Pax Silica? The threat of water insecurity as data centers require millions of gallons of water for cooling systems that computer servers need.

Bases Conversion and Development Authority President and CEO Joshua Bingcang assured the public in a Palace briefing on Thursday, July 23 that the project will have its own water supply and will not encroach on the local community’s sources.

There are alternatives for the hub, according to Bingcang: surface water harvesting, storage, treatment, and recycling. Bingcang said they plan to establish water impounding areas as well.

“At kung may surplus kami, pwede pa namin i-share ito sa community around,” Bingcang said. (And if we have surplus, we can even share this to the communities around.)

Play Video

The hub at New Clark City is set to host mineral processing and semiconductor fabrication industries.

Those opposed to the project claim negative impacts on farmers and Aeta communities such as diverting water from locals. In militant group Bagong Alyansang Makabayan’s opposition to the project, they said the Philippines will become a “forward operating base in an economic and technological war” that the United States is waging against China.

Similarly, Akbayan Party is calling for a probe on whether the data centers and other parts of the hub will “place unsustainable demands on our country’s electricity and water resources” and impose unjust costs on host communities.

Delayed submission of climate targets

The Philippines has yet to submit its revised climate targets to the United Nations, more than a year past deadline.

Parties to the Paris Agreement submit Nationally Determined Contributions (or NDCs) – the emission reduction targets that countries assign themselves.

Submission and implementation of these targets are part of the collective effort to reduce emissions and save the planet from the climate crisis.

Opposition to mining in biodiverse areas

Recently, locals from Sibuyan Island, Romblon, sounded the alarm on planned mining activities of Altai Philippines Mining Corporation after the company secured an endorsement from a local council.

Sibuyanons have started a petition urging Marcos, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources, and the local government to stop the mining project.

There is mining opposition in Palawan province as well. In Brooke’s Point, residents put up a community barricade to protest the activities of Calmia Nickel Incorporated.

Mining cobalt, lithium, nickel, among others, positions the Philippines in the global supply chain of critical minerals for the renewable energy shift. But many locals and clean energy advocates cite the constitutional right to a balanced and healthful ecology and their call for a just energy transition.

RALLY. Environmental groups along with human rights, indigenous peoples and faith-based organizations, hold a protest in front of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources in Quezon City on March 4, 2024, to commemorate the 29th anniversary of the Philippine Mining Act of 1995. Photo by Jire Carreon/Rappler

Flood control scandal, of course

If the President wants a good narrative in his SONA, he can pick up where he left off: the flood control controversy he set in motion last year.

Flood control corruption is at the top of issues that Filipinos want to hear about in Marcos’ fifth SONA, according to recent Pulse Asia survey. The latest development? The Office of the Ombudsman found the President’s cousin, former House speaker Martin Romualdez, the “central figure” in the scandal. Romualdez’ camp belied the accusation.

Beyond accountability however, questions remain on the what flood control measures the country really needs. Environmentalists are demanding a shift in the government’s approach to disaster risk reduction.

Experts and advocates have been recommending more investments on green solutions to mitigate flood: regeneration of watershed ecosystems, and preservation of mangrove forests and wetlands.

Are there issues in your province or locality that should merit more attention from the national government? Let us know in the Environment and Science channel of the Rappler Communities. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Two Pronged] My ex may become my future boss?
World.content:
Our letter-sender is eager to work as a fitness instructor in Dubai, but is worried as her ex is also working in the same fitness center, and he would be her boss if she took the job

Rappler’s People section runs an advice column by couple Jeremy Baer and clinical psychologist Dr. Margarita Holmes.

Jeremy has a master’s degree in law from Oxford University. A banker of 37 years who worked in three continents, he has been training with Dr. Holmes for the last 10 years as co-lecturer and, occasionally, as co-therapist, especially with clients whose financial concerns intrude into their daily lives.

Together, they have written two books: Love Triangles: Understanding the Macho-Mistress Mentality and Imported Love: Filipino-Foreign Liaisons.

Dear Dr Holmes and Mr Baer,

I am a fitness instructor at the best fitness chain in the country. I have been doing this for many years. My sister, who just came back from Dubai after working there for five years as a fitness trainer herself, asked

me to take her place. She said the people she worked with and her bosses were very nice. I also know the pay is so much higher than I could get here, even after working for 10+ years.

I was eager to go since money is getting so difficult to earn in the Philippines. But then I discovered that my ex is also working in the same fitness center my sister worked at. He would be my boss there.

My ex and I did not break up well. I was the reason. Being young and immature, I did not want to end the relationship. I was very angry about our break up and behaved in a manner a lady would not have done. I am ashamed because he did not deserve such treatment.

He is now happily married, with one child. My sister says this should not stop me from going.

What do you think?

– Allyson

Dear Allyson,

It seems that you have weighed the pros and cons of working abroad, such as the better pay versus the absence of family and friends, and are happy to embrace the life of an overseas worker.

The good news is that you have identified the job; the fly in the ointment is that your ex would be your boss.

To make matters worse, your breakup was bad and your behavior was, by your own account, reprehensible so all this is causing you to doubt the wisdom of this move.

Now it appears as though your decision depends very significantly upon your sister’s central role in this saga. She was in Dubai and she had the job that you are now considering, she knows your ex, she knows your history with him. And most importantly she is advising you that the breakup should not be a significant obstacle to your taking the job.

The question therefore is the extent to which you can rely upon your sister’s assessment of the situation.

On this issue we unfortunately have no information so can offer little help but to suggest that you discuss the matter very thoroughly with her before taking a decision.

Another factor to take into account is that your ex is now happily married. This should mitigate some of your concern, as should the likelihood that you are now more mature and should now be capable of managing a normal work-based relationship with him.

If, however, you still have doubts, there is the comfort that the world offers a lot more opportunities than just this single job in Dubai.

As you are already contemplating a move overseas, you probably have the necessary credentials and documents etc. to consider destinations other than Dubai. You may also have contacts with other Filipinos abroad. All in all, you have choices that are not limited to this one position and therefore the chance of employment that will both suit you and come without the baggage of a past relationship.

Best of luck,

– JAF Baer

Dear Allyson,

Thank you very much for your letter. Mr Baer, thank you very much also for laying out all the logical pros and cons to her accepting (or refusing) the job offer and thus writing a very good advice column by assuaging most of Allyson’s fears.

However, since this is much more than an advice column (or so I like to think 🤔) allow me to add below what I learned from Peter Hollins’s The Science Of Self Discipline (2017) that I feel strongly relates to your situation right now.

Of course, I may be overreacting. Maybe you do not have to read Hollis’s book because you have behaved maturely since then and you do not have to change your environment to work in your favor.

Think about it. You have accepted sole responsibility for the terrible way your breakup happened and it also seems you have not behaved this immaturely over a man since. Or are you worried that seeing him will trigger the same reactions and you will backslide?

If that, indeed, is the case and you are worried you will regress, then remind yourself how hesitant you felt about Dubai in the first place. You can use this hesitance and discomfort as training ground the same way surfers use discomfort as encouragement. Surfers ride the wave of discomfort yet refrain from acting on it. Surfers do not fight the ocean but learn to move with it.

How can you do that? Baby steps, Allyson, truly small steps: Actively seek out small doses of discomfort, rejection, cold, boredom, to become familiar with what true discomfort actually feels like, so it stops having so much power over your choices.

Finally, be kind to yourself. An unkind you would interpret your past behavior as simple immaturity. Not true. You were probably just operating without a system.

Your past failures are not necessarily evidence of a broken character; they are evidence of missing structure.

Your goal now is to have a structure. To build habits so consistent and an environment so aligned with your goals that discipline eventually becomes automatic, it becomes your identity. When you reach that point, you do not have to fight yourself every morning, you just become someone who does the thing, because that is who you are now. That shift from willpower to identity, from effort to habit, from struggle to second nature.

Do you think, dearest Allyson, that you might be able to do this once you get to Dubai-or even before?

Please be kind to yourself. Do not consistently berate yourself because you didn’t structure your environment or discipline yourself so consistently that the old you would’ve behaved immaturely. Do not berate yourself, asking silly questions like: Why did I not realize it then? Why did I have to behave so immaturely when we broke up?!!?

Because if you knew then what you do now, of course you would have behaved differently. But you didn’t (behave maturely) because you didn’t (know then what you knew now). The answer is that simple.

All the best!

– MG Holmes

– Rappler.com

World.title: Iran war spreads to Red Sea and Caspian, Gulf quiet as US forgoes strikes
World.content:
ON THE ARABIAN SEA. Military helicopters and personnel operate in a location given as the Arabian Sea in this screengrab obtained from a video released by US Central Command on July 25, 2026.

The US military says its naval blockade against Iran 'remains in full effect' but did not explain why it halted a streak of 13 nights of escalating strikes

Signs of the Iran war’s spread emerged this weekend despite a pause in US strikes, as Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked Saudi oil installations along the Red Sea coast and Iran accused Ukraine of targeting an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea.

The US military said on Saturday, July 25, that its naval blockade against Iran “remains in full effect” but did not explain why it halted a streak of 13 nights of escalating strikes. Asked about the pause, a senior official in President Donald Trump’s administration said Trump “has always been clear that his preference is diplomacy, but he has shown Iran what will happen if they fail to come to the table in a serious way.”

There were also no reports on Saturday of attacks from Iran on neighboring countries, like those that have been taking place daily in response to the US attacks.

Trump has decided, for now, to back away from earlier plans to ramp up attacks on Iran, the New York Times reported on Saturday night, citing two people briefed on the discussion. The president and his advisers, according to the Times, have concerns about expanding the conflict, depleting defense stockpiles, alienating Persian Gulf allies and affecting energy supplies and the global economy.

Despite the lull in the Gulf, fighting between Iran’s Houthi allies and Saudi Arabia on Saturday indicated the war, which has already disrupted energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz, could affect a second major shipping route and reignite Yemen’s civil war.

Separately, Iran’s Foreign Ministry accused Ukraine of attacking an Iranian commercial vessel in the ​Caspian Sea, saying it resulted in an explosion that killed ‌a sailor and injured another.

Earlier on Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a social media post praised the results of “long‑range strikes” in the Caspian Sea, alluding to vessels shipping military cargo, but did not identify the nationality of the targets.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry summoned ​Ukraine’s chargé d’affaires in Tehran to convey its protest over what it described as a “hostile and criminal” attack, Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported.

The Iranian denunciation coincided with comments ​by Zelenskiy that Kyiv had noted Russia was passing ​on its satellite observations in the Middle East to Iran to enable it to direct ‌strikes ⁠in the region.

War threatens to spread to Yemen

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group struck sites belonging to Saudi state oil company Aramco in Jizan and Yanbu. Video shared on social media and verified by Reuters showed a large column of smoke rising from the direction of the Aramco refinery in Jizan.

Two Asia-based trading sources said they had been informed of potential damage to fuel and oil storage sites at Jizan. Aramco did not respond to requests for comment.

In Yanbu, two ballistic missiles aimed at oil installations were intercepted by a US-made Patriot battery operated in Saudi Arabia by the Greek military under an agreement with Riyadh, Greek security sources said.

Yanbu, Saudi Arabia’s main Red Sea oil port, has become a key route for Saudi oil skirting the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has blockaded. Up to 400,000 barrels can be processed daily at the oil refinery in Jizan, a city on the Red Sea close to the Yemeni border.

Saudi-led coalition strikes Hodeidah

In Yemen, the air force of the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government, which has opposed the Houthis for more than a decade, struck Houthi launch sites and arms depots in the Marib and al-Jawf provinces, Yemeni officials said.

Earlier, the Saudi-led military alliance said it bombed Houthi military positions on Friday in the Red Sea coastal city of Hodeidah, although the coalition said it did not target the port facilities.

The Yemeni officials said both sides in Yemen’s civil war were mobilizing forces along the front.

Saudi Arabia has led an Arab coalition battling the Houthis for more than a decade since the Iran-aligned fighters captured Yemen’s capital, Sanaa.

The civil war, during which hundreds of thousands of people died from fighting and famine, has been paused under a ceasefire since 2022. But that truce broke down this month, with the Houthis effectively joining the wider war their Iranian allies have waged since being attacked by the U.S. and Israel five months ago.

The Houthis have declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia over the past week, and Houthi leader Abdul Malik al-Houthi said all Saudi oil facilities could be targets. On Thursday, the Houthis struck two Saudi tankers in the Red Sea.

American forces recently resumed their own blockade on Iranian ports. US Central Command, whose coverage area includes the Middle East, said it disabled a ship whose crew attempted to run the blockade despite “repeated warnings” on Friday in the Gulf of Oman. – Rappler.com

World.title: Vehicle mows down crowd at Berlin Pride festival, killing 1
World.content:
CALLED OFF. People walk past an emergency vehicle after the annual Berlin's Christopher Street Day Pride parade was called off, after a car crashed into the crowd at Tiergarten park, leaving several people injured, in Berlin, Germany, July 26, 2026.

Police say the vehicle struck multiple people after charging into the city's central Tiergarten park close to the Brandenburg Gate.

BERLIN, Germany – One person has been killed and 17 injured, with some in life-threatening condition, after a vehicle mowed down a crowd near Berlin’s Pride celebrations on Saturday evening, July 25, setting off a manhunt for those responsible, the police said.

Hours after the apparent attack many details remained unclear, but police said the vehicle struck multiple people after charging into the city’s central Tiergarten park close to the Brandenburg Gate. They later said they had identified an Islamist as a suspect and were seeking his arrest.

“According to our latest information, the vehicle drove … into the Tiergarten around 10 pm (2000 GMT), injuring several people in the process, and then came to a standstill after hitting a tree here in the Tiergarten,” a police spokesperson at the scene said.

“It was empty, which is why we are currently working intensively to track down the perpetrator or perpetrators.”

Eight seriously injured

Among the injured, eight had serious injuries and of those, three were in life-threatening condition, a fire brigade spokesperson said.

“We have now identified a suspected perpetrator. Measures against this suspected perpetrator, who has not yet been arrested, are underway. However, this suspected perpetrator is known to the police as a member of the Islamist scene here in Berlin,” the police spokesperson told reporters.

The police said the vehicle was white, describing it as possibly a car or minivan or minibus. Tabloid newspaper Bild cited a witness as saying it was a van and that a man emerged from it and fled on foot.

Hundreds of thousands of people had gathered peacefully in the German capital for the annual Christopher Street Day celebrations, one of Europe’s largest LGBTQ events, before the apparent attack brought it to an abrupt end.

A large number of emergency service vehicles were at the scene.

“It’s one of the worst days for the queer community and a day I personally hoped I’d never have to experience… I’m shocked,” said Julian Miethig, who attended the event.

Christopher Street Day draws hundreds of thousands of people to the German capital each year. The event commemorates the 1969 Stonewall uprising in New York and combines a parade with political demands for equality, inclusion and protection against discrimination.

Series of car attacks

First held in West Berlin in 1979, the CSD has grown from a small demonstration into a major fixture of the city’s cultural and political calendar. The parade is the centrepiece of the CSD, but it is accompanied by a range of political, cultural and party events held across the city.

Germany has in recent years suffered a series of incidents in which a car has charged into a crowd, causing deaths.

In May, a man believed to have mental health issues drove his car into a central pedestrian zone of the eastern German city of Leipzig, killing two people and seriously injuring three.

Last year, two people were killed in the western city of Mannheim when a 40-year-old man whom authorities described as psychologically unwell drove a car into a group of pedestrians. Weeks before that, an Afghan national suspected by prosecutors of having carried out a similar attack on a trade union demonstration in Munich, killing two and injuring more than 40, including children.

In December 2024, several people were killed in a car-ramming attack on a Christmas market in the eastern city of Magdeburg. The suspected perpetrator was a psychiatrist from Saudi Arabia with a history of anti-Islamic rhetoric who had lived in Germany for almost two decades. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kabang’s road to recovery: How PETA, vet-guardian saved a horse
World.content:
KABANG AND HIS GUARDIAN ANGELS. PETA's Jana Sevilla (left) and Dr. Steve Ternura check on Kabang the horse in Nagcarlan, Laguna, on July 16, 2026.

Dragged for 25 kilometers before collapsing on a highway in Misamis Oriental, Kabang begins his journey back to health with the help of PETA and his veterinarian-turned-guardian, Dr. Steve Ternura

NAGCARLAN, Laguna – When a video of a horse tied to a moving pickup truck surfaced online in February 2026, it immediately sparked anger.

The horse’s name is Kabang. While many know him then as the horse that ran 25 kilometers and collapsed on a highway in Gingoog, Misamis Oriental, his rescuers describe him as nothing short of gentle and malambing (affectionate).

SAY HELLO TO KABANG. Rescued horse Kabang relaxes in his new home in Nagcarlan, Laguna, on July 16, 2026. All photos by Rappler

Meeting Kabang

Jana Sevilla, senior campaigner of People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) Philippines, first saw the viral video after a news outlet reached out to her for an interview.

“[I was] super angry that someone would do that to an animal — to a horse,” she said.

Sevilla gathered information on Kabang’s owner, Jose Castro, and immediately coordinated with the Bureau of Animal Industry (BAI), which confirmed the owner’s ranch was not registered.

The BAI then issued a show-cause order to Castro for violating Section 2 of the Animal Welfare Act, which states that animal facilities must first obtain a certificate of registration from the bureau before operating.

Soon after, Sevilla flew to Misamis Oriental to personally serve the show-cause order to Castro. She tracked him down through his mother, who directed Sevilla to Castro’s house in Lagonglong, where she met Kabang for the first time.

“When I saw him, he was skinny. He was lethargic. And he looked so sad. His life there had no enrichment at all,” said Sevilla.

TREATS FOR KABANG. PETA’s Jana Sevilla feeds the recovering Kabang.

At the ranch, she took videos of the injured Kabang and sent them to Dr. Janela Silva, who also flew to Misamis Oriental to examine him in person. There, she diagnosed him with severe lameness, hoof inflammation, and hip pain.

Silva recommended taking Kabang to Batangas for an X-ray, which would require Sevilla to secure full custody of the horse.

Trip to Batangas

Securing full custody of Kabang proved to be another challenge. Sevilla wrote to several municipalities for help in filing the case, but often received no response.

Since Kabang needed to reach Batangas as soon as possible, and securing a court order was difficult, PETA decided to make special arrangements with Castro instead.

“The agreement was that we will not file a case against Castro, but he will give the full custody of Kabang to PETA, and he will not be allowed to care for any animals for the rest of his life,” Sevilla explained.

The PETA official recalled that Castro first defended himself and said what he was doing was horse endurance training — using techniques learned from ancestors — for his business.

But Castro eventually agreed to compromise and signed the contract in front of representatives from the Department of Agriculture and the BAI.

After successfully securing custody, PETA made the necessary logistical arrangements for the trip to Batangas.

DOC STEVE. Kabang with his new guardian and veterinarian Dr. Steve Ternura.

6-day travel

The journey was not easy. Securing the documents and travel permits was only the beginning. Luckily, Sevilla was accompanied by Dr. Steve Ternura — the man who was about to change Kabang’s life.

They both remembered how only very few ships allowed livestock, so they had no choice but to travel by land and sea. Accommodations that allowed big animals to stay were equally scarce, leaving Sevilla, Ternura, and their driver with only two nights of sleep in those six days.

Ternura and Sevilla also recalled an incident on the second day of the trip. Kabang panicked over a white vehicle — an incident that first happened in Libertad. This confirmed that what happened to the horse was beyond physical damage.

Throughout the journey, Ternura played a crucial role, staying with Kabang in the horse trailer to keep him comfortable and monitor his condition.

COOLING DOWN. Dr. Steve Ternura gives Kabang a bath.

Kabang connection

Ternura is no stranger to PETA. He has been working with the organization since its Taal Volcano animal rescue project in 2020. But even after years in the profession, Ternura said Kabang’s story was different from those he had witnessed before.

“[Why] would you train a horse for trail riding or trail hiking on the highway, right? And then, the distance is too long,” the veterinarian said.

He described meeting Kabang as one of the highlights of his career, adding that forming a bond with the horse was not difficult.

“It was not hard kasi si Kabang, malambing siya (It was not hard because Kabang is affectionate),” said Ternura, who first met Kabang at the foster farm in Libertad, where he got to know the horse better.

Ternura also shared it was during their ferry ride to Batangas that he decided he wanted to adopt Kabang. After spending several days caring for him, Ternura realized he could do the same long-term — and the rest was history.

KABANG AND DOC. Dr. Steve Ternura spends time with adopted horse Kabang.

Kabang’s new life

Sevilla and Ternura saw visible changes in Kabang. In his new home, Kabang looks happier, healthier, and more comfortable around people.

“Wala na siyang worry sa place niya because he can get all the care that he needs (He doesn’t have any worries anymore because he can get all the care that he needs),” said the veterinarian.

Kabang’s everyday routine now consists of roaming in his paddock in the morning, then getting fed his first meal at 7 am.

Ternura and his fellow caretaker, Jeffrey, ensure Kabang is well fed throughout the entire day. They are, of course, still mindful of his diet. According to Ternura, this is still needed to successfully manage Kabang’s injuries.

He added that Kabang’s recovery could take another four to six months, but the priority now is to further improve his appetite.

Ternura performs a physical checkup on the horse every time he visits the farm, but while he is away tending to other animals, he makes sure to check up on Kabang at least 10 times a day.

QUIET TIMES WITH KABANG. Dr. Steve Ternura tends to Kabang in his paddock.

Protecting animals

People who use business as an excuse to keep animals, Sevilla said, should be held liable.

“If animals are used for business…their welfare is at the least priority, because they are seen as moneymakers, like machines na parang (treated as if) they don’t feel tired.”

She said this is the reason why PETA continues to urge people to stop supporting businesses that use animals.

“Malayo pa tayo (We still have a long way to go),” said Ternura, acknowledging that a lot of things still have to be done for change to happen in the Philippines.

Sevilla urges people to testify and properly report cases of animal cruelty to authorities. She emphasized that posting about them on social media is simply not enough. Legal action has to be taken.

While there is still much work to be done for animal welfare in the Philippines, hope persists for those dedicated to the cause. As Ternura points out, with proper education and awareness, the country can create safer environments for animals like Kabang. – Rappler.com

Charley Dueñas is a Rappler intern and a fourth year AB Communications student from the Ateneo de Manila University.

World.title: Bangko Sentral recycles old peso bills into armchairs for this Davao City classroom
World.content:
The next stop for some worn-out Philippine banknotes is not the shredder or the landfill, but the classroom

MANILA, Philippines – Nearly 100 armchairs made entirely from recycled polymer banknotes have been donated to Doña Pilar L. Marfori Elementary School in Davao City, giving the notes a second life after they were deemed unfit for circulation.

The chairs were turned over on Wednesday, July 22, through the Banknote-to-Armchair Project of the BSP Employees Association Inc. (BSPEAI).

BSP Deputy Governor Mamerto Tangonan, BSP Mindanao Regional Office officer-in-charge Jason Capocao, BSPEAI president Brent Lucero, and Currency Policy and Integrity Department director Eloisa Glindro led the ceremonial turnover to the school, represented by principal Eloisa Questo.

The project transforms damaged or worn-out polymer notes, along with manufacturing byproducts, into durable classroom furniture. The employees’ association partnered with private recycling company Envirotech Waste Recycling Inc. to produce the armchairs.

“Polymer banknotes follow a planned lifecycle from circulation to recycling. End-of-life management is built into their design,” Tangonan said.

Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Deputy Governor Mamerto Tangonan stands in front of a class in Doña Pilar L. Marfori Elementary School in Davao City. Photo by Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas.

Lucero said the Davao City elementary school was selected after the group assessed the needs and priorities of communities on the ground.

The project also highlights one of the BSP’s arguments for shifting from paper to polymer notes: they are designed to last longer and require less frequent replacement. (READ: Senators, farmers question design of new P1,000 polymer bills)

From 2022 to May 2026, the BSP said just 0.02% of the P1,000 polymer banknotes issued to banks were returned to the BSP because they were already worn out or damaged. By comparison, 54.75% of the P1,000 paper banknotes issued over the same period were eventually returned in worn-out or damaged condition.

The BSP said it had also yet to receive any unfit lower-denomination polymer notes since the new P50, P100, and P500 polymer bills were first released in December 2024. – Rappler.com

World.title: Fire destroys P3.8-M gov’t school property in Zamboanga City
World.content:
BLAZING FIRE. The fire of still unknown origin that razed a school building of the Taluksangay Elementary School in Zamboanga City early Sunday, July 26, 2026. The city fire district placed the damage to property at P3.8 million. (Photo from the Zamboanga City Fire District)

ZAMBOANGA CITY – An estimated P3.8 million worth of government school property went up in smoke early Sunday in this city.

Supt. Leo Pioquinto, Zamboanga City Fire District (ZCFD) marshal, said the fire destroyed a two-story 10-classroom school building in Taluksangay Elementary School.

“The fire that consumed the school building started around 4:28 a.m. and was contained at about 5:04 a.m.,” he said in a report.

Article continues after this 

READ: Fire razes homes in Zamboanga City, displacing 23 families

There was no fatality or injury reported.

Pioquinto said they have yet to determine the fire’s origin as investigation continues.

Four fire trucks from the Bureau of Fire Protection’s ZCFD responded to the incident. They were backed by two water tankers from the City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office.

World.title: PNP ready for 5th Marcos Sona, urges maximum tolerance during rallies
World.content:
Personnel from various government agencies and media organizations conduct final preparations inside and outside the House of Representatives in Quezon City, July 24, 20226, ahead of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s fifth State of the Nation Address (SONA) on July 27. (Photo by NIÑO JESUS ORBETA / INQUIRER.net)

MANILA, Philippines—All security preparations for President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s fifth State of the Nation Address (Sona) on Monday are complete, said the Philippine National Police (PNP).

PNP has deployed over 20,000 cops set to secure key areas while observing maximum tolerance during rallies.

“All security protocols have been completed and we are already in the process of phased deployment in areas that require police presence,” said PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. in a statement on Sunday.

Article continues after this 

“We’ve done this before. We prepared for this important event—and we are ready,” noted Nartatez.

The National Capital Region Police Office earlier said it had inspected critical areas along Commonwealth Avenue, from St. Peter Parish Church to the Sandiganbayan, including IBP Road, the House of Representatives, and the Batasan Police Station.

Aside from providing security for the president’s Sona, police personnel will assist in traffic management along Commonwealth Avenue and surrounding areas of the Batasang Pambansa.

The PNP chief also reminded police personnel to observe maximum tolerance in handling rallies and urged protesters to cooperate with authorities, and comply with existing regulations to help maintain peace and order.

“Our personnel are also ready to secure protest actions across the country. We likewise ask for the cooperation of everyone who will participate in the rallies,” said Nartatez

Article continues after this 

“Let us respect one another’s rights and maintain peace and order on this day,” he added.

The PNP has not monitored any serious security threat related to this year’s Sona but remains vigilant against any attempt to disrupt peace and order during the event.Earlier, the PNP said it would “exhaust all peaceful means” to stop protesters from burning effigies during rallies.

Article continues after this 

Read: PNP to ‘exhaust all peaceful means’ to stop effigy-burning at Sona

July 27 also marks the anniversary of the founding of the Iglesia ni Cristo, a religious movement which held a surprise rally on June 30, drawing over 12,000 participants.

“As of now, they have not made any announcement on whether they will push through with their celebration or where it will be held,” PNP public information chief Col. Allen Rae Co told the Inquirer. /apl

World.title: Parañaque voters ratify boundary changes for 5 coastal villages
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

MANILA, Philippines — Voters in five coastal barangays in Parañaque City overwhelmingly ratified Saturday an ordinance altering their existing territorial boundaries adjoining the reclaimed areas in Manila Bay.

Official results released by the Commission on Elections (Comelec) showed that 11,597 voters voted “Yes” to City Ordinance No. 2023-19, which alters the existing territorial boundaries of Barangays Baclaran, Tambo, Don Galo, La Huerta, and San Dionisio in the city.

On the other hand, a total of 2,254 people voted “No” against the ratification.

Article continues after this 

READ: Comelec to hold plebiscite in 5 barangays in Parañaque City

The Plebiscite Board of Canvassers proclaimed the approval of the ordinance after canvassing all 151 plebiscite returns from the five barangays, where 13,873 out of 79,251 registered voters participated.

Comelec Spokesperson John Rex Laudiangco said the July 25 polls were recorded as the fastest plebiscite canvassing after the winner was proclaimed just several hours after voting ended.

“The fastest plebiscite canvassing on record, with the Certificate of Canvass and Proclamation having been issued and promulgated within 6 hours from the close of polls,” he said.

World.title: Senate probe into electricity bill spikes sought
World.content:
The Department of Energy reported that the Philippines had the highest electricity costs in Southeast Asia as of June 2026, with average rates pegged at P12.43 per kilowatt-hour. — NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

MANILA, Philippines — A resolution seeking an inquiry into the increase in electricity prices has been filed in the Senate in aid of legislation to protect power consumers.

Sen. Erwin Tulfo, chairperson of the Senate energy panel, said he filed Senate Resolution No. 535 to ensure that electricity rates remain reasonable.

“While electric distribution utilities and generation companies are entitled to recover prudent and legitimate costs necessary to maintain reliable electric service and undertake essential capital investments, consumers likewise have the right to fair, transparent, accurate, and reasonable electricity charges and access to timely and effective complaint resolution mechanisms,” Tulfo said in a statement.

Article continues after this 

The senator also questioned the government’s capability to help consumers affected by bill shocks.

“Is the government really powerless here? For instance, if an electric cooperative’s service is awful and the people are fed up with it, are we helpless?” he asked.

“We cannot let our countrymen just accept this, especially with wage rates remaining stagnant,” Tulfo added.

READ: PH power rates highest in Asean in June; further hikes loom

READ: Fuel costs, peso depreciation drive power rate hikes—Meralco

Article continues after this 

Tulfo vowed, as chairperson of the energy panel, to find a solution to rising power rates.

He said: “We will find out how to temper these high electricity prices and make them affordable for Filipinos. In this day and age, access to power is a right and not a mere luxury. Every Filipino deserves fair electricity rates.”

Article continues after this 

Recently, the Department of Energy reported that the Philippines had the highest electricity costs in Southeast Asia as of June 2026, with average rates pegged at P12.43 per kilowatt-hour. /mcm /atm

World.title: Shabu worth over P491,000 seized, 3 nabbed in Bicol buy-busts
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

LEGAZPI CITY — Authorities arrested three drug personalities and recovered more than P491,000 worth of shabu (crystal meth) on July 25 in separate operations in Camarines Norte and Albay.

In Panganiban town, Camarines Norte, suspects identified as “Batoy” and “Sonny”—both residents of Albay province—were arrested after selling a sachet of shabu to an undercover agent at 8:50 p.m.

The operatives recovered P10,200 worth of shabu during the operation.

Article continues after this 

READ: P3.74M ‘shabu’ seized in Camarines Sur buy-bust

In Daraga town, Albay, operatives from the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency and the Philippine National Police arrested a suspect identified as “Bodgie” in a separate buy-bust operation.

Col. Noel Nunez, chief of the Albay police, said in a report on Sunday that the suspect, tagged as a high-value drug personality, sold a sachet of suspected shabu to an undercover agent in Barangay (village) Malabog at 3:11 p.m.

During the body search, they recovered 14 sachets containing 70 grams of shabu worth P481,440, a caliber .22 gun, and five bullets.

World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — The Police Regional Office (PRO) Mimaropa has arrested the region’s most wanted person, who is facing 10 counts of qualified rape, during a law enforcement operation in Rizal town, Palawan, the agency said Sunday.

Operatives of the Rizal Municipal Police Station arrested the suspect on Saturday in Purok Balite, Barangay Punta Baja.

They were assisted by the Regional Intelligence Unit 4B–Palawan Provincial Intelligence Team, Palawan Provincial Intelligence Unit, 1st Palawan Provincial Mobile Force Company, and the Rizal Municipal Law Enforcement Team.

Police said the arrest was carried out by virtue of 10 warrants of arrest issued by the court for qualified rape. Each warrant carries no recommended bail.
