These principles are based on freedom of choice, the provision of adequate housing and, wherever possible, the restoration of rights to former property. Under Azerbaijan’s new legislation, however, the state is considered to have fulfilled its obligations once it offers housing, while refusing that offer results in the loss of IDP status. This weakens the principle that return should be voluntary.

Official position and expert assessments

Pro-government media outlets, including Milli.az, Report.az and APA, have presented the amendments in a positive light, using phrases such as “restoring property rights”, “sustainable social support” and “providing a legal framework for the Great Return programme”.

MP Vugar Bayramov has also argued that the three-year transition period demonstrates the state’s continued commitment to social support. Official statements emphasise that the new housing is transferred into private ownership rather than provided on a rental basis, which the authorities say will encourage people to settle permanently in the region.

At the same time, independent observers and some human rights advocates argue that the changes restrict freedom of choice, fail to fully restore land rights and raise other concerns. They also point to the contrast between the urban lifestyles that many IDPs have built over the past three decades and the newly established rural settlements, as well as the risks of unemployment and inadequate infrastructure.

The status of internally displaced persons in Azerbaijan

World.title: EU’s 21st sanctions package targets Kulevi oil terminal and cryptocurrency platforms in Georgia
World.content:
Georgia in the EU’s 21st sanctions package

The European Union’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia includes an oil refinery in the Georgian town of Kulevi and several cryptocurrency platforms.

The sanctions against the Kulevi refinery, which processes and sells Russian oil, include a six-month grace period. The ban on transactions will take effect after six months unless the refinery changes its business practices.

The Kulevi refinery had previously been considered for inclusion in the EU’s 20th package of sanctions against Russia, but was ultimately removed from the sanctions list.

At the time, the EU said that “the Georgian authorities and the port operator had made positive commitments.” This was stated in a letter from the EU’s Special Envoy, David O’Sullivan, to Georgian Foreign Minister Maka Botchorishvili.

What does the new sanctions package include?

The EU’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia, which is expected to take effect shortly, was formally approved by the permanent representatives of the EU member states on 23 July 2026.

The sanctions are expected to enter into force on 23 July following approval by EU leaders and their publication in the Official Journal of the European Union.

The measures target sectors of the Russian economy that generate significant revenue for Moscow’s war in Ukraine, including energy, financial services and the cryptocurrency sector.

The package also imposes sanctions on more than 50 companies and organisations involved in supplying military goods and weapons to Russia.

It includes the EU’s largest-ever round of individual sanctions, targeting a total of 218 entities — 48 individuals and 170 legal entities.

It is one of the most significant expansions of the EU’s sanctions regime in the past four years.

Sanctions against the Kulevi refinery

“The package introduces the possibility of banning transactions with oil refineries listed in Russia and third countries that process Russian crude oil and petroleum products. Under these measures, the EU is imposing a ban on transactions with the Georgian oil refinery in Kulevi, which processes and trades Russian oil. The ban will take effect in six months,” the EU said in a statement.

According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, citing a source familiar with the matter, the introduction of a six-month deadline is unprecedented in EU sanctions policy.

The same source said the decision reflected Tbilisi’s willingness to meet the EU’s requirements, which became apparent during discussions over sanctions related to the port.

This means that if the Kulevi refinery continues processing Russian oil over the next six months, it will become subject to EU sanctions. The refinery’s owner, Black Sea Petroleum, announced on 1 July 2026 that it would begin full-scale processing of non-Russian crude from August or September.

According to Georgia’s National Statistics Office, domestic exports rose sharply in January 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, driven largely by exports of petroleum products.

Petroleum and petroleum products ranked as Georgia’s second-largest export category in January 2026, with exports worth $58.7 million, accounting for 12.2% of the country’s total exports.

Cryptocurrency platforms added to the sanctions list

The EU has imposed transaction bans on 14 cryptocurrency platforms based in Georgia, Panama, the United Arab Emirates, Kyrgyzstan, Belarus and the Marshall Islands.

For the first time, the EU has introduced a mechanism allowing it to impose a complete ban on transactions between EU companies and cryptocurrency platforms that help Russia circumvent sanctions.

The measure also applies to crypto service providers operating in third countries if they facilitate activities that serve Russian interests.

What does the inclusion of Georgian companies in the sanctions package mean for Georgia?

The inclusion of the Kulevi refinery in the EU’s 21st sanctions package has already sparked debate in Georgia.

“The EU’s 21st sanctions package is a national disgrace: Georgian assets are being used as cannon fodder for Russia’s war machine. By allowing the Kremlin to circumvent sanctions, those in power are betraying our sovereignty. Georgia’s place is in Europe — we will never become a loophole for Russian aggression,” Georgia’s fifth president, Salome Zourabichvili, wrote on X.

Analyst Lela Djedjelava said sanctions against such an important economic asset would have an impact on the Georgian economy.

“The consequences will become increasingly visible over time. The reality is that the Kulevi refinery is probably not the only facility that could be exposed for cooperating with Russia. If other businesses in Georgia are also hit by sanctions, it will naturally have a very negative impact on the country.”

Gedevan Popkhadze, one of the leaders of the opposition Coalition for Change, said the EU sanctions against the Kulevi refinery were the result of the Georgian government’s inaction.

“If you are not helping Ukraine, why are you helping Russia? If you do not want war, why are you acting in favour of one of the parties to the conflict? We must clearly understand that these sanctions are not a message to the Kulevi refinery itself — they are a message to Georgia’s de facto government. It should realise that claiming to be neutral is hypocrisy.”

Georgia in the EU’s 21st sanctions package

World.title: Opinion: ‘There is no longer peace in Georgia’
World.content:
Opinion on the latest events in Georgia

Professor at Ilia State University and literary critic Zaal Andronikashvili comments on the events that unfolded in Georgia on 22 July 2026, including the arrest of a journalist, a shooting in central Tbilisi, and an attack on an opposition stand-up comedian.

He writes that there is no longer peace in Georgia and blames Bidzina Ivanishvili and his Georgian Dream party.

Journalist Vakho Sanaia was sentenced to 14 days of administrative detention over satirical social media posts about members of the Georgian Dream party. A shooting took place in central Tbilisi on 22 July, leaving four people injured, including two minors. One of the minors later died in hospital. Comedian Onise Okriashvili, a critic of the government, was brutally beaten at his home. Before the attack, he had been the target of a disinformation campaign on pro-government television channels.

Zaal Andronikashvili: “It is important to find the right name for what is happening in Georgia. The situation is new, and historical parallels apply only in part.

Since at least 2019, during the ‘Gavrilov Night’ protests, Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party have done everything possible to prevent a peaceful transfer of power. Some scholars describe this as a ‘coup from above’.”

This “coup from above” is not peaceful.

Anyone who believes that Georgia is at peace today is deeply mistaken. Beyond dragging Georgia into a geopolitical confrontation on Russia’s side — at an enormous cost to the country — Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party are waging an asymmetric, hybrid civil war against the overwhelming majority of the Georgian population.

Part of this hybrid civil war consists of unlawful restrictive legislation enforced only against certain groups of citizens and against civil society as a whole.

There is also financial repression aimed at depriving opponents of the regime of their livelihoods, as well as the deliberate destruction of education and culture. Alongside this come aggression, hopelessness, and an absence of love and empathy elevated to the level of state policy.

There is micro-level violence — encouraging crime and fostering a culture of impunity that ultimately erodes trust in the law, the justice system, and the very idea of justice. There is macro-level violence carried out by the police and special forces, along with many other elements.

“I repeat: this is not peace.

It is a hybrid civil war waged by a regime that controls the police, the legislature and the country’s financial resources against the majority of Georgia’s population, especially its most active citizens. Its goal is to suppress, subjugate and ultimately enslave them.

The other side has nothing but the truth and peaceful resistance. But the truth is a powerful, almost invincible weapon — and it can never truly be defeated.

Despite this asymmetric civil war, whose domestic objective is to cement the regime permanently in power and make the current government irreplaceable, while its foreign policy goal is to sever Georgia once and for all from the European values-based community and turn it into a banana republic under a quasi-colonial regime, Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party have failed to win this unequal conflict.

Peaceful resistance is alive. The people have not been broken. They have not been intimidated.

Those who support the regime today, or choose silent complicity, should look at Russia.

People there also believed that if they kept quiet and buried their heads in a bowl of caviar, none of it would affect them. Other people’s children would die, someone else would go to prison, someone else’s life would be ruined. Perhaps someone would stop greeting them, but they could live with that.

In reality, supporting injustice always comes at a price. Injustice and lawlessness may begin by targeting only selected groups, but they very quickly spread to everyone.

By supporting injustice, you create an environment in which that injustice will inevitably reach you in one form or another.

But people are willing to ignore it until it affects them personally. There is a powerful metaphor in the Gospel of Matthew (26:52): ‘All who draw the sword will die by the sword.’ This is not really about the sword itself, but more broadly about the laws of social reality and their universal nature.

There is no peace in Georgia. Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party are responsible for that.”

Opinion on the latest events in Georgia

World.title: First H5 bird flu case confirmed on SA metro beach
World.content:
The CSIRO says two native birds found dead on separate beaches in South Australia have tested positive for the H5 strain of bird flu.

It is the first time a case has been confirmed on a SA metropolitan beach.

The two additional cases were flagged yesterday as suspected cases.

A greater crested tern was found near Robe on South Australia's Limestone Coast, while another greater crested tern was found at a beach ramp near the Semaphore Surf Life Saving Club, north-west of Adelaide.

Acting Australian chief veterinary officer Sam Hamilton said there have now been 20 confirmed or presumed positive detections of H5 bird flu in Australia.

"All of these have been individual wild seabirds found in coastal locations," Dr Hamilton said in a statement.

"There remains no evidence of any mass mortality events and there are no detections in poultry or in our agricultural production system.

There are now seven confirmed H5 bird flu cases in SA. (ABC Goldfields & Esperance: Tara de Landgrafft)

"The risk to human health remains low."

SA Environment Minister Emily Bourke said on Saturday the bird found in Robe was located 4 kilometres from the location where the first Australian seabird confirmed to have the H5 strain of bird flu was found.

"Unfortunately, we are finding that these two cases are in our local [bird] species," Ms Bourke said.

Previous confirmed cases involved migratory birds from the sub-Antarctic region.

South Australia's first confirmed case was in a giant petrel found on the Fleurieu Peninsula on June 14.

As of today, there are seven confirmed cases in SA, 10 in WA, and two in NSW.

Queensland confirmed its first H5 bird flu case yesterday after a dead petrel was found on Moreton Island, east of Brisbane.

Before the two suspected cases were confirmed on Sunday, Premier Peter Malianauskas said the government's policy in response to the bird flu remains the same.

"We still don't have any evidence of it being anywhere near poultry facilities or the poultry industry, which of course is the biggest risk that we're keeping a close eye on," Mr Malinauskas said.

The premier said despite there being evidence of the bird flu in the native Australian bird population, he had received advice it cannot be "automatically assumed that means a spread throughout the population."

"But that's nonetheless something we have to continue to monitor," the premier said.

World.title: Body found after house fire in NSW coastal town
World.content:
Police are investigating a house fire at Kiama on the NSW south coast, after a person was found dead in the home on Saturday night.

Authorities were called to the property on Manning Street just before 9:30pm, finding a house engulfed in flames.

Fire and Rescue NSW (FRNSW) responded with eight fire trucks and about 28 firefighters, and were assisted by the NSW Rural Fire Service and police.

NSW Police have confirmed the body of a person, who is yet to be formally identified, was located at the scene following the fire.

Investigators are still working to confirm the cause of the blaze but have told the ABC it is not being treated as suspicious.

The home in Kiama was destroyed by the blaze. (Supplied: Darin Sullivan)

FRNSW acting superintendent Peter Murray said crews worked to contain the fire to the property, which was located in a residential street in the coastal town, but the home was extensively damaged by the blaze.

"Fire crews worked to help make the site safe before handing the scene over to the NSW Police," Mr Murray said in a statement to the ABC.

Winter fire safety

Kiama state MP Katelin McInerney said the incident was "incredibly sad" and expressed her "deepest sympathies to [the deceased's] family and friends" in a statement posted to social media on Sunday morning.

"Thank you to the local first responders who acted so swiftly and worked to put out the blaze and responded with professionalism and compassion at a such a confronting scene," Ms McInerney said in the statement.

" With winter now truly upon us, please check all your smoke alarms are working, batteries are in, ensure heaters are plugged in correctly and used safely, and that you have fire blankets in the kitchen and bedroom. "

It comes a fortnight after another fatal Illawarra house fire, which claimed the life of a woman in Coniston, near Wollongong.

Investigations are ongoing into the blaze at Kiama and a report will be prepared for the coroner.

World.title: Runaway train with no driver travelled faster than 60km/h
World.content:
Railway safety officials are looking into an incident involving a runaway coal train in the Hunter Valley.

The fully laden coal train was unmanned and travelled several kilometres, including through level crossings.

Pacific National, which hauls coal from mines in the Hunter Valley, has confirmed the incident in a statement to the ABC.

"Pacific National can confirm that an incident involving one of its coal services occurred in the Hunter Valley during the early hours of 25 July 2026," the statement read "There were no injuries to our crew or any members of the public, and there was no collision or derailment. "Pacific National immediately notified Australian Rail Track Corporation (ARTC) network control and the Office of the National Rail Safety Regulator. "Safety is Pacific National's highest priority. We take this incident extremely seriously and are fully cooperating with the regulator and all relevant authorities to understand exactly what occurred and identify any actions required to prevent a recurrence."

The train stopped near Glennies Creek, where crews worked to clear the line just before midday. (ABC Upper Hunter: Courtney Yeandle)

The ABC understands the fully laden train started rolling independently downhill during a crew change at Camberwell between Singleton and Muswellbrook just after midnight on Saturday morning and that it reached speeds in excess of the safe operating speed of 60 kilometres per hour.

Pacific National did not respond to a specific set of questions about how the train came to be unmanned and what speed the train reached.

The train was stopped near a level crossing at Glennies Creek. (ABC Upper Hunter: Courtney Yeandle)

The Office of the National Rail Safety Regulator said in a statement it was investigating the incident.

"The Office of the National Rail Safety Regulator (ONRSR) has this morning deployed a team of rail safety officers, investigators and rolling stock specialists to the Hunter Valley where a fully loaded coal train has been involved in a runaway incident. "Fortunately, nobody was injured." "ONRSR issued a Non-Disturbance Notice to ensure the scene is preserved and is now investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident. "In addition to assessing and inspecting the scene, ONRSR is seeking information and documentation from the rail transport operator."

The incident stopped coal and passenger train movements for 36 hours. (ABC Upper Hunter: Courtney Yeandle)

The incident held up coal and passenger movements on the line for 36 hours.

The Australian Rail Track Corporation said a locomotive sustained significant wheel damage and that there was not a derailment.

The line was cleared just after midday on Sunday.

World.title: Sister of missing kayaker 'heartbroken' as search wraps up
World.content:
The sister of Shane Wilson, the man feared drowned after he disappeared while fishing on the Goulburn River, says she was "heartbroken" to hear the search for him was ending.

Mr Wilson, 53, was fishing from a kayak on the Goulburn River on Saturday, July 18, when the boat overturned.

A week after a search was initiated, Victoria Police said the recovery effort had ended.

"Sadly, with the passage of time and environmental conditions in the area, police hold grave concerns for the man’s welfare and have been working to recover his body," a spokesperson said.

Melissa Teague said Shane Wilson was an "incredible" brother who always made time for her. (Supplied: Melissa Teague)

Mr Wilson's sister, Melissa Teague, said her family was "incredibly disappointed" that the search was ending.

"I’m angry," she said.

"It feels like the search is being scaled back before we’ve had the chance to bring Shane home, and that’s devastating for us.

"We were told to prepare ourselves for the possibility that Shane may never be found. Hearing those words while we’re desperately waiting for answers was absolutely heartbreaking."

Ms Teague said she had a close relationship with her brother, who was 13 years older than her.

"He always made time for me," she said.

"We’d cook potato gems together and watch all my favourite cartoons.

"He’d play with me on the trampoline, teach me things, and when he was painting around the house, he’d hand me a little pot of water and a paintbrush so I thought I was helping."

The SES assisted in the multi-agency search. (Facebook: SES Chiltern)

A week-long search

Emergency Services were called to the river on July 18, after a witness on the riverbank raised the alarm about Mr Wilson.

Victoria Police, the Country Fire Authority, Lifesaving Victoria and the State Emergency Service (SES) were involved in the search.

An SES spokesperson had said Mr Wilson was a "strong swimmer", but the current was "flowing quite rapidly".

Mr Wilson was not wearing a life jacket.

Police did not respond to questions about why the search had concluded but confirmed they had been in contact with the family regarding the developments along the way.

"Officers will revisit the area if further information is received or if there are any new developments," a spokesperson said.

Melissa Teague says she misses talking to her older brother. (Supplied: Melissa Teague)

Ms Teague said she never called Mr Wilson by his first name; he was always 'brudda' to her.

"Ever since I was little, I couldn't say 'brother', so I called him 'brudda'. It just stuck," she said.

Ms Teague said Mr Wilson would call her regularly "nearly every day on his drive home from work, usually complaining about Melbourne traffic".

"Those everyday conversations are what I miss the most. He wasn't just my big brother … he was my best friend," Ms Teague said.

World.title: Largest display of Melanesian artefacts in Southern Hemisphere 'put to sleep'
World.content:
South Australia's Pacific Island community has come together to say goodbye to the largest display of Melanesian artefacts in the Southern Hemisphere.

The South Australian Museum will hibernate the 2,500-piece display to off-site storage for a years-long restoration project.

Pacific Island community member Wasodawa Mathews said it was "very special" to help put culturally significant crocodile artefacts to sleep during the Melanesian lullaby ceremony.

"I was talking to them and reassuring them more or less, that they are going to be safe," Ms Mathews said.

Wasodawa Mathews says artefacts that aren't displayed should "go back to their rightful place". (ABC News)

"I want to make sure that the crocodile is rested properly, and the spirits will stay with the crocodile."

Ms Mathews, who moved to Australia from Papua New Guinea 40 years ago, said she had mixed emotions.

"I think not knowing the future of it makes me sad, that they're going to put it to rest today," she said.

" It's very, very important that if they don't want the crocodiles displayed, then they have to go back to their rightful place. "

Collection to return to same space: museum director

South Australian Museum director Samantha Hamilton said the museum was committed to bringing the collection back, in the same space, in coming years, although the project did not have a timeline for its completion.

"A lot of these materials have been on display for a few decades now ... it's our responsibility now to put these items to rest," Ms Hamilton said.

Ms Hamilton said the conservation and preservation project was being undertaken in consultation with Pacific communities.

Members of the SA Pacific Island community held a ceremony to put the Pacific Cultures Gallery collection "to sleep". (ABC News: Peta Doherty)

Pacific Island community member Fred Ovia also felt emotional about saying goodbye to the collection, which he said he often visited with his grandchildren.

He said he could not "help but feel the history" behind the collection.

"Who built it? What was he like? What was she like? That creates this emotion in me that knowing that something that comes from where I come from landed here in Australia," he said.

Most of SA Museum's collection originated from Papua New Guinea, spanning from the late 19th century until the First World War.

Most of the artefacts originate from Papua New Guinea, spanning from the late 19th century until the First World War. (ABC News: Peta Doherty)

Mr Ovia said he hoped the preservation project would give the younger generation a chance to enjoy the artefacts in decades to come.

"This is not a permanent thing, it's not going away," he said.

"It's not being put into storage where it'll disappear and not be seen again.

"We've been verbally assured that this will come back."

The collection will also be digitalised in 3D and the museum said it would put on pop-up exhibitions.

Concerns raised over restoration project

But retired City of Adelaide senior heritage architect John Greenshields, who also spent 11 years working in PNG, questioned the need for the restoration project.

He was also concerned about moving some of the exhibits, saying one of them — a nearly 100-year-old Trobriand hut — could not be taken apart and removed from the museum without almost permanently destroying it.

Retired heritage architect John Greenshield objects to the 'hibernation' of SA Museum's Pacific Island collection. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

While conservation work is underway, the gallery space will be used to host national and international touring exhibitions.

Mr Greenshields said he was concerned the restoration project was motivated by funding.



"I think the museum is desperate to have a space where they can attract blockbuster-type ticketed exhibitions," he said.

But Ms Hamilton dismissed the suggestion.

"This space is not where we want to have our travelling exhibitions, it's just not," she said.

"We want this to be the Pacific cultures gallery, and we are working towards other solutions."

People are encouraged to visit the museum before the end of the month to see the conservation project as it begins. (ABC News: Peta Doherty)

'It's time to rest them'

Ms Hamilton, a material scientist who has a PhD in preserving Indigenous artefacts, said the museum's detailed condition records highlighted the need for the project.

"[They are] organic materials and they do deteriorate," she said.

"Some of the things that cause [deterioration] are light, temperature, humidity, and pests, and also things like dust.

"Over time these things accumulate, and they are actually irreversible. It's time to rest them."

Ms Hamilton also refuted suggestions that the hut would not survive moving, saying the museum was working with specialist conservators from Artlab to disassemble, pack and move items.

"The highest quality care is being taken," she said.

The SA Museum's director says the conservation and preservation project is being undertaken in consultation with Pacific communities. (ABC News: Peta Doherty)

Ms Hamilton said the Pacific Island community would be involved in designing the collection's "re-awakening" and hoped future displays would better represent other Melanesian nations.

"The community will think about what themes they want to explore, what stories they want to tell [and] there will then be a process of going into the storage and selecting those objects," she said.

The gallery is scheduled to close to the public from Monday August 3.

World.title: 'How do I not have enough money to live?' The nomadic life of a bee drover
World.content:
With her swag rolled out and her campfire lit, Sophia Croker is in her happy place.

She's in the middle of nowhere, but right beside the thing that matters most: her bees.

"Nothing about my lifestyle is normal," she says.

"Who else gets to say they sleep in their swag under the stars every night and they don't know where their next destination is going to be?"

Loading...

Sophia loves her nomadic life as a commercial beekeeper, trucking hundreds of hives around rural New South Wales and Victoria chasing honey flows and pollinating crops.

But behind the passion and devotion is a hidden struggle that's forcing Australia's beekeepers to call it quits.

"I'd be lying if I said I haven't sat and gone, 'Is this worth it?'"

A deadly bee parasite, competition with imported honey, and rising fuel costs are devastating the industry.

" The price we get for our honey doesn't cover the cost of production at the moment. "

But as many businesses leave the industry, this 23-year-old is doubling down.

She's determined not only to stay but to make sure more people know the truth behind the honey in their kitchen cupboards.

Becoming 'The Bee Drover'

Even though beekeeping has been in her family for over a century, Sophia didn't dream of following in their footsteps.

Loading TikTok content

But her life changed dramatically when she was an 18-year-old university student, and the offer came up to buy 120 hives from a beekeeper leaving the industry.

It was a $40,000 investment.

"All of a sudden I was starting a company and at the bank taking out my first ever loan."

And so began the fourth generation of beekeepers in the family, which started with Sophia's great-grandmother carting hives through the citrus orchards of Beelbangera on her push bike in the 1920s.

In five years, Sophia has doubled her hives and also helps manage her dad's, meaning they're moving up to 2,000 hives at a time.

They're constantly on the move, either chasing honey flows, finding areas where plants are in bloom and producing nectar, or being contracted on farms to pollinate crops.

"We get to see so much land that people will ever see in their lifetimes; it's so special."

Sophia now documents her work and lifestyle on social media as "The Bee Drover", where she also hopes to bring greater awareness to the challenges facing the industry.

The buzzkill

The deadly varroa mite parasite is devastating beekeeping businesses, prompting warnings of a potential food crisis, as at least 60 per cent of hives are wiped out.

The pest arrived in Australia in 2022 and has drastically changed beekeeping practices and costs.

" I knew the moment I found my first mite, it was going to change the way I bee keep forever. "

And it has.

"Every beekeeping technique, just throw it out the window."

Because of the intensive treatments required to manage varroa mite, Sophia says her workload has increased fivefold.

Sophia says rising fuel costs and the cost of treating hives for varroa mite are making beekeepers question whether the lifestyle is worth it. (Supplied)

The cost of treatments, along with higher fuel prices and more imported honey on Australian shelves, means running a business is almost not viable.

" I was crunching numbers at the end of the season and I was like, 'How do I still not have enough money to live, to eat food?' "

Sophia says honey production alone would not keep her business alive, so pollinating crops like almonds had become an important source of income.

"This is a critical industry.

"One in every three mouthfuls of food that we consume is because of pollinators.

"We do need beekeepers, that's the reality."

'Beekeeping gets in your blood'

And that reality is what drives The Bee Drover.

Sophia admits she's been under "unbelievably high stress".

"But my dad says beekeeping gets in your blood, and I think that's kind of true.

" My family has been so passionate about it for over a century, the idea of walking away breaks my heart a bit. "

Loading

She hopes her storytelling series can help change consumer behaviour.

"We need some more things in place to safeguard our industry from fake and adulterated honey.

"How we do that is out of my hands; I'm just a beekeeper.

"I just love telling our story because I think it's such a cool story to tell."

World.title: Young men in the crosshairs of 'morally disturbed' online crime
World.content:
Jack thought he'd met a potential date on Hinge. Turns out he'd matched with his blackmailer.

"I matched with this woman on Hinge and pretty quickly she asked to move over to Instagram," Jack said of the exchange in 2024.

The conversation shifted from Hinge to Instagram. (Supplied/BTN High)

After a few basic questions, the conversation took a turn.

Messages exchanged between Jack and the blackmailer. (Supplied/BTN High)

Jack was asked how he felt about exchanging nudes.



"I was kind of nervous about it, that it's not something that I'm used to," he said.

"They were not overly pushy, but kind of encouraging me, and … at the time, in the moment, it was like, 'Oh, this person's like, kind of interested enough to be patient and try to sort of help make the moment happen.'"

Jack was asked to exchange nude photos. (Supplied/BTN High)

Jack received an explicit photo and eventually felt comfortable enough to send one back.

The exchange continued for about 10 minutes.

"It started to feel a little bit weird because there was no real exchange of words in between, which I guess was kind of my expectation," Jack said.

Then the threats began.

"That was when they sent me, obviously, like a pre-written, very long message," Jack said.

"It was a screenshot of a group set up with all of my contacts on Instagram, and then a message."

Jack says he was sent a threat that looked pre-written. (Supplied/BTN High)

He was the victim of a sextortion scam — a form of blackmail involving the non-consensual sharing of sexual images, either for money, manipulation or for the gratification of the perpetrator.

"Sextortion is when really morally disturbed people try to exploit human sexuality, which is a totally natural, fundamental part of human life," Jack said.

Authorities say this type of scam is on the rise around the world.

Who is being targeted?

Between July 1, 2025 and December 31, 2025, eSafety received 2,206 individual complaints of sexual extortion in Australia.

Most victims were young men and boys, some younger than 15.

"Unfortunately we're starting to see these organised criminals targeting younger, younger people, younger boys, 14, 15, 16. That's a little bit more rare, but we really worry about that," eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant said.

eSafety received the most complaints about sexual extortion from men aged 18 to 24. (Supplied: eSafety Commissioner)

Authorities say advances in AI are making the problem worse, giving criminals easy access to an alias or helping them create deep-fake sexualised images.

That's what happened to Mateo.

Mateo was targeted on Snapchat by a sextortion scammer. (BTN High)

"A couple of years ago, I received a friend request online through Snapchat from someone who I believed to be genuine," he said.

"It said I had about 40 mutual friends with them. Even their Snap score was, like, high enough to be legitimate.

"So all the signs did point towards it being a real person, and I do like to think of myself as pretty switched on online."

Mateo accepted the friend request after seeing they had 40 mutual friends. (Supplied/BTN High)

But as soon as Mateo accepted the request, he was threatened with fake nudes of himself.

"I went back into my chat with them, and then they had these fake, like, explicit images that they had facilitated to make it look like I had sent them," he said.

"They said if I don't send them money, they would leak all these pictures to all these group chats with my friends and family.

"They were asking for about $500 at the time."

Mateo received this threat. (Supplied/BTN High)

Mateo says that even though the images weren't real, the impact was.

"I remember thinking my reputation, my relationships could be destroyed in a matter of seconds," he said.

"And it was really weird because I felt really vulnerable just from my bedroom, which is not — it wasn't the best feeling.

"My first instinct was, 'Should I just pay them?' But I learned that giving them what they want definitely will not make it stop.

"So the best thing to do is stop engaging, keep the evidence, report it, and tell someone you trust."

Mateo reported his blackmailer to the police in 2023.

Jack and Mateo's scammers did not release the images.

What is being done?

The Australian Federal Police (AFP) says it takes sextortion reports seriously.

"Sextortion is a terrible crime," Human Exploitation branch commander Joanne Cameron said.

Joanne Cameron says it can be hard to convict sextortionists because they are often based overseas. (BTN High)

But prosecutions can be difficult.

"It's really hard for the police to find these offenders and investigate, bring them to court like we normally would and prosecute them, because they're often overseas," Commander Cameron said.

Ms Inman Grant said there were some "major" organised criminals behind the scams.

"One is known as the Yahoo Boys, and they're based out of Nigeria," she said.

"But we also are seeing call centres being weaponised in the evening in places like Manila or Delhi. So they can come from anywhere."

Julie Inman Grant says there are organised criminals behind sextortion. (ABC News: Craig Hansen)

That is why the eSafety Commissioner has asked for social media and messaging platforms to take more responsibility.

"Social media companies aren't doing enough," Ms Inman Grant said.

"The only reason I could think of that they wouldn't want to protect their users and, say, get rid of those fake and impostor accounts is because it doesn't support their revenue generation and business model."

The social media companies contacted by BTN all said they took sextortion seriously and had proactive and reactive measures in place to address it.

Loading...

A Meta spokesperson said the company was using technology to detect grooming and sextortion in chats with minors, that it blurred nude images in DMs and warned people of the risks before they sent them.

A Snapchat spokesperson said it was able to detect and remove predators before they caused harm, and that it had 24/7 safety teams that acted on reports.

A TikTok spokesperson said the platform actively removed content, terminated accounts and prevented scammers from creating new ones when there was clear evidence of unlawful behaviour.

Jack says he and his friends were able to laugh about the experience afterwards. (BTN High)

It is not your fault

Dealing with sextortion can be a traumatic experience.

"My immediate reaction was shock and my heart started racing," Jack says.

"But … I didn't feel like the world was caving in on me.

"I immediately sort of thought to call my best friend and get her support. She was an absolute angel, guardian angel."

While he was on the phone with his best friend, Jude, the scammer continued to flood Jack's inbox with threats and spammed him with calls.

Jack eventually picked up.

"I was just kind of stalling them as much as I could whilst my friend passed any information I got over to the police," he says.

Jack says he took power away from his blackmailer by refusing to feel ashamed.

"I was confident that I'd behaved with enough integrity that people's perception of me wouldn't be that bad if it did come out," he says.

Jack says he refused to feel ashamed about the ordeal. (Supplied/BTN High)

Jack and Mateo's blackmailers were not charged.

Two years later, Jack says the whole situation actually brought him and his friends closer together.

"Me and my friends were able to, to laugh about [it] afterwards and kind of see a more positive side of the situation, have an outcome that wasn't just OK, but almost like a funny story, a memory that we bonded over rather than something that was horrific to deal with," he says.

What to do if you are targeted

If you're the victim of a sextortion scam, authorities say you should not panic and you should not pay.

Sextortion threats rise Major online platforms are accused of failing to deploy readily available technology to detect well-known blackmail tactics.

"So what you do need to do is first of all stop the chat with that person completely. You can collect some information about that person, whether it's their profile or the URL or what platform you're on," Commander Cameron said.

"You can report it to the platform, and they can block the accounts. You can report it to eSafety for the take-down of that material if it's circulating."

Ms Inmam Grant said eSafety had a "98 per cent success rate in terms of getting intimate imagery down".

"So what might seem like the end of the world as you're going through it — there are people who are here to help and who want to help," she said.

Subscribe to the BTN Newsletter Do you want to be notified when the next BTN High stories arrive? Join our weekly newsletter.

Commander Cameron says coming forward won't get you into trouble.

"The seriousness of sextortion, that's the issue, and you being victimised is the issue, and that's our focus … to help you get out of that situation," she said.

While being caught in the middle of a scam like this might feel isolating, Jack and Mateo say it's important to remember that you're not alone.

"Speak to someone as soon as you can, especially a friend or a loved one, because there is no shame in doing something like this," Jack said.

"The person who has all the shame is the scammer, not you."

"Asking for help is a sign of strength. It's not embarrassment," Mateo said.

World.title: Star rugby teen turns down PNG as Lomax is unveiled as ‘Chief 005’
World.content:
Updated SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Star rugby teen turns down PNG as Lomax is unveiled as ‘Chief 005’ Iain Payten Updated July 26, 2026 — 4:46pm ,first published 1:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian rugby has had a major win with rising superstar Treyvon Pritchard turning down the PNG Chiefs and Sydney Roosters to sign a long-term contract extension with the Queensland Reds and Rugby Australia. But the Chiefs haven’t wasted any time in moving on, with cross-code star Zac Lomax confirming on Sunday he will be headed to PNG on a three-year deal in 2028. Treyvon Pritchard scores his first Super Rugby try for Queensland in May. Getty Images Pritchard became the most in-demand teenager across both codes this year after the Chiefs made him one of their first targets ahead of the 2028 arrival of the NRL expansion club. In his first year out of school, Pritchard made his debut for the Reds in Super Rugby Pacific and the utility back – who plays centre, wing and fullback – was dominant for the Junior Wallabies at the recent under-20s world championships in Georgia.



This masthead revealed Pritchard, 19, and his 21-year-old brother, Kadin (who plays for the Brumbies), were pursued by the PNG Chiefs and made tax-free offers after meeting club officials in Brisbane. The Roosters also joined the chase and recently expressed interest in bringing Treyvon to the Bondi club when his deal with rugby expired at the end of 2027. But after Rugby Australia and the Reds countered with a strong offer for Treyvon to extend his stay, the outstanding youngster agreed to terms on a three-year deal late last week, according to informed sources unable to comment publicly due to the confidentiality of the negotiations. Zac Lomax has signed with the PNG Chiefs. Getty Images The PNG Chiefs, who saw Pritchard as having a future in the halves in league, were informed of his decision last week. As forecast, the Chiefs have finalised a three-year deal with Lomax after flying him and his partner to Port Moresby on the weekend. Lomax was announced as “Chief 005” on the club’s social media accounts on Sunday along with footage of him being introduced to the crowd at a PNG domestic league game.



“I am super honoured to have committed to you guys,” Lomax said. “We are going to shock the NRL, I am telling you, and I can’t wait to be a part of it.” Lomax is sidelined with a groin injury, but is expected to return to action in for to six weeks. He will see out his deal with the Western Force and RA before returning to league at the end of 2027. The Chiefs are also deep in discussions with Joey Manu to make a return from rugby.



Securing Pritchard is a significant victory for Australian rugby. Many teenage stars have moved to the NRL in the past decade. Eleven players who featured in the recent State of Origin series had played for Sydney or Brisbane schoolboy rugby teams and junior rep rugby. The importance of Pritchard’s retention sits alongside Max Jorgensen last year re-signing through to the end of 2031, but the true value will likely grow in the coming years as the youngster continues to develop and get more time on the game’s biggest stages. Like Jorgensen, he will become a face of the game in Australia. The potential for Pritchard to become an Olympian in 2028 was no doubt one of rugby’s selling points, given he is also an accomplished sevens player.



The Junior Wallabies narrowly missed the semi-finals of the under-20s event in Georgia, but the teenager was named in the team of the tournament after some eye-catching performances, including one against eventual runners-up France. Pritchard’s sizzling footwork, speed and strength helped him beat 25 defenders in three pool games and run for 350 metres, of which 250 metres were post-contact. But his tournament was cut short by a broken leg, suffered in a hip-drop tackle against Wales. He underwent surgery last week. It is hoped Pritchard will be back in action to potentially play for Australia A in late October against the USA. If fit, some argue Pritchard should even go on the Wallabies’ spring tour, even if only on a non-playing development basis. Former Wallabies coach Michael Cheika used that approach for several years, and took young future stars such as Taniela Tupou, Rob Valetini, Izzy Perese, Jack Dempsey and Andrew Kellaway away between 2016 and 2018. New Wallabies coach Les Kiss will gather with his first squad in Sydney this week, after naming a 34-player group last week for the two Tests against Japan on August 8 in Osaka and August 15 in Townsville.



Speaking about his selection plans for the first few months of his tenure, Kiss revealed he would continue to experiment with players to “explore the depth” ahead of the World Cup next year. “It’s important that the players that played the recent [Nations Championship] series are seen, and [that] they see me and the new coaching team,” Kiss said on Nine’s Wide World of Sports on Sunday. “But over the next, you know, 10 Test matches, I’m going to stretch it out a bit and make sure I see a few players as well in other positions.” But Kiss said five-eighth would not be a position he plans to chop and change unnecessarily. “There have been challenges in that position over the last two years – injuries have got in the way, and we haven’t been able to get consistency,” he said.



“I’ve stuck with the three that they had in the Nations Cup. I want to try and keep that as consistent as possible in the next few Test matches.” Waratahs defy doubters to win seventh title After an uncharacteristic mid-season wobble when they lost two games, the Waratahs not only resumed normal service in smashing the Fijian Drua in the Super Rugby Women’s grand final on Saturday, they arguably broke new ground. The Tahs bounced back from defeats in the regular season to the Western Force and Queensland to smash Fiji 34-17 in Ba, in a six-tries-to-three performance to claim a record seventh Super W-Super Rugby Women’s title in nine seasons. Loading



Two tries from the home side in the final 10 minutes reduced the winning margin after the Waratahs dominated for most of the game and established a 34-5 lead, courtesy of two tries to Amelia Whitaker and one each to Rosie Ferguson, Maya Stewart and Desi Miller. Returning Wallaroos fullback Caitlyn Halse was also in the middle of much of it, with lovely assists. But while the star backs doing their thing was par for course in another NSW title, there was no question the powerhouse performance from the Waratahs forwards was the driving force in the win. In what was arguably the most complete Waratahs performance in any of their Super W deciders, their forwards muscled up from the outset and dominated Fiji at their strength. The sharp connection of forwards and backs then built up momentum for NSW that proved, at times, unstoppable. Wallaroos prop Faliki Pohiva was immense in attack and defence, and her second-half try was just reward for a superb game. The 25-year-old from western Sydney was also named player of the final. Faliki Pohiva crashes over for a try in a superb overall performance. Getty Images



The NSW pack allowed dynamic halves Tia Hinds and Waiaria Ellis to apply huge pressure. Despite only being two games into their new partnership, the duo have during the past two weeks made a strong claim to be the Wallaroos halves, too. The skill and strength of the Waratahs forwards in Fiji points to the potential for a competitive showing against the Auckland Blues women next Saturday in Sydney in the Women’s Super Rugby champions final. The Blues also completed a hat-trick of Super Rugby Aupiki titles when they snatched victory from Matatū, scoring a late try to beat the South Islanders 28-21. The trans-Tasman winner’s showdown began last year when the Blues dispatched NSW 36-5. The Waratahs celebrate their Super Rugby Women’s crown. Getty Images



The Blues pack was able to get on top in the forwards and stretch the Matatū defence out wide thereafter, and that has been the pattern for a lot of trans-Tasman Test rugby as well. But the smartly coached Waratahs pack showed enough in Fiji to suggest they will be up for the battle against the Blues on Saturday. Waratahs captain Emily Chancellor paid tribute to the 34 players who had played during an injury-plagued season for NSW, which had rivals hoping the sky blue juggernaut might have finally run out of steam. “I want to shout out to every single player that’s been part of this program this year,” Chancellor said. “What an incredible group. I feel like rugby in Australia wrote us off – we lose two games and that’s it for us. This is the response, and I’m so proud of this team. I couldn’t be more proud of the way we played today and the belief we have in each other.” The Women’s Super Rugby champions final will be played at Leichhardt Oval on Saturday.

World.title: Malvern bungalow sells for $2.66m to buyer who wants to tear it down
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Malvern bungalow sells for $2.66m to buyer who wants to tear it down Wes Mountain July 26, 2026 — 4:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Californian bungalow in a coveted Malvern street sold for $2.66 million at auction on Saturday, with the buyer planning to tear it down to build her “dream home”. The well-maintained three-bedroom house at 32 Jordan Street is on a 576-square-metre block and features original Baltic pine floors, front verandah and classically landscaped gardens, all walking distance to Tooronga Road shops, Harold Holt Swim Centre and High Street. It had a price guide of $2.2 million to $2.4 million, and a reserve of $2.35 million. The house was sold as part of a deceased estate. The property was one of 692 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne last week. By Saturday evening, Domain Group had recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 55 per cent from 464 reported results throughout the week, while 94 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate.



After last week’s preliminary clearance rate almost hit the 60 per cent threshold that indicates a balanced market, this week’s results suggest the market continues to favour buyers, despite a shortage of supply in the traditionally quieter winter months. The clearance rate was 72 per cent this time last year. Related Article Auctions Downsizer cries with joy as she wins $866,000 northern Melbourne home Ray White Ashburton agent Max Hedley said bidding for Jordan Street opened at $2.2 million, with four bidders competing. Two main bidders traded $50,000 increments throughout, sending the eventual price more than $300,000 above the reserve. “It was unexpected,” Hedley said. “It just kept going.” He believed that while the market for homes over $2 million had slowed, the scarcity of original Malvern properties had led to a “surprising” result.



“In those ... streets in Malvern, there’s not a lot of properties left like that,” he said. The property was advertised with an artist’s impression of a potential renovation – subject to council approval – and Hedley said the buyer, who lived in nearby Caulfield East, had purchased to “take it down and rebuild”. An artist’s impression of what a potential update to the Malvern home could look like, subject to council approval. Ray White Ashburton “It just showcases the fact that the heart is still beating for the right properties,” Hedley said. In Yarraville, a freestanding two-bedroom Victorian passed in on a single vendor bid of $950,000, despite a campaign with “a lot of love” for the home.



Nestled in the Yarraville village, a “short stroll” to shops and the historic Sun Theatre, 16 Norfolk Street features a north-facing yard, modern updates and had a price guide of $950,000 to $1 million, with a reserve of $1.05 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. While updated, Compton Green agent Dee Gibson said the vendors had preserved much of the original Victorian features, including its pressed iron ornamentation. “It’s quite a quaint, beautifully styled home,” she said.



Gibson said the auction opened with a vendor bid of $950,000 and passed in without either of two previously interested parties putting their hand up. Related Article Melbourne house prices ‘A long winter for house prices’: Melbourne market’s steepest drop in four years “It seems typical of the market at the moment,” she said, noting the sale would now convert to private treaty. She thought it was in a difficult spot for the current market, but was sure it would find the right buyer. “The first home buying market is still strong,” she said. “When we get to the $1 million mark ... that’s where there’s that stretch. Can buyers go the extra mile for something a bit better? That’s the question.”



In Port Melbourne, a two-bedroom modern townhouse sold in post-auction negotiations for $1.14 million to a “seasoned purchaser and seller” who beat an eager but nervous first home buyer. Split across two levels, 6/97-101 Cruikshank Street features light-filled rooms, a red-brick facade and large balcony, and is a short walk to Port Melbourne beach and Gasworks Arts Precinct. It had a price guide of $1.1 million to $1.2 million and a reserve of $1.14 million. Buxton Port Phillip agent Nancy Yang said the opening $1 million bid came from the first home buyer – the first bid of his home-buying journey. From there, the two bidders went back and forth, with $5000 bids from the first home buyer and larger $10,000 and $20,000 bids from the more “seasoned” eventual buyer. The home passed in at $1.12 million, after the first home buyer hit the top of his budget, selling in post-auction negotiations.



Yang said the buyer lived with her parents while saving to make her next move, and would be sharing the home with her dog, using the second bedroom to work from home. The home had been an investment property “for many years”, but Yang said the vendors were selling following state and federal tax changes. “The market’s not down,” she said, noting that renters were getting a better opportunity to buy after an “exponential” rise in rents, competing with Sydney and Brisbane buyers who were still keen on Melbourne investment properties. “It’s just a re-shifting.”

World.title: Trump is back announcing a 2028 presidential bid. It’s dangerous to assume he’s joking
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Opinion Trump is back announcing a 2028 presidential bid. It’s dangerous to assume he’s joking Cory Alpert Former White House staffer July 26, 2026 — 4:42pm

July 26, 2026 — 4:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Six years into his presidency, Donald Trump has ended his boycott of the annual White House Correspondents Dinner. In a speech that included numerous attacks on his political enemies, Trump started and ended by joking about his plans to run again for president. He pulled out a “Trump 2028” hat, with the tagline “rewrite the rules”, that is now for sale on his website for $US55 ($79). Presidents are expected to make jokes at this dinner, as Trump did on Friday night. But Trump has spent most of his second term making sure that no one can be certain if he really is joking about running for a third term, despite the explicit ban in the US Constitution. Trump’s will-he-won’t-he drama has instead frozen Republican efforts for succession planning. In 2016, when Barack Obama was term-limited, both parties had already begun their unofficial primaries by this point and we know from Joe Biden’s late withdrawal in 2024 just how damaging it can be when a figurehead of the party won’t let go. Was President Donald Trump attempting to throw his hat in the ring at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner on Friday? AP Trump started playing this game in March 2025, weeks after being sworn in for a second time, when he told NBC News that he was serious about a third term and spoke about the ways it could be possible. He has mentioned running again at least 18 times, moving between jokes and serious escalations, before conceding at the end of 2025 that the Constitution prohibited him from running again. Because he keeps opening and closing the door, no one can quite be sure what Trump intends to do, but it has empowered the president while freezing the Republican Party.



Those in Trump’s bubble seem to be confused as well. Hats are for sale. One of Trump’s closest allies in the House, Tennessee congressman Andy Ogles, has proposed a constitutional amendment that would permit Trump, but not predecessors like Obama or Clinton, to run for a third term. Steve Bannon has said that Trump will run again, with his strategy to be revealed at “the appropriate time”. Chief of staff Susie Wiles has said that Trump is not serious about a third term, and that he’s aware of the constitutional limits. Speaker Mike Johnson has said that Trump is “trolling” Democrats and that the president enjoys seeing the opposition party with their “hair on fire”. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump’s power is at its peak. He has reason to be fearful of what’s coming Cory Alpert Former White House staffer And yet, when Alan Dershowitz, the lawyer who was on the defence team for Donald Trump’s first impeachment, released a book-length plan on how Trump can remain in office, a White House spokesperson said only that the American people would be lucky enough to keep Trump in office. It is a mistake to dismiss all of Trump’s rhetoric as unserious, as many do. Yes, some quips appear to be improv, off the cuff and unconsidered. Many more of his ideas are only discarded after they meet the institutional realities of Congress, the courts, or the markets.



But hyperbole has been a feature of his Trump’s campaigning, and he’s been deadly serious on what might have once seemed like outlandish plans for massive tariff increases, slashes to government programs, and expansion of immigration enforcement. This air of uncertainty gives Trump continued leverage over his party as the 2028 nominating contest begins to take shape. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance are the leading contenders for the Republican nomination in 2028 and have built profiles that extend well past their official roles. But no candidate can offer a future that extends beyond Trump while this ambiguity about his intentions hangs over their party. Contrast that with the work that the Democratic Party is doing to shape their primary. It has spent a year reshuffling its early primary calendar, this week landing on my home state of South Carolina as the important first state, replacing Iowa’s historic role. Prospective candidates have been travelling, raising money and publishing the obligatory campaign books. Republicans are not only asking who should lead their party but who Trump might eventually permit to succeed him. Those are two very different questions.



It is impossible to predict what Trump will do in 2028. If he sought to get his name on the ballot, election officials in each state would make the initial decisions, likely along partisan lines. Those decisions could be expected to end up at the Supreme Court, which although ideologically conservative has been willing to step in when Trump claims too much unilateral authority over the Constitution. Just last month, they overruled his effort to revoke birthright citizenship, saying he had no singular authority to change constitutional rules Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump’s three-pronged threat to American democracy Peter Hartcher Political and international editor But Trump does not need a plausible path to the ballot to have power over the race. As long as the possibility remains alive, every potential Republican successor must wait and demonstrate their loyalty. The question of Trump running for a third term should be settled under the Constitution. The 22nd amendment says that “no person shall be elected to the office of president more than twice”. It also prohibits tricks like the one Trump has openly mused about, in which he runs as JD Vance’s vice-president, only to replace Vance on their first day in office. The vast majority of constitutional scholars have said there is no loophole that Trump can reasonably exploit. But the Republican Party is largely still behaving as though its future depends on what Trump decides. By making sure that no firm ground exists on which any candidate can stand, Trump has turned political uncertainty into leverage over his party. They remain paralysed by his influence.



The irony of this moment is that the White House Correspondents Dinner in 2012 is where Barack Obama told Trump to his face that he would never be president. A decade and a half later, it’s where Trump is keeping alive the question of if he will ever stop being president. Cory Alpert is a PhD researcher at the University of Melbourne looking at the impact of AI on democracy. He previously served the Biden-Harris administration. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Bailey-Ashcroft double act powers Lions to seventh straight win
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Bailey-Ashcroft double act powers Lions to seventh straight win Nick Wright July 26, 2026 — 4:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The price tag being attached to Zac Bailey’s name must be increasing by the day, as the Brisbane Lions’ sensation produced a masterclass to extend his side’s winning run to seven. The Gabba became the 26-year-old’s stomping ground once again as the two-time defending champions conquered Port Adelaide 19.12 (129) to 9.13 (67). Zac Bailey was in top form. via Getty Images The off-contract Bailey, who is being headhunted by Adelaide and reportedly weighing up a multi-million dollar long-term deal to make the move, was a man on a Sunday afternoon mission – kicking three goals and finishing with 26 disposals. In a clash which largely became a seesawing tussle for ascendancy in the first half, Brisbane’s class ultimately proved to be too much for a young Power outfit to overcome, with Bailey’s third-quarter surge building the momentum needed to keep their rivals at arm’s length.



It began as the Will Ashcroft show, whose deft dribble through traffic for the contest’s first goal was swiftly followed by an assist for Kai Lohmann’s first of two majors. Ashcroft continued his knack for producing memorable moments by kicking his second from a tight set shot angle as the three-quarter time siren sounded, before emerging from the break with a pair of goal assists for Logan Morris and Eric Hipwood. Will Ashcroft of the Lions in action during the round 20 clash. AFL Photos via Getty Images Those moments sparked a fourth-quarter onslaught, kicking seven goals to two, after only leading by nine points at halftime – an incredible Charlie Cameron mark to kick his second goal in his 200th Lions appearance the moment of the term, before he added a third from a set shot. During the rare moments Ashcroft was kept contained – still finishing with 30 touches – Bailey took charge.



His speed was a constant nightmare for Port Adelaide, but it was his support play that was equally pivotal – lurking near a spoil and launching a 50-metre angled shot for his second goal, a far more impressive effort than his uncontested mark in the opening term for his first. It was not long before he had his third, as Cam Rayner – who produced two magic goals through contests of his own – shrugged off a tackle and found a handball for his superstar teammate to strike cleanly. Balyn O’Brien of the Power competes for the ball against Charlie Cameron and Hugh McCluggage of the Lions. via Getty Images While superstar Lachie Neale was kept relatively quiet, the Ashcroft-Bailey combination kept the Power guessing and signalled that this team had endless ways to win and pile on the pressure.



Is the McCluggage of old back? Josh Dunkley teased during the week that Hugh McCluggage was closing in on the sort of performance which typified his career-best 2025 campaign, having spent plenty of time on the sidelines to nurse a calf issue sustained back in Opening Round. “It’s obviously tough being injury interrupted and trying to manage all those different things, but we know Hughy’s best is not too far away,” Dunkley said. Hugh McCluggage. via Getty Images “Last preseason [leading into 2025] he actually missed a lot of it, and came back and had one of his best years ever, so I’m sure he got a few lessons from that experience.



“I think he’s not too far away from being that dominant player we know he can be.” Dunkley’s premonition ended up being bang on the money, with producing his most involved performance of the season as the Power sought to lock down his midfield teammate, Lachie Neale. McCluggage’s 29 possessions were his most in a game this year, and he added a goal to his resume when he was left unmarked inside 50. What was perhaps most pleasing about his outing was the amount of work he did in contest, and he appeared to be moving more freely than he has at any point in 2026. It is an ominous sign for the rest of the competition as Brisbane cemented their standing in the top four. They were winning without getting the best out of the All Australian, but if they start doing so now, even the ladder-leading Dockers will be watching of their shoulder.



Will Oscar add a new layer to Lions’ assault? While the Lions have restored their ambitions for a third-straight flag on the back of what is now a seventh-straight win, they may be about to get stronger still. Prized off season recruit Oscar Allen has not been sighted in a Brisbane jumper for roughly three months after suffering a foot fracture in the round seven battle with Adelaide, but his performance in reserve grade will come as a relief to coach Chris Fagan. Fagan hinted during the week Allen’s rain-effected comeback through the VFL last week was a difficult gauge on whether he was fit enough to line up in the top level, but the former West Coast captain’s two goals and 10 disposals against North Melbourne would no doubt be a relieving sight. Young forward Logan Morris has been a consistent pillar up front for the premiers this season, and he took his season goal tally to 47 with a three-goal haul on Sunday.



But should Allen force his way back into the fold, it will simply add another layer to this Brisbane attack which is gathering momentum. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Pleased as Punch: Orphaned monkey receives 2500 birthday cards
World.content:
WorldAsiaAnimals Pleased as Punch: Orphaned monkey receives 2500 birthday cards Emily Smith July 26, 2026 — 4:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Punch the monkey rose to fame after being abandoned by its mother and left only with a stuffed toy orangutan for comfort. The orphaned macaque was bullied by other monkeys at Ichikawa City Zoo, near Tokyo, and would often be seen wandering its enclosure alone. Punch plays at Ichikawa City Zoological and Botanical Garden east of Tokyo this week. AP Photo/Eugene Hoshiko But as Punch turns one on Sunday, the monkey is surrounded by new friends and has been inundated with thousands of birthday cards from fans around the world. Many of the cards and other messages fill the walls at an indoor Punch exhibit, where visitors can watch a video chronicling the animal’s early days.



It is believed Punch was abandoned by its mother because of exhaustion. Zookeepers nursed the monkey and gave it the toy to develop its gripping ability – something newborn macaques need to survive. “As Punch was trying very hard, struggling to live each day, his two keepers did everything they could while other staff watched over him,” the head of the zoo, Takashi Yasunaga, said. The zoo has been inundated with thousands of birthday cards for Punch from fans around the world. AP Photo/Eugene Hoshiko Many of the cards and other messages fill the walls at an indoor Punch exhibit. AP Photo/Eugene Hoshiko Punch still attracted big crowds, and had received some 2500 birthday cards from inside and outside Japan, Yasunaga added.



Kumi Ishizawa, a Kobe resident who was at the exhibit, said she learnt of Punch’s story from social media earlier this year. From then on, overcoming her illness to see the monkey became her goal. “He moved me ... I kept on telling myself that I’m going to get well and come visit to see Punch,” said Ishizawa, who has recovered and visited the zoo after a business trip. Six-day-old Punch with his stuffed orangutan in a basket at the zoo. Ichikawa City Zoological and Botanical Garden via AP Loading “And here I am, I made it. I’m very happy I could finally see him in person.”



Yeye Lights, a long-time Ichikawa resident, had never visited the zoo until her daughter told her about Punch, and now has an annual visitor pass. “I have a cake for Punch-kun, I’m celebrating with my friends,” Lights said, using an affectionate Japanese honorific for boys. World.title: Brisbane Lions flick switch, turn off Power in second-half rout
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Brisbane Lions flick switch, turn off Power in second-half rout July 26, 2026 — 4:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brisbane have continued their push for an historic second premiership “three peat” this century, demolishing a depleted Port Adelaide by 59 points for a seventh successive victory. But the Lions had to work hard to shake off the Power, who hung in until midway through the third quarter before the home side exploded, kicking 14 to 5 goals in a crushing second half to win 19.12 (126) to 9.13 (67). The result leaves Chris Fagan’s men fourth on the ladder, a game clear of Adelaide with four rounds to play, and with challenging games against Carlton, Hawthorn, the Gold Coast Suns and Collingwood to come. Brisbane Lions livewire Charlie Cameron. AFL Photos On form, however, the Lions should fear none of them.



While the Power worked hard early to close space and force the Lions to use the ball more by hand instead of employing their usual precise kicking game, the Lions had too much class and too many avenues to goal. Sunday’s game split open in the second half, with both sides going goal for goal from the centre ball-up before the Lions cut loose, finishing with seven majors to three in the third quarter. The decisive blows were struck by Sam Draper, who plucked a centre-square ruck contest and galloped to 60 metres before launching, and Will Ashcroft, who extended the Lions’ lead to 29 points on the siren. Port Adelaide finally folded in the last quarter as the Lions shifted into overdrive, turning what had been a hard-fought game into a procession. Ashcroft was superb with two goals from 30 possessions, while Zac Bailey was destructive with three majors from his 26 and Harris Andrews was typically impassable in defence with 13 marks.



Perhaps the most encouraging sign was the inside game of Hugh McCluggage, who had his best match for the year, finishing with 29 possessions, five clearances and a goal as an inside midfielder. The Lions’ defensive intent was shown late in the final quarter, when Draper spoiled a Port shot on goal on the line and celebrated as if he had kicked one himself. Brisbane’s forwards also fired, with Logan Morris, Kai Lohmann and Charlie Cameron kicking three goals apiece. Jason Horne-Francis was a shining light for Port, keeping them in the contest with a superb kicking exhibition that resulted in nine score involvements and three direct assists. But without Port’s usual centre-square assassin Zak Butters, Horne-Francis lacked midfield support, with the Power doing well to stay with the Lions for as long as they did.



They were also let down by their set-shot kicking, with spearhead Mitch Georgiades ending with 2.4 for the game. AAP
