World.title: Chickens, Chairman Mao and spiced tea with the neighbours: Welcome to ‘the real China’
World.content:
WorldAsiaChina relations Chickens, Chairman Mao and spiced tea with the neighbours: Welcome to ‘the real China’ Lisa Visentin Updated July 26, 2026 — 4:07pm ,first published July 26, 2026 — 9:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What in the World, a free weekly newsletter from our foreign correspondents, is sent every Thursday. Below is an excerpt. Sign up to get the whole newsletter delivered to your inbox. Xingming village, China: Perched atop a hill in a small village in central China, Li Zhiying’s family guesthouse has a spectacular view. Just beyond the front door is a vista of a pristine reservoir, ringed by pine forests and framed by mountain ranges flossed with low-hanging clouds. Li Zhiying grew up in poverty in Hunan province in central China and later returned to his hometown to open a guesthouse. Lisa Visentin Along the cul-de-sac that winds past his house, Li’s neighbours tend crops of beans, chillies, pumpkin and corn in small plots near their homes.



Village dogs bark and scrap in the street and chickens roam freely. By the roadside, an elderly man is picking the Sichuan peppercorns that will spice the tea and tingle the tongues of neighbours who will pop by in the evening for a daily ritual of gossip and card-playing. I’ve come to Li’s hometown of Xingming in China’s central Hunan province to spend three days exploring a different side of the modern China story that frequently makes headlines. The ordinariness of rural life. Loading Xingming village, in Hunan Province, central China. Lisa Visentin A snapshot of the so-called “real China” that’s more representative of everyday life for millions of Chinese people than dancing robots, drone light shows and the breakneck speed of AI development that is reshaping tech hubs in Beijing, Shenzhen and Hangzhou.



The evening I arrive, we wander down the street to the home of the retired village party secretary, a local Communist Party official, whose wife is serving slices of watermelon and tea in plastic cups to any neighbour who stops for a chat. Neighbours pop by in the evening for a daily ritual of gossip and card-playing. Lisa Visentin “Hello Australia, welcome, please enjoy our village,” one elder tells me, using a translation app. This is Chairman Mao country, where portraits of China’s former supreme leader hang in the homes of older villagers, his reputation unspoiled by history’s verdict – in the West at least – of the calamity caused by the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution. “Mao is like a god to us,” a local party cadre from the neighbouring province tells me over lunch at the guesthouse. “He understood the ordinary people.”



The nearest market is 5 kilometres away in a small, unremarkable township, where everyone is curious about the visiting foreigner (me). There’s plenty of pointing and waving and lots of smiles. “Never!” an old villager running a pork stall responds when I ask how often foreigners come to the market. Nearby, a man is loading hunks of fresh meat into the boot of his car lined with just a piece of cardboard. Another vendor is selling a freshly slaughtered whole dog, its fur shaved off but skin intact. It’s a confronting sight for the uninitiated, though Li tells me he has never seen dog meat for sale here before.



By his own admission, Li forewarns would-be guests that his home is located in a remote rural village that most Chinese people have never heard of. There’s no tourist infrastructure, and quotidian village life is slow-paced and perhaps even boring. “If you are looking for a comfortable, easy introduction to China, this may not be the place,” he says on the guesthouse website. Li Zhiying and his friend, Li Mi, paddling on the reservoir that sustains the local village. Lisa Visentin But he believes visitors will be charmed by the warmth and authenticity of the locals, and the unrefined beauty of the Chinese countryside. For the most part, this is not the side of China that has bedazzled the wave of influencers who have arrived under the government’s soft-power masterstroke of visa-free travel, which has now been extended to more than 70 countries, Australia included.



They have flooded Instagram and TikTok with effusive videos about China’s smartphone-powered megacities, with a cashless economy, gleaming skyscrapers, robots that deliver food to the hotel door, and futuristic electric vehicles that cruise silently around clean streets. The comparison is stark. There’s little tangible wealth in villages such as Xingming, but community bonds are strong. People eat what they grow, or fish from the reservoir, and share what they have with their neighbours. Villagers fish from the reservoir. Lisa Visentin Some of the older generation speak patchy Mandarin, preferring their local dialect. This has tethered them to their home province and added to the language barriers with outsiders who arrive, as I have, reliant on AI tools to navigate them. ChatGPT, though an impressive translator, struggles with dialects. Younger people, meanwhile, have decamped for the cities looking for work, often leaving behind their children to be raised by their grandparents.



“My children have gone to work in the 3D printing industry,” one woman says, as she picks beans from her garden while her granddaughter plays nearby. But the crushing poverty that once afflicted Xingming, and mired families such as Li’s in destitution, has largely been eliminated. Portraits of Mao Zedong are a common sight in the homes of older residents in parts of rural China. Lisa Visentin To get to Xingming from Beijing, it’s a five-hour journey on high-speed rail to the nearest station in Yueyang – a small, lower-tier city by Chinese standards with only 5 million people (about the size of Sydney). Then it’s an hour-long drive through the countryside. I’ve come specifically to meet Li, a softly spoken 36-year-old architect turned aspiring AI developer, whose life has skirted the same grooves as China’s own recent trajectory in many ways.



He rose out of poverty off the back of China’s economic juggernaut, which from the 1990s onwards lifted hundreds of millions of people like him with it. Li then crested the wave of the country’s property boom before crashing with its collapse, shuttering his own construction company within six months of opening it in 2022. Since then, he’s looked for ways to reinvent himself, firstly in e-commerce, joining a friend’s large online company selling adult products to consumers all over the world on platforms like Amazon and Taobao – a lucrative pivot that was especially profitable in the US market until US President Donald Trump’s tariff war upended global supply chains. Now he’s dabbling in the emerging tech economy, splitting his time between Xingming and Shenzhen – the gravitational epicentre of China’s entrepreneurial classes – where he is teaching himself AI and building a small online game. At the same time, he has been running the guesthouse. The 14-bedroom homestay is a relatively new addition to Xingming, one he designed himself, overseeing its construction in 2016 during the runaway years of China’s real estate bubble. To build it, he scrimped, saved and borrowed money from friends in a bid to deliver on his parents’ dream for their son to return home and share his success with the family.



Its minimalist open-plan aesthetic – with sharp lines, exposed brick, timber panelling and floor-to-ceiling glass windows – is a strikingly incongruous landmark in the small village. It’s also an unrecognisable improvement on the basic brick flat that once stood in the same spot and where his mother cooked over an open wood stove that doubled as heating. As a child, his family was too poor to afford a bicycle, so he and his brother walked two hours through the mountains to attend school, a journey they made twice a week, sleeping at the school quarters in between. North Asia correspondent Lisa Visentin has lunch with Li Zhiying’s family and neighbours at the guesthouse in Xingming village. “We could only afford to eat meat a handful of times a year. As for clothes, we often wore the same clothes for five or six years, unless we literally outgrew them,” he tells me. “I think everyone in China has felt the economic growth, and people in rural areas have felt it very noticeably too.



“If you had visited rural China 30 years ago, there was basically not a single paved or asphalt road in most rural areas. All the toilets in the countryside were simple pit latrines. Our waste was used to fertilise the vegetables.” Related Article China relations Not a solo performance, but a symphony: What China’s leader thinks about AI These days the roads are sealed, and the village has reliable power and sewerage systems. Many of his neighbours have rebuilt bigger, multi-storey houses in recent years, and many families have at least one car. Li’s ticket out was that he was academically gifted, won a scholarship to study architectural design at university and was supported by government policies that helped low-income families. He graduated into a rapacious property market, at one point securing a well-paid job with Country Garden, China’s biggest real estate developer. Laden with billions of dollars of debt, Country Garden has been teetering on the brink of collapse since 2023. Its crisis, along with the implosion of other major developers, has hollowed out China’s middle-class wealth and left an economic wound so deep that even the nation’s breakout AI industries haven’t come close to healing it.



When Li’s guesthouse first opened before COVID-19 hit, it was fully booked on weekends, but since then, the slow post-pandemic recovery and lagging domestic economy have seen bookings dwindle as Chinese consumers sit on their savings. During my stay last weekend, I was the only guest, although more travellers arrived the day I checked out. As China opens up to foreign tourists, Li hopes more will find their way to villages such as Xingming. “If you travel China, 70 to 80 per cent of the places are like this. It is also very beautiful here. Although the big cities are also a real part of China, this is what China truly is.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Red V reality check as Titans rain on Gutherson’s 250th parade
World.content:
Dragons 18 Dragons 38 SportNRLNRL 2026 Red V reality check as Titans rain on Gutherson’s 250th parade Dan Walsh July 26, 2026 — 4:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was the Spoonbowl that really wasn’t. And despite finally locking in a long-term coach with a batch of promising local juniors to build around, the Dragons have copped the reality check they didn’t really need. The Gold Coast’s 38-18 win on Sunday afternoon all but confirms the inevitable. St George Illawarra are now eight points adrift of the 16th-placed Wests Tigers with seven games left in their season. Space will have to be made in the trophy cabinet for the first wooden spoon in the joint-venture’s history. It was a tough milestone afternoon for Clint Gutherson and the Dragons. Getty Images The Titans entered the match sitting second last on the NRL ladder. However, with both teams showing better form than typical cellar dwellers – and the visitors well clear of the bottom – this contest never truly felt like a Spoonbowl. Newly installed full-time coach Dean Young will be all too aware, though, after the Dragons failed to match their improvements of the past six weeks.



Their right-edge defence was picked apart far too easily as the Gold Coast scored three first-half tries by targeting Kyle Flanagan and the teammates either side of him. An early 40-20 from Daniel Atkinson was undone by other long kicks that sailed out on the full and conceded seven-tackle sets. Josh Kerr needlessly landed himself on report within seconds of coming from the bench by belting Titans halfback Zane Harrison late and off the ball. Keano Kini had a field day targeting the Dragons middle. Getty Images And Clint Gutherson’s 250th NRL outing had him involved in everything – good, bad and otherwise. It was Gutherson who started a promising, sun-kissed afternoon at Jubilee Oval when he had seemed to be on a fool’s errand, ducking down the short-side from dummy-half and was swarmed by three Titans defenders.



His last-gasp offload for an unmarked Tyrell Sloan proved otherwise. From there though, it was pretty much all Gold Coast. Incoming Dragons recruit Phillip Sami gave Red V fans an unwelcome taste of what they can expect from him next year when he finished off a 40-metre raid. Clint Gutherson leads the Dragons out with his family. Getty Images Beau Fermor’s offload laid on both that try and the 13th minute follow-up from Jaylan de Groot, with both long breaks coming after Flanagan was isolated in defence. Gutherson was hammered by Jojo Fifita before Val Holmes spilled his fullback’s inside ball a moment later. Within one tackle, the Titans had a 16-6 lead when de Groot strolled through a flimsy Dragons defensive line for his second.



True to form, Gutherson had a hand in St George Illawarra’s return salvo as he popped Hamish Stewart into the backfield before Flanagan finished the play off. After a late offside penalty saw Jayden Campbell push the Gold Coast’s half-time lead out to 18-12, hooker Oliver Pascoe sped through the Dragons middle to start the second-half scoring. When Campbell duped Flanagan with a couple of dummies and sped straight past him, the Titans had a fourth win from their past seven starts in the bag. A late Jacob Liddle try was never changing that, especially when Tino Fa’asuamaleaui answered with his first four-pointer of the season. The Dragons have a promising crop of local juniors, as well as Keaon Koloamatangi and Scott Drinkwater leading their recruits next season. But they also have the wooden spoon and looked every bit a last-placed side on Sunday.

World.title: Star rugby teen turns down PNG as Lomax is unveiled as ‘Chief 005’
World.content:
Updated SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Star rugby teen turns down PNG as Lomax is unveiled as ‘Chief 005’ Iain Payten Updated July 26, 2026 — 4:46pm ,first published 1:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian rugby has had a major win with rising superstar Treyvon Pritchard turning down the PNG Chiefs and Sydney Roosters to sign a long-term contract extension with the Queensland Reds and Rugby Australia. But the Chiefs haven’t wasted any time in moving on, with cross-code star Zac Lomax confirming on Sunday he will be headed to PNG on a three-year deal in 2028. Treyvon Pritchard scores his first Super Rugby try for Queensland in May. Getty Images Pritchard became the most in-demand teenager across both codes this year after the Chiefs made him one of their first targets ahead of the 2028 arrival of the NRL expansion club. In his first year out of school, Pritchard made his debut for the Reds in Super Rugby Pacific and the utility back – who plays centre, wing and fullback – was dominant for the Junior Wallabies at the recent under-20s world championships in Georgia.



This masthead revealed Pritchard, 19, and his 21-year-old brother, Kadin (who plays for the Brumbies), were pursued by the PNG Chiefs and made tax-free offers after meeting club officials in Brisbane. The Roosters also joined the chase and recently expressed interest in bringing Treyvon to the Bondi club when his deal with rugby expired at the end of 2027. But after Rugby Australia and the Reds countered with a strong offer for Treyvon to extend his stay, the outstanding youngster agreed to terms on a three-year deal late last week, according to informed sources unable to comment publicly due to the confidentiality of the negotiations. Zac Lomax has signed with the PNG Chiefs. Getty Images The PNG Chiefs, who saw Pritchard as having a future in the halves in league, were informed of his decision last week. As forecast, the Chiefs have finalised a three-year deal with Lomax after flying him and his partner to Port Moresby on the weekend. Lomax was announced as “Chief 005” on the club’s social media accounts on Sunday along with footage of him being introduced to the crowd at a PNG domestic league game.



“I am super honoured to have committed to you guys,” Lomax said. “We are going to shock the NRL, I am telling you, and I can’t wait to be a part of it.” Lomax is sidelined with a groin injury, but is expected to return to action in for to six weeks. He will see out his deal with the Western Force and RA before returning to league at the end of 2027. The Chiefs are also deep in discussions with Joey Manu to make a return from rugby.



Securing Pritchard is a significant victory for Australian rugby. Many teenage stars have moved to the NRL in the past decade. Eleven players who featured in the recent State of Origin series had played for Sydney or Brisbane schoolboy rugby teams and junior rep rugby. The importance of Pritchard’s retention sits alongside Max Jorgensen last year re-signing through to the end of 2031, but the true value will likely grow in the coming years as the youngster continues to develop and get more time on the game’s biggest stages. Like Jorgensen, he will become a face of the game in Australia. The potential for Pritchard to become an Olympian in 2028 was no doubt one of rugby’s selling points, given he is also an accomplished sevens player.



The Junior Wallabies narrowly missed the semi-finals of the under-20s event in Georgia, but the teenager was named in the team of the tournament after some eye-catching performances, including one against eventual runners-up France. Pritchard’s sizzling footwork, speed and strength helped him beat 25 defenders in three pool games and run for 350 metres, of which 250 metres were post-contact. But his tournament was cut short by a broken leg, suffered in a hip-drop tackle against Wales. He underwent surgery last week. It is hoped Pritchard will be back in action to potentially play for Australia A in late October against the USA. If fit, some argue Pritchard should even go on the Wallabies’ spring tour, even if only on a non-playing development basis. Former Wallabies coach Michael Cheika used that approach for several years, and took young future stars such as Taniela Tupou, Rob Valetini, Izzy Perese, Jack Dempsey and Andrew Kellaway away between 2016 and 2018. New Wallabies coach Les Kiss will gather with his first squad in Sydney this week, after naming a 34-player group last week for the two Tests against Japan on August 8 in Osaka and August 15 in Townsville.



Speaking about his selection plans for the first few months of his tenure, Kiss revealed he would continue to experiment with players to “explore the depth” ahead of the World Cup next year. “It’s important that the players that played the recent [Nations Championship] series are seen, and [that] they see me and the new coaching team,” Kiss said on Nine’s Wide World of Sports on Sunday. “But over the next, you know, 10 Test matches, I’m going to stretch it out a bit and make sure I see a few players as well in other positions.” But Kiss said five-eighth would not be a position he plans to chop and change unnecessarily. “There have been challenges in that position over the last two years – injuries have got in the way, and we haven’t been able to get consistency,” he said.



“I’ve stuck with the three that they had in the Nations Cup. I want to try and keep that as consistent as possible in the next few Test matches.” Waratahs defy doubters to win seventh title After an uncharacteristic mid-season wobble when they lost two games, the Waratahs not only resumed normal service in smashing the Fijian Drua in the Super Rugby Women’s grand final on Saturday, they arguably broke new ground. The Tahs bounced back from defeats in the regular season to the Western Force and Queensland to smash Fiji 34-17 in Ba, in a six-tries-to-three performance to claim a record seventh Super W-Super Rugby Women’s title in nine seasons. Loading



Two tries from the home side in the final 10 minutes reduced the winning margin after the Waratahs dominated for most of the game and established a 34-5 lead, courtesy of two tries to Amelia Whitaker and one each to Rosie Ferguson, Maya Stewart and Desi Miller. Returning Wallaroos fullback Caitlyn Halse was also in the middle of much of it, with lovely assists. But while the star backs doing their thing was par for course in another NSW title, there was no question the powerhouse performance from the Waratahs forwards was the driving force in the win. In what was arguably the most complete Waratahs performance in any of their Super W deciders, their forwards muscled up from the outset and dominated Fiji at their strength. The sharp connection of forwards and backs then built up momentum for NSW that proved, at times, unstoppable. Wallaroos prop Faliki Pohiva was immense in attack and defence, and her second-half try was just reward for a superb game. The 25-year-old from western Sydney was also named player of the final. Faliki Pohiva crashes over for a try in a superb overall performance. Getty Images



The NSW pack allowed dynamic halves Tia Hinds and Waiaria Ellis to apply huge pressure. Despite only being two games into their new partnership, the duo have during the past two weeks made a strong claim to be the Wallaroos halves, too. The skill and strength of the Waratahs forwards in Fiji points to the potential for a competitive showing against the Auckland Blues women next Saturday in Sydney in the Women’s Super Rugby champions final. The Blues also completed a hat-trick of Super Rugby Aupiki titles when they snatched victory from Matatū, scoring a late try to beat the South Islanders 28-21. The trans-Tasman winner’s showdown began last year when the Blues dispatched NSW 36-5. The Waratahs celebrate their Super Rugby Women’s crown. Getty Images



The Blues pack was able to get on top in the forwards and stretch the Matatū defence out wide thereafter, and that has been the pattern for a lot of trans-Tasman Test rugby as well. But the smartly coached Waratahs pack showed enough in Fiji to suggest they will be up for the battle against the Blues on Saturday. Waratahs captain Emily Chancellor paid tribute to the 34 players who had played during an injury-plagued season for NSW, which had rivals hoping the sky blue juggernaut might have finally run out of steam. “I want to shout out to every single player that’s been part of this program this year,” Chancellor said. “What an incredible group. I feel like rugby in Australia wrote us off – we lose two games and that’s it for us. This is the response, and I’m so proud of this team. I couldn’t be more proud of the way we played today and the belief we have in each other.” The Women’s Super Rugby champions final will be played at Leichhardt Oval on Saturday.

World.title: Malvern bungalow sells for $2.66m to buyer who wants to tear it down
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Malvern bungalow sells for $2.66m to buyer who wants to tear it down Wes Mountain July 26, 2026 — 4:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Californian bungalow in a coveted Malvern street sold for $2.66 million at auction on Saturday, with the buyer planning to tear it down to build her “dream home”. The well-maintained three-bedroom house at 32 Jordan Street is on a 576-square-metre block and features original Baltic pine floors, front verandah and classically landscaped gardens, all walking distance to Tooronga Road shops, Harold Holt Swim Centre and High Street. It had a price guide of $2.2 million to $2.4 million, and a reserve of $2.35 million. The house was sold as part of a deceased estate. The property was one of 692 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne last week. By Saturday evening, Domain Group had recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 55 per cent from 464 reported results throughout the week, while 94 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate.



After last week’s preliminary clearance rate almost hit the 60 per cent threshold that indicates a balanced market, this week’s results suggest the market continues to favour buyers, despite a shortage of supply in the traditionally quieter winter months. The clearance rate was 72 per cent this time last year. Related Article Auctions Downsizer cries with joy as she wins $866,000 northern Melbourne home Ray White Ashburton agent Max Hedley said bidding for Jordan Street opened at $2.2 million, with four bidders competing. Two main bidders traded $50,000 increments throughout, sending the eventual price more than $300,000 above the reserve. “It was unexpected,” Hedley said. “It just kept going.” He believed that while the market for homes over $2 million had slowed, the scarcity of original Malvern properties had led to a “surprising” result.



“In those ... streets in Malvern, there’s not a lot of properties left like that,” he said. The property was advertised with an artist’s impression of a potential renovation – subject to council approval – and Hedley said the buyer, who lived in nearby Caulfield East, had purchased to “take it down and rebuild”. An artist’s impression of what a potential update to the Malvern home could look like, subject to council approval. Ray White Ashburton “It just showcases the fact that the heart is still beating for the right properties,” Hedley said. In Yarraville, a freestanding two-bedroom Victorian passed in on a single vendor bid of $950,000, despite a campaign with “a lot of love” for the home.



Nestled in the Yarraville village, a “short stroll” to shops and the historic Sun Theatre, 16 Norfolk Street features a north-facing yard, modern updates and had a price guide of $950,000 to $1 million, with a reserve of $1.05 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. While updated, Compton Green agent Dee Gibson said the vendors had preserved much of the original Victorian features, including its pressed iron ornamentation. “It’s quite a quaint, beautifully styled home,” she said.



Gibson said the auction opened with a vendor bid of $950,000 and passed in without either of two previously interested parties putting their hand up. Related Article Melbourne house prices ‘A long winter for house prices’: Melbourne market’s steepest drop in four years “It seems typical of the market at the moment,” she said, noting the sale would now convert to private treaty. She thought it was in a difficult spot for the current market, but was sure it would find the right buyer. “The first home buying market is still strong,” she said. “When we get to the $1 million mark ... that’s where there’s that stretch. Can buyers go the extra mile for something a bit better? That’s the question.”



In Port Melbourne, a two-bedroom modern townhouse sold in post-auction negotiations for $1.14 million to a “seasoned purchaser and seller” who beat an eager but nervous first home buyer. Split across two levels, 6/97-101 Cruikshank Street features light-filled rooms, a red-brick facade and large balcony, and is a short walk to Port Melbourne beach and Gasworks Arts Precinct. It had a price guide of $1.1 million to $1.2 million and a reserve of $1.14 million. Buxton Port Phillip agent Nancy Yang said the opening $1 million bid came from the first home buyer – the first bid of his home-buying journey. From there, the two bidders went back and forth, with $5000 bids from the first home buyer and larger $10,000 and $20,000 bids from the more “seasoned” eventual buyer. The home passed in at $1.12 million, after the first home buyer hit the top of his budget, selling in post-auction negotiations.



Yang said the buyer lived with her parents while saving to make her next move, and would be sharing the home with her dog, using the second bedroom to work from home. The home had been an investment property “for many years”, but Yang said the vendors were selling following state and federal tax changes. “The market’s not down,” she said, noting that renters were getting a better opportunity to buy after an “exponential” rise in rents, competing with Sydney and Brisbane buyers who were still keen on Melbourne investment properties. “It’s just a re-shifting.”

World.title: Trump is back announcing a 2028 presidential bid. It’s dangerous to assume he’s joking
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Opinion Trump is back announcing a 2028 presidential bid. It’s dangerous to assume he’s joking Cory Alpert Former White House staffer July 26, 2026 — 4:42pm

July 26, 2026 — 4:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Six years into his presidency, Donald Trump has ended his boycott of the annual White House Correspondents Dinner. In a speech that included numerous attacks on his political enemies, Trump started and ended by joking about his plans to run again for president. He pulled out a “Trump 2028” hat, with the tagline “rewrite the rules”, that is now for sale on his website for $US55 ($79). Presidents are expected to make jokes at this dinner, as Trump did on Friday night. But Trump has spent most of his second term making sure that no one can be certain if he really is joking about running for a third term, despite the explicit ban in the US Constitution. Trump’s will-he-won’t-he drama has instead frozen Republican efforts for succession planning. In 2016, when Barack Obama was term-limited, both parties had already begun their unofficial primaries by this point and we know from Joe Biden’s late withdrawal in 2024 just how damaging it can be when a figurehead of the party won’t let go. Was President Donald Trump attempting to throw his hat in the ring at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner on Friday? AP Trump started playing this game in March 2025, weeks after being sworn in for a second time, when he told NBC News that he was serious about a third term and spoke about the ways it could be possible. He has mentioned running again at least 18 times, moving between jokes and serious escalations, before conceding at the end of 2025 that the Constitution prohibited him from running again. Because he keeps opening and closing the door, no one can quite be sure what Trump intends to do, but it has empowered the president while freezing the Republican Party.



Those in Trump’s bubble seem to be confused as well. Hats are for sale. One of Trump’s closest allies in the House, Tennessee congressman Andy Ogles, has proposed a constitutional amendment that would permit Trump, but not predecessors like Obama or Clinton, to run for a third term. Steve Bannon has said that Trump will run again, with his strategy to be revealed at “the appropriate time”. Chief of staff Susie Wiles has said that Trump is not serious about a third term, and that he’s aware of the constitutional limits. Speaker Mike Johnson has said that Trump is “trolling” Democrats and that the president enjoys seeing the opposition party with their “hair on fire”. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump’s power is at its peak. He has reason to be fearful of what’s coming Cory Alpert Former White House staffer And yet, when Alan Dershowitz, the lawyer who was on the defence team for Donald Trump’s first impeachment, released a book-length plan on how Trump can remain in office, a White House spokesperson said only that the American people would be lucky enough to keep Trump in office. It is a mistake to dismiss all of Trump’s rhetoric as unserious, as many do. Yes, some quips appear to be improv, off the cuff and unconsidered. Many more of his ideas are only discarded after they meet the institutional realities of Congress, the courts, or the markets.



But hyperbole has been a feature of his Trump’s campaigning, and he’s been deadly serious on what might have once seemed like outlandish plans for massive tariff increases, slashes to government programs, and expansion of immigration enforcement. This air of uncertainty gives Trump continued leverage over his party as the 2028 nominating contest begins to take shape. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance are the leading contenders for the Republican nomination in 2028 and have built profiles that extend well past their official roles. But no candidate can offer a future that extends beyond Trump while this ambiguity about his intentions hangs over their party. Contrast that with the work that the Democratic Party is doing to shape their primary. It has spent a year reshuffling its early primary calendar, this week landing on my home state of South Carolina as the important first state, replacing Iowa’s historic role. Prospective candidates have been travelling, raising money and publishing the obligatory campaign books. Republicans are not only asking who should lead their party but who Trump might eventually permit to succeed him. Those are two very different questions.



It is impossible to predict what Trump will do in 2028. If he sought to get his name on the ballot, election officials in each state would make the initial decisions, likely along partisan lines. Those decisions could be expected to end up at the Supreme Court, which although ideologically conservative has been willing to step in when Trump claims too much unilateral authority over the Constitution. Just last month, they overruled his effort to revoke birthright citizenship, saying he had no singular authority to change constitutional rules Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump’s three-pronged threat to American democracy Peter Hartcher Political and international editor But Trump does not need a plausible path to the ballot to have power over the race. As long as the possibility remains alive, every potential Republican successor must wait and demonstrate their loyalty. The question of Trump running for a third term should be settled under the Constitution. The 22nd amendment says that “no person shall be elected to the office of president more than twice”. It also prohibits tricks like the one Trump has openly mused about, in which he runs as JD Vance’s vice-president, only to replace Vance on their first day in office. The vast majority of constitutional scholars have said there is no loophole that Trump can reasonably exploit. But the Republican Party is largely still behaving as though its future depends on what Trump decides. By making sure that no firm ground exists on which any candidate can stand, Trump has turned political uncertainty into leverage over his party. They remain paralysed by his influence.



The irony of this moment is that the White House Correspondents Dinner in 2012 is where Barack Obama told Trump to his face that he would never be president. A decade and a half later, it’s where Trump is keeping alive the question of if he will ever stop being president. Cory Alpert is a PhD researcher at the University of Melbourne looking at the impact of AI on democracy. He previously served the Biden-Harris administration. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Bailey-Ashcroft double act powers Lions to seventh straight win
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Bailey-Ashcroft double act powers Lions to seventh straight win Nick Wright July 26, 2026 — 4:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The price tag being attached to Zac Bailey’s name must be increasing by the day, as the Brisbane Lions’ sensation produced a masterclass to extend his side’s winning run to seven. The Gabba became the 26-year-old’s stomping ground once again as the two-time defending champions conquered Port Adelaide 19.12 (129) to 9.13 (67). Zac Bailey was in top form. via Getty Images The off-contract Bailey, who is being headhunted by Adelaide and reportedly weighing up a multi-million dollar long-term deal to make the move, was a man on a Sunday afternoon mission – kicking three goals and finishing with 26 disposals. In a clash which largely became a seesawing tussle for ascendancy in the first half, Brisbane’s class ultimately proved to be too much for a young Power outfit to overcome, with Bailey’s third-quarter surge building the momentum needed to keep their rivals at arm’s length.



It began as the Will Ashcroft show, whose deft dribble through traffic for the contest’s first goal was swiftly followed by an assist for Kai Lohmann’s first of two majors. Ashcroft continued his knack for producing memorable moments by kicking his second from a tight set shot angle as the three-quarter time siren sounded, before emerging from the break with a pair of goal assists for Logan Morris and Eric Hipwood. Will Ashcroft of the Lions in action during the round 20 clash. AFL Photos via Getty Images Those moments sparked a fourth-quarter onslaught, kicking seven goals to two, after only leading by nine points at halftime – an incredible Charlie Cameron mark to kick his second goal in his 200th Lions appearance the moment of the term, before he added a third from a set shot. During the rare moments Ashcroft was kept contained – still finishing with 30 touches – Bailey took charge.



His speed was a constant nightmare for Port Adelaide, but it was his support play that was equally pivotal – lurking near a spoil and launching a 50-metre angled shot for his second goal, a far more impressive effort than his uncontested mark in the opening term for his first. It was not long before he had his third, as Cam Rayner – who produced two magic goals through contests of his own – shrugged off a tackle and found a handball for his superstar teammate to strike cleanly. Balyn O’Brien of the Power competes for the ball against Charlie Cameron and Hugh McCluggage of the Lions. via Getty Images While superstar Lachie Neale was kept relatively quiet, the Ashcroft-Bailey combination kept the Power guessing and signalled that this team had endless ways to win and pile on the pressure.



Is the McCluggage of old back? Josh Dunkley teased during the week that Hugh McCluggage was closing in on the sort of performance which typified his career-best 2025 campaign, having spent plenty of time on the sidelines to nurse a calf issue sustained back in Opening Round. “It’s obviously tough being injury interrupted and trying to manage all those different things, but we know Hughy’s best is not too far away,” Dunkley said. Hugh McCluggage. via Getty Images “Last preseason [leading into 2025] he actually missed a lot of it, and came back and had one of his best years ever, so I’m sure he got a few lessons from that experience.



“I think he’s not too far away from being that dominant player we know he can be.” Dunkley’s premonition ended up being bang on the money, with producing his most involved performance of the season as the Power sought to lock down his midfield teammate, Lachie Neale. McCluggage’s 29 possessions were his most in a game this year, and he added a goal to his resume when he was left unmarked inside 50. What was perhaps most pleasing about his outing was the amount of work he did in contest, and he appeared to be moving more freely than he has at any point in 2026. It is an ominous sign for the rest of the competition as Brisbane cemented their standing in the top four. They were winning without getting the best out of the All Australian, but if they start doing so now, even the ladder-leading Dockers will be watching of their shoulder.



Will Oscar add a new layer to Lions’ assault? While the Lions have restored their ambitions for a third-straight flag on the back of what is now a seventh-straight win, they may be about to get stronger still. Prized off season recruit Oscar Allen has not been sighted in a Brisbane jumper for roughly three months after suffering a foot fracture in the round seven battle with Adelaide, but his performance in reserve grade will come as a relief to coach Chris Fagan. Fagan hinted during the week Allen’s rain-effected comeback through the VFL last week was a difficult gauge on whether he was fit enough to line up in the top level, but the former West Coast captain’s two goals and 10 disposals against North Melbourne would no doubt be a relieving sight. Young forward Logan Morris has been a consistent pillar up front for the premiers this season, and he took his season goal tally to 47 with a three-goal haul on Sunday.



But should Allen force his way back into the fold, it will simply add another layer to this Brisbane attack which is gathering momentum. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Pleased as Punch: Orphaned monkey receives 2500 birthday cards
World.content:
WorldAsiaAnimals Pleased as Punch: Orphaned monkey receives 2500 birthday cards Emily Smith July 26, 2026 — 4:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Punch the monkey rose to fame after being abandoned by its mother and left only with a stuffed toy orangutan for comfort. The orphaned macaque was bullied by other monkeys at Ichikawa City Zoo, near Tokyo, and would often be seen wandering its enclosure alone. Punch plays at Ichikawa City Zoological and Botanical Garden east of Tokyo this week. AP Photo/Eugene Hoshiko But as Punch turns one on Sunday, the monkey is surrounded by new friends and has been inundated with thousands of birthday cards from fans around the world. Many of the cards and other messages fill the walls at an indoor Punch exhibit, where visitors can watch a video chronicling the animal’s early days.



It is believed Punch was abandoned by its mother because of exhaustion. Zookeepers nursed the monkey and gave it the toy to develop its gripping ability – something newborn macaques need to survive. “As Punch was trying very hard, struggling to live each day, his two keepers did everything they could while other staff watched over him,” the head of the zoo, Takashi Yasunaga, said. The zoo has been inundated with thousands of birthday cards for Punch from fans around the world. AP Photo/Eugene Hoshiko Many of the cards and other messages fill the walls at an indoor Punch exhibit. AP Photo/Eugene Hoshiko Punch still attracted big crowds, and had received some 2500 birthday cards from inside and outside Japan, Yasunaga added.



Kumi Ishizawa, a Kobe resident who was at the exhibit, said she learnt of Punch’s story from social media earlier this year. From then on, overcoming her illness to see the monkey became her goal. “He moved me ... I kept on telling myself that I’m going to get well and come visit to see Punch,” said Ishizawa, who has recovered and visited the zoo after a business trip. Six-day-old Punch with his stuffed orangutan in a basket at the zoo. Ichikawa City Zoological and Botanical Garden via AP Loading “And here I am, I made it. I’m very happy I could finally see him in person.”



Yeye Lights, a long-time Ichikawa resident, had never visited the zoo until her daughter told her about Punch, and now has an annual visitor pass. “I have a cake for Punch-kun, I’m celebrating with my friends,” Lights said, using an affectionate Japanese honorific for boys. World.title: Brisbane Lions flick switch, turn off Power in second-half rout
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Brisbane Lions flick switch, turn off Power in second-half rout July 26, 2026 — 4:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brisbane have continued their push for an historic second premiership “three peat” this century, demolishing a depleted Port Adelaide by 59 points for a seventh successive victory. But the Lions had to work hard to shake off the Power, who hung in until midway through the third quarter before the home side exploded, kicking 14 to 5 goals in a crushing second half to win 19.12 (126) to 9.13 (67). The result leaves Chris Fagan’s men fourth on the ladder, a game clear of Adelaide with four rounds to play, and with challenging games against Carlton, Hawthorn, the Gold Coast Suns and Collingwood to come. Brisbane Lions livewire Charlie Cameron. AFL Photos On form, however, the Lions should fear none of them.



While the Power worked hard early to close space and force the Lions to use the ball more by hand instead of employing their usual precise kicking game, the Lions had too much class and too many avenues to goal. Sunday’s game split open in the second half, with both sides going goal for goal from the centre ball-up before the Lions cut loose, finishing with seven majors to three in the third quarter. The decisive blows were struck by Sam Draper, who plucked a centre-square ruck contest and galloped to 60 metres before launching, and Will Ashcroft, who extended the Lions’ lead to 29 points on the siren. Port Adelaide finally folded in the last quarter as the Lions shifted into overdrive, turning what had been a hard-fought game into a procession. Ashcroft was superb with two goals from 30 possessions, while Zac Bailey was destructive with three majors from his 26 and Harris Andrews was typically impassable in defence with 13 marks.



Perhaps the most encouraging sign was the inside game of Hugh McCluggage, who had his best match for the year, finishing with 29 possessions, five clearances and a goal as an inside midfielder. The Lions’ defensive intent was shown late in the final quarter, when Draper spoiled a Port shot on goal on the line and celebrated as if he had kicked one himself. Brisbane’s forwards also fired, with Logan Morris, Kai Lohmann and Charlie Cameron kicking three goals apiece. Jason Horne-Francis was a shining light for Port, keeping them in the contest with a superb kicking exhibition that resulted in nine score involvements and three direct assists. But without Port’s usual centre-square assassin Zak Butters, Horne-Francis lacked midfield support, with the Power doing well to stay with the Lions for as long as they did.



They were also let down by their set-shot kicking, with spearhead Mitch Georgiades ending with 2.4 for the game. AAP

World.title: Chickens, Chairman Mao and spiced tea with the neighbours: Welcome to ‘the real China’
World.content:
WorldAsiaChina relations Chickens, Chairman Mao and spiced tea with the neighbours: Welcome to ‘the real China’ Lisa Visentin Updated July 26, 2026 — 4:07pm ,first published July 26, 2026 — 9:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What in the World, a free weekly newsletter from our foreign correspondents, is sent every Thursday. Below is an excerpt. Sign up to get the whole newsletter delivered to your inbox. Xingming village, China: Perched atop a hill in a small village in central China, Li Zhiying’s family guesthouse has a spectacular view. Just beyond the front door is a vista of a pristine reservoir, ringed by pine forests and framed by mountain ranges flossed with low-hanging clouds. Li Zhiying grew up in poverty in Hunan province in central China and later returned to his hometown to open a guesthouse. Lisa Visentin Along the cul-de-sac that winds past his house, Li’s neighbours tend crops of beans, chillies, pumpkin and corn in small plots near their homes.



Village dogs bark and scrap in the street and chickens roam freely. By the roadside, an elderly man is picking the Sichuan peppercorns that will spice the tea and tingle the tongues of neighbours who will pop by in the evening for a daily ritual of gossip and card-playing. I’ve come to Li’s hometown of Xingming in China’s central Hunan province to spend three days exploring a different side of the modern China story that frequently makes headlines. The ordinariness of rural life. Loading Xingming village, in Hunan Province, central China. Lisa Visentin A snapshot of the so-called “real China” that’s more representative of everyday life for millions of Chinese people than dancing robots, drone light shows and the breakneck speed of AI development that is reshaping tech hubs in Beijing, Shenzhen and Hangzhou.



The evening I arrive, we wander down the street to the home of the retired village party secretary, a local Communist Party official, whose wife is serving slices of watermelon and tea in plastic cups to any neighbour who stops for a chat. Neighbours pop by in the evening for a daily ritual of gossip and card-playing. Lisa Visentin “Hello Australia, welcome, please enjoy our village,” one elder tells me, using a translation app. This is Chairman Mao country, where portraits of China’s former supreme leader hang in the homes of older villagers, his reputation unspoiled by history’s verdict – in the West at least – of the calamity caused by the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution. “Mao is like a god to us,” a local party cadre from the neighbouring province tells me over lunch at the guesthouse. “He understood the ordinary people.”



The nearest market is 5 kilometres away in a small, unremarkable township, where everyone is curious about the visiting foreigner (me). There’s plenty of pointing and waving and lots of smiles. “Never!” an old villager running a pork stall responds when I ask how often foreigners come to the market. Nearby, a man is loading hunks of fresh meat into the boot of his car lined with just a piece of cardboard. Another vendor is selling a freshly slaughtered whole dog, its fur shaved off but skin intact. It’s a confronting sight for the uninitiated, though Li tells me he has never seen dog meat for sale here before.



By his own admission, Li forewarns would-be guests that his home is located in a remote rural village that most Chinese people have never heard of. There’s no tourist infrastructure, and quotidian village life is slow-paced and perhaps even boring. “If you are looking for a comfortable, easy introduction to China, this may not be the place,” he says on the guesthouse website. Li Zhiying and his friend, Li Mi, paddling on the reservoir that sustains the local village. Lisa Visentin But he believes visitors will be charmed by the warmth and authenticity of the locals, and the unrefined beauty of the Chinese countryside. For the most part, this is not the side of China that has bedazzled the wave of influencers who have arrived under the government’s soft-power masterstroke of visa-free travel, which has now been extended to more than 70 countries, Australia included.



They have flooded Instagram and TikTok with effusive videos about China’s smartphone-powered megacities, with a cashless economy, gleaming skyscrapers, robots that deliver food to the hotel door, and futuristic electric vehicles that cruise silently around clean streets. The comparison is stark. There’s little tangible wealth in villages such as Xingming, but community bonds are strong. People eat what they grow, or fish from the reservoir, and share what they have with their neighbours. Villagers fish from the reservoir. Lisa Visentin Some of the older generation speak patchy Mandarin, preferring their local dialect. This has tethered them to their home province and added to the language barriers with outsiders who arrive, as I have, reliant on AI tools to navigate them. ChatGPT, though an impressive translator, struggles with dialects. Younger people, meanwhile, have decamped for the cities looking for work, often leaving behind their children to be raised by their grandparents.



“My children have gone to work in the 3D printing industry,” one woman says, as she picks beans from her garden while her granddaughter plays nearby. But the crushing poverty that once afflicted Xingming, and mired families such as Li’s in destitution, has largely been eliminated. Portraits of Mao Zedong are a common sight in the homes of older residents in parts of rural China. Lisa Visentin To get to Xingming from Beijing, it’s a five-hour journey on high-speed rail to the nearest station in Yueyang – a small, lower-tier city by Chinese standards with only 5 million people (about the size of Sydney). Then it’s an hour-long drive through the countryside. I’ve come specifically to meet Li, a softly spoken 36-year-old architect turned aspiring AI developer, whose life has skirted the same grooves as China’s own recent trajectory in many ways.



He rose out of poverty off the back of China’s economic juggernaut, which from the 1990s onwards lifted hundreds of millions of people like him with it. Li then crested the wave of the country’s property boom before crashing with its collapse, shuttering his own construction company within six months of opening it in 2022. Since then, he’s looked for ways to reinvent himself, firstly in e-commerce, joining a friend’s large online company selling adult products to consumers all over the world on platforms like Amazon and Taobao – a lucrative pivot that was especially profitable in the US market until US President Donald Trump’s tariff war upended global supply chains. Now he’s dabbling in the emerging tech economy, splitting his time between Xingming and Shenzhen – the gravitational epicentre of China’s entrepreneurial classes – where he is teaching himself AI and building a small online game. At the same time, he has been running the guesthouse. The 14-bedroom homestay is a relatively new addition to Xingming, one he designed himself, overseeing its construction in 2016 during the runaway years of China’s real estate bubble. To build it, he scrimped, saved and borrowed money from friends in a bid to deliver on his parents’ dream for their son to return home and share his success with the family.



Its minimalist open-plan aesthetic – with sharp lines, exposed brick, timber panelling and floor-to-ceiling glass windows – is a strikingly incongruous landmark in the small village. It’s also an unrecognisable improvement on the basic brick flat that once stood in the same spot and where his mother cooked over an open wood stove that doubled as heating. As a child, his family was too poor to afford a bicycle, so he and his brother walked two hours through the mountains to attend school, a journey they made twice a week, sleeping at the school quarters in between. North Asia correspondent Lisa Visentin has lunch with Li Zhiying’s family and neighbours at the guesthouse in Xingming village. “We could only afford to eat meat a handful of times a year. As for clothes, we often wore the same clothes for five or six years, unless we literally outgrew them,” he tells me. “I think everyone in China has felt the economic growth, and people in rural areas have felt it very noticeably too.



“If you had visited rural China 30 years ago, there was basically not a single paved or asphalt road in most rural areas. All the toilets in the countryside were simple pit latrines. Our waste was used to fertilise the vegetables.” Related Article China relations Not a solo performance, but a symphony: What China’s leader thinks about AI These days the roads are sealed, and the village has reliable power and sewerage systems. Many of his neighbours have rebuilt bigger, multi-storey houses in recent years, and many families have at least one car. Li’s ticket out was that he was academically gifted, won a scholarship to study architectural design at university and was supported by government policies that helped low-income families. He graduated into a rapacious property market, at one point securing a well-paid job with Country Garden, China’s biggest real estate developer. Laden with billions of dollars of debt, Country Garden has been teetering on the brink of collapse since 2023. Its crisis, along with the implosion of other major developers, has hollowed out China’s middle-class wealth and left an economic wound so deep that even the nation’s breakout AI industries haven’t come close to healing it.



When Li’s guesthouse first opened before COVID-19 hit, it was fully booked on weekends, but since then, the slow post-pandemic recovery and lagging domestic economy have seen bookings dwindle as Chinese consumers sit on their savings. During my stay last weekend, I was the only guest, although more travellers arrived the day I checked out. As China opens up to foreign tourists, Li hopes more will find their way to villages such as Xingming. “If you travel China, 70 to 80 per cent of the places are like this. It is also very beautiful here. Although the big cities are also a real part of China, this is what China truly is.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.
